en: The Kṛtyakalpataru (The Wish-Fulfilling Tree of Duties)
Composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara.
The Section on Śrāddha Rites
Auspicious Invocation
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.

That virtuous soul who daily gratifies men with boundless *hantakāra* offerings, the host of ancestors with *kavya* offerings that are truly auspicious, and the assembly of immortals with abundant *havya* offerings;
whose mind-swan is endowed with the essence of bliss flowing from the ocean of meditation upon Śrīnātha.
This wise Śrī Lakṣmīdhara composes the fourth book, the Śrāddhakāṇḍa. [The Promise]
The nature of the śrāddha, its divisions, the times, and the places; thereafter, the sacrificial foods, things to be avoided, and the examination of the brāhmaṇas.
Those who purify the rows [of guests] must be avoided; those unworthy of the row are excluded from the invitation.
For one who has been invited, there are observances beginning from the invitation up until the invocation at the śrāddha.
The excellence of the ancestral rite (śrāddha), hospitality, the sequence of duties,
the general rules of procedure, and the ritual concerning silent recitation and the seating of guests.
The ritual resolve (saṅkalpa) for the mantra used during the serving of food constitutes the rule for the meal;
here too, the rules for recitation (japa) and so forth apply, and the rites follow in sequence after the śrāddha.
[2] The essential nature of the ancestors and others, the praise of the śrāddha in due order,
the śrāddha with raw grain (āma-śrāddha), and likewise the śrāddha for one whose father is still living.
Next is the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha for one who has two fathers;
immediately following that is the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha, and after performing that, the subsequent śrāddha.
In this context, even those entitled to perform the *śrāddha* perform a *śrāddha* based on prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
Immediately following that, the *śrāddha* for one who is still living is described here.
Thus, by the learned Lakṣmīdhara, through the words of various eminent sages,
the section on Śrāddha for the thirty-two Parvas is explained.
Now, the nature of the Śrāddha.
Now follows the ritual for the *śrāddha*. Regarding this, Hārīta [A. 12] says:

"Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for the *śrāddha*. Prajāpati is the year. Of that, the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*), the bright fortnight (*śukla*), and the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) belong to the gods. The southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), the dark fortnight (*tāmisra*), and the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) belong to the ancestors (*pitṛ*). There is no other state [of time], because it is the whole; thus they are worshipped in both ways. Because of their intermixture, they are worshipped day by day. Furthermore, regarding this, they cite the following:

He whose two paths carry the oblations to the gods and the offerings to the ancestors, of whom half belongs to the gods and half likewise to the ancestors, and of whom the moments of time are the root—that very one who sacrifices shall attain immortality through the seasons.

The two fortnights are the bright (*śukla*) and the dark (*tāmisra*). Since time is thus divided for the gods and the ancestors, the entirety of time is subsumed under these two modes; therefore, there is "no other state" (*nānyabhāvaḥ*), meaning no alteration, because of their being mixed according to the distinctions of forenoon, afternoon, and so forth. "Day after day they are sacrificed to in both ways" means by the two modes distinguished as forenoon, afternoon, and so on. "These two paths" refers to those called the path of the gods (*devayāna*) and the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*). From this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the injunction for the general performance of the *śrāddha* is inferred. (1)

[4] The nature of the *śrāddha* has been clearly stated by Āpastamba. As Āpastamba says (2.16.1–4): "Now, Manu proclaimed this rite under the name *śrāddha*, for the sake of the ultimate welfare of progeny. In this rite, the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are the deities, while the Brahmins serve the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire. It should be performed month after month; the afternoon of the waning fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) is preferable. Thus it is said.

The term *śrāddha-śabdam* means that which has the word "śrāddha" as its designator. As for the statement, "But the Brāhmaṇa is for the purpose of the Āhavanīya fire," this is because he serves as the locus for the disposal of the substance, just like the Āhavanīya fire. By this, it is implied that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the primary rite of *śrāddha* consists in the renunciation of the substance intended for the ancestors, up until its acceptance by the Brāhmaṇas. However, in other instances such as the *daiva-śrāddha* and so forth, the use of the word *śrāddha* is figurative (*gauṇa*), intended to extend those specific ritual properties [to the secondary rites], just as the word *agnihotra* is applied to the *homa* of the Kauṇḍapāyinas. Furthermore, in this context, each individual ancestor—such as the father and others—is a deity (*devatā*) separately, not the group collectively.

"One should first offer food to the Viśvedevas with the mantra *namo viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ* to two [guests] facing east; then, to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, by name and lineage (*nāma-gotra*), to those facing north"—
since Viṣṇu [73.13–14] specifies each [ancestor] individually as the object of the offering,
one should then [offer] warm food mixed with sesame seeds and smeared with honey and ghee.
Having taken it again with the *devatīrtha* using the *praṇava* alone.
Having said, "This is your food," one should offer sacrifice to all the gods, saying: "O [Name], of the [Gotra] lineage, this is your food; *svadhā*! Homage!"

This is also because of the statement in the *Brahmapurāṇa*. As for the plural number used in such sentences as “one should give to the ancestors on the new moon day,” that does not refer to the act of naming [the ancestors] in accordance with their status as individual deities established by other means of knowledge, as in the case of “The Gargas should be fed. Nor is there the status of deity for the father and others together with their wives; for there is no evidence for such a thing. On the contrary:
[5] One should not offer separately to women, except on the anniversary of death (avasānadina);
for it is recorded in the Smṛti that their satisfaction comes solely from the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) offered to their own husbands.

Thus, in the statement of Śātātapa, because it is declared that only the share of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) belonging to the husband is the cause of the wife's satisfaction, there exists evidence that is indeed the opposite [of your claim].

Thus ends the section on the nature of the *śrāddha* in the *Śrāddhakāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsāndhivigrahika*) and son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
Now, the classifications of Śrāddha rites.
Viśvāmitra says: The daily (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), the optional (kāmya), the ancestral rite for prosperity (vṛddhi-śrāddha), the rite of offering the pinda to the ancestors (sapiṇḍana),
the monthly rite (pārvaṇa), and the eighth, performed at a social gathering (goṣṭhī) for the sake of purification, should be known [as the types of śrāddha].
The ninth is declared to be the limb of ritual action (karmāṅga), and the tenth is remembered as the divine (daivika).
The eleventh is declared for journeys (yātrā), and the twelfth is remembered for the purpose of nourishment (puṣṭi).
This has been explained in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"The śrāddha that is performed day after day is proclaimed as 'nitya' (obligatory). Devoid of the Vaiśvadeva rite, it may, however, be performed with water alone in the event of incapacity."
The śrāddha known as ekoddiṣṭa is said to be occasional (naimittika);
it too should be performed without [an offering to] the gods, and one should feed an odd number of twice-born brahmins.

O Lord of Birds, that which is prescribed for one desiring [a specific result] for the sake of accomplishing a desired object is also said to be performed according to the Pārvaṇa rite. That śrāddha which is performed on an occasion of prosperity is called a Vṛddhi-śrāddha.
One should perform all circumambulations in the forenoon while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder;
one should prepare four vessels containing scented water and sesame seeds,
and pour the vessel of the deceased (preta) into the vessels of the ancestors for the purpose of the *arghya* offering.
This Sapindikarana rite is to be known by means of the two verses beginning with "ye samānāḥ";
the remainder should be identical to the Nitya-śrāddha, and the Ekoddista rite applies to women as well.
[7] That which is performed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is declared to be pārvaṇa;
or that which is performed on a festival day (parvan) is declared to be pārvaṇa.
That śrāddha which is performed in a social gathering is called a *goṣṭhī-śrāddha*;
it is for the satisfaction of the ancestors and for the happiness resulting from the assembly of many learned men.
That which is performed for the sake of purification, namely the feeding of Brahmins,
is declared by the wise, O Vainateya, to be for the purpose of purification.
At the time of the impregnation rite (niṣeka), during the Soma sacrifice, likewise at the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), and also at the rite for obtaining a male child (puṃsavana),
the Śrāddha is to be understood as an integral part of the ritual action itself.
That śrāddha which is performed with reference to the gods is here called *daivika*;
it should be performed diligently on the seventh lunar day and subsequent days, using distinguished sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
If one who is traveling to another country performs a Śrāddha with clarified butter, it is declared to be for the purpose of a journey; and the same applies at the time of entry, without a doubt.
The ancestral rite (śrāddha) performed for the nourishment of the body, as well as for the accumulation of wealth,
should be understood as being for the sake of prosperity, or merely figurative.
7. [The seventh chapter]

"Vṛddhi" refers to the birth of a son and similar occasions. Regarding the statement, "The remainder should be equal to the obligatory (nitya)," what is intended is the *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa* rites that must necessarily be performed with mantras. Therefore, the meaning is this: since the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* consists of both elements, in its *pārvaṇa* portion it is equal to the *pārvaṇa*, and in its *ekoddiṣṭa* portion it is equal to the *ekoddiṣṭa*; thus, the collection of specific subsidiary rites (*aṅga-jāta*) should be applied accordingly. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the *ekoddiṣṭa* is also for a woman," here the term *ekoddiṣṭa*—by association with the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite—actually denotes the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* itself, which is mentioned incidentally in connection with women. In the phrase "or it is performed on a festival day (*parvan*)," the word *parvan* refers to the solstices (*saṃkrānti*) and so forth. "Gathering" (*goṣṭhī*) here refers to a group of those performing the *śrāddha*. Regarding "for the sake of the happiness of prosperity": when a *śrāddha* is to be performed simultaneously by many learned men due to some cause, and separate cooking and other resources are unavailable, the *śrāddha* that is performed by pooling their resources to complete the ritual materials is called a *goṣṭhī-śrāddha*; such is the view of Śaṅkhadhara. The passage beginning with "at the time of impregnation (*niṣeka*) and at the Soma sacrifice" is an illustration of Vedic (*śrauta*) and Smārta rites. The *śrāddha* performed upon traveling to another country and upon entering one's home should be understood as being for the purpose of a pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*), namely, after having completed a pilgrimage and upon returning home; this is based on the statement from the *Brahma-purāṇa* beginning with "whoever anyone... "In the case of bodily nourishment" refers to when one must perform elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like that serve as causes for bodily nourishment.
Thus ends the section on the varieties of *śrāddha* in the *Śrāddhakāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the great *Mahāsāndhivigrahika* and son of Śrī Mahāhṛdayadhara.
Now, the times for the Śrāddha ceremony.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya [1.217–218] states:
"The new moon day, the Aṣṭakās, an occasion of prosperity (vṛddhi), the dark fortnight, the two solstices,
the availability of materials, the excellence of Brahmins, the equinoxes, and the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign."
Vyatīpāta, Gajacchāyā, the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
and a personal inclination toward performing a Śrāddha— these are proclaimed as the times for Śrāddha.
‘Vyatīpāta’ is a specific astronomical conjunction (yoga) occurring at the moment when the declinations of the sun and the moon are equal. ‘Gajacchāyā’ is as described in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
“The conjunction of the Maghā constellation and the thirteenth lunar day is known as Kuñjaracchāyā;
it occurs when the moon is situated in Maghā and the sun is positioned in Hasta.”

“The three Aṣṭakās of the new moon, the three Anvaṣṭakās, the full moon of Māgha, the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight following that, and the ripening of rice and barley—Prajāpati has declared these to be the obligatory times for the Śrāddha.”
One who does not perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) for these [ancestors] falls into hell.
The transit of the sun; the two equinoxes; especially the two solstices; the *vyatīpāta* yoga; one's own birth-star (*janmarkṣa*); and a time of prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
Prajāpati has declared these to be the obligatory times for *śrāddha*.
Whatever *śrāddha* is offered on these occasions conduces to infinity.
The full moon day of Māgha; for it is so established by common usage.
"Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors, a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, when the moon has waned..."
One should perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month.
The wise know that the monthly *śrāddha* for the ancestors is the *anvāhārya*;
and that should be performed with effort using commendable meat.

"Pitṛyajña" here refers to the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. "Piṇḍānvāhāryaka" means that which is brought (āhriyate) or performed after (anu) the rice-balls (piṇḍān); thus, it is the Darśa-śrāddha. "Māsānumāsika" means occurring every month. Regarding the phrase "the monthly [offering] for the ancestors," the meaning is that the wise know the monthly Darśa-śrāddha to be that which must be performed as something to be brought after the rice-balls. By this, the technical name "Piṇḍānvāhāryaka" is established; the etymological explanation is stated for the purpose of prescribing its specific quality. "With meat" (āmiṣeṇa) means with commendable meat, such as the flesh of a rhinoceros and so forth.
[11] Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [2.81–92]:
"The *Piṇḍānvāhāryaka* Śrāddha is recommended when the moon has waned,
during the third part of the day, and not too close to the time of twilight."
When the fourth watch of the fourteenth day completes its course and the new moon is waning, at that very time the Śrāddha is prescribed.

As for what was said—that the moon does not become visible on that very day—it should be understood as being with reference to its waning; and the statement "when the king has waned" is likewise [to be understood in this sense].
And as for what was said regarding [the moon being seen] even while it is visible, that refers to the fourteenth day;
one should wait for the new moon, or perform the offering at its very end.
In the eighth part of the fourteenth day, the moon becomes exhausted;
and in the eighth part of the new moon (amāvāsyā), it is said to become minute once again.
The new moon day of Āgrahāyaṇī as well as that which occurs in the month of Jyeṣṭha—
those who know the movements of the moon declare these two to be special.

In this case, the moon remains in the first watch [of the night] with one-quarter of a digit remaining; right at its end, it undergoes complete waning—thus say those who know the circle of luminaries.
In that year in which there are thirteen lunar months, the third [lunar month] is not observed;
thus one should understand the course of the moon.
When that [day] has ended, one should give [the gift] in the afternoon.
If the fourteenth day should ever be mixed with the new moon,
some know that as "kharvitā," while others say, "Approach it."
One should observe the new moon day as it increases on the following day;
the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) should then take place after three or even more watches [of the night].
One should always perform the *caru* offering at the beginning of the fortnight and so forth;
other wise men, however, perform it in the forenoon even when [the moon] is pierced.

[12] "When the moon has waned" (*kṣīṇe rājani*) means when the moon has diminished. "In the third part" (*tṛtīyāṃśe*) refers to the third division of the day divided into three parts, that is to say, the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). "The watch of the fourteenth day" (*caturdaśīyāmaṃ*) means the period of the fourteenth day. "The fourth" (*turīyaṃ*) means the fourth. "One should fill it" (*pūrayet*); the connection is that the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is waning. Having raised the objection regarding a contradiction with the Vedic texts on the visibility of the moon—beginning with the words "on whichever day indeed" (*yadahas tv eva*)—a resolution was provided, because "non-visibility" is an indicative mark for "waning. As for the statement of Gobhila [1.7.9], "Even when it is visible at one time," that also refers to such a fourteenth day. "At its end" (*tadante*) means during the remainder of the fourteenth day. This alternative should be understood when the new moon does not extend into the time suitable for the *śrāddha*. Otherwise, however, the first alternative alone applies. Regarding the phrase "the eighth part of the new moon": when the eighth part of the new moon on the preceding day is capable of extending into the afternoon of the following day, then, because even a minute form of the moon exists and there is no waning, the *śrāddha* must not be performed then. For this very reason, where the new moon neither increases nor wanes, but rather, through a standstill (*viṣṭambha*), the possibility of the new moon occurring in the afternoon of both days arises, then the *śrāddha* must be performed on the previous day alone, according to Manu’s statement: "It is recommended when the moon has waned. In the cases of the new moons of Āgrahāyaṇa and Jyeṣṭha, due to the peculiar motion of the moon according to the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*), the aforementioned method—"it wanes in the eighth part of the fourteenth day"—is impossible; therefore, the meaning is that the *śrāddha* must be performed on the subsequent day, even in its eighth part. "Only at its end" (*tadanta eva*) means only at the end of the new moon. By the word "dwarfed" (*kharvitāṃ*), it is stated that [the moon] is unfit for performance due to censure. Others, however, interpret "approach her" (*upeṣvám*) as "approach her for the sake of performing the rite. Thus, he states the settled rule regarding the options with the words "increasing" (*vardhamānāṃ*) and so forth. By this, it is stated that in the case of an increasing new moon, one mixed with the fourteenth day is to be rejected; otherwise, in the case of waning or a standstill, only that mixed with the fourteenth day is to be accepted for the purpose of performance. Now, an objection: if the new moon is increasing, then by performing the rite on that very new moon, the rites to be performed on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), such as the *caru* offering to the beginning of the fortnight, would also follow as being performed on the second day—even though that is strictly forbidden. And that is absolutely prohibited.
The fourth part of the lunar day (parvan) and the first three moments of the following day (pratipad) are to be known as the time for sacrifice, as prescribed by the wise for the morning.

This is because Bodhāyana has stated that only this much time constitutes a constituent part (*yajñāṅga*) of the sacrifice; and because there is a statement of censure in the Taittirīya Śruti regarding the second-day overlap, beginning with: "This indeed is the sacrifice named Sumanā. Regarding this, he says: "Some perform [the sacrifice] on the previous day alone, while other wise men do so even when there is an overlap. By this, the following is meant: since the time for the sacrifice—which is joined with the morning and free from the second lunar day—is already established, the time joined with the second day is censured. However, when that [proper time] is not obtained, that [time joined with the second day] itself becomes a constituent part of the sacrifice. This was stated in connection with the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), as found in the Brāhma Purāṇa.
When the Śravaṇa asterism occurs on the new moon day, which is indeed destructive of demons and sacred to Viṣṇu,
then a śrāddha offered to the ancestors is said to be inexhaustible.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.14.7–9; 15–16]:
"When the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is conjoined with Anurādhā, Viśākhā, or Svātī, the host of ancestors attains satisfaction for eight years at the śrāddha."
When the new moon occurs under the asterisms of Puṣya, Ārdrā, or Punarvasu,
then the ancestors, when honored, attain satisfaction for twelve years.
[14] On the day of the constellation Ārdrā, for those desiring the satisfaction of the ancestors, it is presided over by Vāsava;
however, the new moon day under the constellation Śatabhiṣaj is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
If the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha ever coincides with the lunar mansion Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj),
that time is supreme for the ancestors.
For this is not obtained by those of little merit, O King.
O King, if at that time Dhaniṣṭhā should indeed be present,
then water and food offered to the ancestors will grant them complete satisfaction.
For ten thousand years by humans born in that family.
If, at that very time, the Pūrvabhādrapadas occur when that rite is performed for the ancestors,
they attain supreme satisfaction through it.
The ancestors sleep for a thousand yugas.
‘Maitra’ is Anurādhā; ‘Raudra’ is Ārdrā; ‘Vāsava’ is Dhaniṣṭhā; ‘Ajaikapāt’ is Pūrvabhādrapadā; ‘Vāruṇa’ is Śatabhiṣak. Kātyāyana says:
One should perform the Śrāddha with faith, even if it consists only of vegetables; one should not let the dark fortnight pass by. "Month after month," says the Śruti.
Baijavāpa says:
"One should perform the Śrāddha in the dark fortnight after having prepared the food;
'having prepared' means having cooked it."
In the dark fortnight, the lunar days beginning with the tenth, excluding the fourteenth, are recommended for the Śrāddha;
other days are not so.
Just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight,
so too the afternoon is superior to the forenoon for the performance of a śrāddha.
[15] In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "A man who is dependent on others, a traveler, or even one who is destitute, may always subsist during the dark fortnight with milk, roots, fruits, and vegetables."
One should offer water with sesame seeds during a śrāddha with a mind purified by devotion;
for the ancestors do not eat the sacrificial offering of one who performs it with impurity.
Alas, they do not satisfy those [deities] with devotion; instead, they drink the blood from their own bodies and bring about total destruction at every step.
Therefore, out of fear, the wise person should constantly offer libations to the ancestors.
Yama says: At the end of the fortnight, one who knows the Vedas should offer [oblations] to them in the afternoon,
near water, upon dūrvā grass, on *darbha* grass, and on sand.

"To them"—that is, to the ancestors—because it has been stated by Yama in this very context: "The ancestors do not accept [the offerings] from him. "On *darbha* grasses" means on places made of *darbha* grass; the same applies to *dūrvā* grass and so forth.
Likewise: "On the full moon of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, or Māgha, [one should feed] three or five twice-born men."
One should satisfy the ancestors first; that [offering] of his is said to be inexhaustible.
The meaning of this is: having performed the *śrāddha*, one should again feed three or five Brahmins separately; that results in inexhaustible fruit. Gautama [15.1–4]:

Now, one should offer the *śrāddha* to the ancestors on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), or during the latter fortnight of the month starting from the fifth day according to the *śrāddha* rite, or at all times when the materials, the place, and the Brahmins are available. The restriction of time is according to one’s capacity.

[16] This aforementioned restriction of time, such as the new moon day and so forth, should be understood to apply to one who is capable, possesses the requisite materials and other factors, and is free from illness. However, in the event of incapacity, one does not incur a transgression even by failing to perform it.
Vasiṣṭha [11.43]: One should offer to the ancestors on the full moon days of Śrāvaṇa and Āgrahāyaṇī, and also on the Anvaṣṭakī. The Nigama says:

For one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the worship of the ancestors should be performed with funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) alone, or he may also feed Brāhmaṇas, according to the earlier scriptural injunction. This should be done on whichever day occurs during the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*). However, it should be performed especially on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), or whenever there is an abundance of the eightfold offerings (*aṣṭakā*), a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), an auspicious lunar day (*tithi*), the necessary materials (*dravya*), or qualified Brāhmaṇas.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "The sixteen days when the sun has entered the sign of Virgo are equal to sacrificial rites; what is given during them is indeed inexhaustible."
Likewise:
"In the dark fortnight of the month of Aśvayuja, the śrāddha should be performed day by day;
or for three-quarters of the fortnight, or for one-third, or even for half."
Especially with *śyāmāka* grains, which are well-known and dear to the ancestors;

"day by day" (*dine dine*) means every single day, that is, throughout the entire fortnight. "Reduced by one-third" (*tribhāgahīnam*) means starting from the fifth day. "One-third" (*tribhāgam*) means starting from the tenth day. "Half" (*ardham*) means starting from the eighth day of the fortnight. Likewise:
As long as the sun remains in the signs of Virgo and Libra in succession, that is the time for the śrāddha; at that time, the city of the departed spirits is empty.

[17] “‘The time for the *śrāddha* lasts that long’ means that for one who, due to some cause, has not completed the *śrāddha* during the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) following the new moon, the period for the *śrāddha* is prescribed to last as long as the sun remains in Libra (*tulā*).
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: “O King, this fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*) known on earth as being ‘endowed with lamps’ (Dīpāvalī)...”
If one does not give [an offering] in that [period], it is as if nothing has been given to the ancestors during the Mahālaya.

"In the *Mahālaya*," that is, during the latter fortnight when the moon is in the sign of Virgo; as stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "One should perform the *śrāddha* at the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), as well as at the two solstices (*ayana*), on the occasion of the loss of a lunar day (*dinalopa*), during the *vyatīpāta* yoga, and when both the moon and the sun are eclipsed."
‘Dinalopa’ refers to that day and night during which there is contact with three days.
Likewise, it is said that a śrāddha performed on the beginnings and ends of the yugas yields inexhaustible merit.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"For the offering to the ancestors, there should be three Aṣṭakās at the root [of the lunar month];
indeed, that which occurs in the dark fortnight is the most excellent, and it is called the 'Aindrī'."
The second [offering] should be dedicated to Prajāpati, and the third to the Viśvedevas;
the first must always be performed with sacrificial posts (yūpa), and likewise, the other should be performed with meat.
The third [Anvaṣṭakā] should be performed with potherbs; this is the rule regarding the materials.
Indeed, the Anvaṣṭakā for the ancestors is ordained as a constant obligation.
And whatever other fourth [tithi] there may be, one should perform that especially;
and whoever should constantly perform a śrāddha on these [days], even at the cost of his entire wealth.
He swiftly attains blessings and rejoices both in this world and the next;
for at the times of the lunar festivals (parvan) the ancestors [are gratified], and at the times of the lunar days (tithi) the deities.
All [ancestors] come to that householder, like cows to a watering place—
even those who might otherwise go away unhonored on the Aṣṭakā days— if they are honored by him.
His hopes become fruitless both in this world and the next, forever.

[18] ‘At the root’ means at the beginning, that is to say, at the primary occasion. Since the *aṣṭakā* consists of both lunar days (*tithi*) and festival days (*parvan*), the worship of the gods and ancestors must necessarily be performed. As stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: “On the first *aṣṭakā*, which falls on the day of Indra, one should satisfy the ancestors with vegetables.”
On the second day, one should offer libations to Prajāpati with pure months.
On the third lunar day dedicated to Viśvedevas, one should offer cakes according to the prescribed order;
during the rainy season, however, on the fourth day itself, one should always offer pure leafy vegetables.
"Pure" means praiseworthy. And here, the option regarding vegetables and so forth is determined by the differences between the Vedic branches (śākhās).
Devala says:
All odd lunar days are more highly honored than even ones;
and among times, both the months of Māgha and Proṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada) are most highly honored.
For between the two fortnights, the dark fortnight is indeed more honored for the ancestral rites (śrāddha).
This examination of lunar days has been stated; now they shall explain it with respect to the constellations (nakṣatras).
Uttarā, Śravaṇa, Tiṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Prajāpati (Rohiṇī), Hasta, Śatabhiṣaj, Svāti, Citrā, Pitrya (Maghā), and then Āśvina.
These asterisms are always praised for rites pertaining to the ancestors;
however, other asterisms are occasionally mentioned for specific reasons.
Or again, that time at which one might obtain a brahmin endowed with virtues and worthy as a recipient— that indeed would be the honored time for the *śrāddha*.

"The three 'Uttaras'" [are Uttara-phalgunī, Uttara-āṣāḍhā, and Uttara-bhādrapadā]. "Prajāpati" refers to Rohiṇī, which has Prajāpati as its deity. "'Pitryam'" is Maghā. "'Āśvinam'" is Aśvinī. "'The others'" refers to Dhaniṣṭhā and the subsequent asterisms. "'By reasons'" refers to such factors as the conjunction with the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha.
Hārīta says: When materials for the offering are available at a sacred site (tīrtha), one need not observe a specific time;
this is remembered as a constant, superior rite for the ancestors to be performed monthly.
[19] Having obtained a worthy Brahmin as a recipient, the Śrāddha rite is prescribed to be performed immediately;
this applies also to the Aṣṭakā rites, those for prosperity (Abhyudaya), pilgrimages, and occasions of birth.

"One should not wait for a specific time" means one should not await the afternoon of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) or other such times. "Excessive" (*atireka*) means additional; "fixed" (*dhruva*) means obligatory. Regarding "the *aṣṭakās*" and so forth: the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha* and others are to be performed every month. Paiṭhīnasi [asks]:
"What is the time, place, substance, and the twice-born [invited] for the *śrāddha*?"
The place is Vārāṇasī; the substance is such things as the flesh of a rhinoceros; the twice-born person is one who purifies the company at a meal, and so forth.
Śātātapa says:
"Upon the arrival of new water, upon new grain, and likewise upon the roofing of a house..."
The ancestors, however, long for food on the Aṣṭakā days and under the Maghā asterisms;
therefore, one should always be diligent in giving to learned Brāhmaṇas.
"At 'navodaka' means at the beginning of the rains. "Among the Brāhmaṇas"—the word "when they have arrived" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Manu [3.273–274]: "One should offer whatever is mixed with honey on the thirteenth day."
That too would indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season and under the constellation Maghā.
"May there be born in our family one who would give us milk-rice with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth day, during the time when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east."
"In the shadow of the elephant to the east" means when the shadow of the elephant has moved toward the eastern direction.
Vasiṣṭha [11.39–40]: The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather,
wait upon the son who has been born, just as birds wait upon the peepul tree.
"With honey, meat, śāli rice, milk, and milk-rice—
this man will offer us the śrāddha during the rainy season under the asterism Maghā."
Śaṅkha, Likhita,
and Yama: "The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather,
praise the son who has been born, just as birds rejoice over a fig tree."
With honey, meat, rhinoceros flesh, milk, or milk-rice,
he will grant us satisfaction during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism.
There are also two verses sung by the ancestors:
"May there be born in our lineage some supreme among men..."
During the rainy season, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should remain concentrated in meditation.
He who performs a śrāddha with honey-abundant milk-rice (pāyasa) throughout the entire month of Kārttika, or even on the day when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east;
Paiṭhīnasi says:
"Whether it be a son or a grandson, whoever among us gives [a goat] made of all metals on the thirteenth lunar day during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism..."
Thus the ancestors look on. "With all-copper" means with a goat that is entirely red in color.
Likewise, Devala says in the context of sacrificial oblations (haviṣya):
"Or a goat that is entirely red."
Yājñavalkya [1.261]: Whatever one gives while staying at Gayā is said to be entirely infinite;
likewise on the thirteenth day of the rainy season, and especially under the Maghā asterism.
Śaṅkha says: When the full moon day of Pauṣa has passed, having reached the thirteenth lunar day conjoined with the Maghā constellation,
one should indeed perform the Śrāddha rite with honey and milk-rice (pāyasa).

[21] In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, under the asterism of Maghā, during the rainy season, Yama [releases] the deceased ancestors from the abode of Yama."
Having left his own city empty, he departs from the human world,
tormented by hunger and proclaiming the evil deeds he himself committed.
Desiring [merit] for their sons and grandsons, they offer milk-rice mixed with honey;
therefore, one should satisfy her there according to the prescribed rite with that milk-rice.
Likewise, that man who obtains from another's house even a single mouthful of food mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, or even cold water, [attains great merit].
Whether he himself sustains his life by means of mere alms,
or whether he nourishes his body every day by selling himself;
He too should perform the śrāddha with various well-accumulated materials,
with great effort on the thirteenth lunar day, during the rainy season, and under the Maghā asterism.
There exists no time superior to this for ancestral rites (śrāddha),
other than that wherein the ancestors themselves directly receive the imperishable nectar (amṛta).

In this context, by considering the statements regarding the thirteenth lunar day as a single syntactical unit, it is understood that on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight following the month of Proṣṭhapadā, a Śrāddha accompanied by rice-balls (piṇḍas) must necessarily be performed by both those who have sons and those who do not. However, when that same day is conjoined with the Maghā asterism, one who has an eldest son should perform a Śrāddha without rice-balls. As stated in the section concerning the latter half of the month when the sun is in Virgo:
"Even there, a great worship should be performed for the ancestors;
however, the offering of rice-balls in that asterism, an eldest son should avoid."

This is because of the statement in the Devīpurāṇa. As for the hearing of censure in passages such as "and they become those who die young," that refers to the performance of optional śrāddhas on the intercalary thirteenth day (trayodaśī) which will be described hereafter.
[22] Following the rules for the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, Manu [6.289–282] states: "By this rule, one should offer the *śrāddha* here three times a year—
during the winter, the summer, and the rainy seasons— and the *pañcayajña* [śrāddha] every day."
The oblation pertaining to the ancestral sacrifice is not prescribed for the common fire;
nor is there a Śrāddha rite without the Darśa sacrifice for a twice-born who has maintained the sacred fires.

"Three times a year" means three times within a year (*saṃvatsara*). This [rule] applies commonly to both those who maintain a sacred fire (*sāgni*) and those who do not (*niragni*). Regarding the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* which is declared as necessarily to be performed during the course of a year, this is an alternative procedure (*anukalpa*) in the event it cannot be accomplished due to some cause such as the lack of available materials. However, the *śrāddha* that is part of the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) must be performed every day, even with water and so forth. For this very reason, Devala, after describing the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, also stated: "One should perform the *śrāddha* according to this rule at some point during the year."
Twice, four times, or as faith permits—month by month, or day by day.

Thus, many alternative options have been demonstrated according to the relative degree of one's capacity or lack thereof. The *śrāddha* performed three times during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons should be performed on any lunar day (*tithi*) when the sun is situated in Virgo (*kanyā*), Aquarius (*kumbha*), or Taurus (*vṛṣa*). However, even for one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), it must be performed specifically on the new moon day (*darśa*). This is because the Southern Fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*), which serves as the constituent element of the fire-oblation (*agnaukaraṇa-homa*) prescribed by the term "Paitṛyajñika" as an ancillary part of the *śrāddha*, does not exist apart from the new moon sacrifice. As for other occasional *śrāddhas*, such as those for the *Aṣṭakās*, since they are to be accomplished using materials like the horn of a deer or similar substances, the fire-oblation as an ancillary rite must simply be performed in whatever fire is available.
Devala says: This ritual for the Śrāddha was proclaimed by Manu as the "Mānava-śrāddhakalpa.
While there may be many rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) during the Aṣṭakās, the Aṣṭakā itself consists of only a single rice-ball.
By this procedure, one should perform the Śrāddha once a year,
twice, four times, or according to the specific rite— either month by month or day by day.
Yama said:
"Indeed, a śrāddha offered upon the sight of Rāhu is said to yield infinite merit."
[23] Viṣṇu [77.8–9]: A wise person should certainly not perform a śrāddha during the two twilights or at night;
however, it may be performed even during those times if there is an eclipse of the moon.
For a śrāddha offered at the sight of Rāhu remains as long as the moon and stars;
endowed with all virtues, it fulfills every desire for the ancestors.
Śātātapa says: One should not perform a śrāddha at night, except during an eclipse;
nor should one ever perform it during either of the two twilights.
Āpastamba [1.16.23–24]:
"And one should not perform a Śrāddha at night, except during an eclipse of the moon."
Manu [3.280]: One should not perform a śrāddha at night, for that is declared to belong to the Rākṣasas;
nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only recently risen.
Now, the times for the optional *śrāddha* rites.

Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: Now follow the rites for specific desires (*kāmya*). On the first lunar day (*pratipad*), women [are obtained]. On the second, the birth of daughters. On the third, horses. On the fourth, small livestock. On the fifth, sons. On the sixth, success in gambling. On the seventh, agriculture. On the eighth, trade. On the ninth, one-hoofed animals. On the eleventh, female attendants. On the twelfth, wealth and grain. On the thirteenth, base metals and preeminence among kinsmen. On the fourteenth, young men die; and for one slain by a weapon, [the result is obtained] on that day. On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), everything [is obtained].
Manu says:
"Performing a śrāddha on the first lunar day (pratipad), one obtains handsome sons;
on the second, daughters; and on the third, bards."
On the fourth day, one obtains small cattle; on the fifth, beautiful sons;
on the sixth, gambling and agriculture; and on the seventh, a man obtains these things.
On the eighth day as well, the giver of a śrāddha always obtains success in trade;
on the ninth day he obtains single-hoofed animals, and on the tenth day, many double-hoofed ones.
Likewise, on the eleventh day, one obtains prosperity and sons endowed with Vedic luster;
on the twelfth day, gold, silver, and base metals.
On the thirteenth day, one attains preeminence among kinsmen; on the fourteenth, one obtains excellent offspring;
and his ancestors who were slain by weapons in battle are gratified.

By offering at the new moon on the fifteenth day, the giver of the śrāddha attains all those vast and heart-pleasing desires that were specified for the first day of the lunar fortnight and the others.

‘Vandinaḥ’ refers to panegyrists; that is to say, they become so immediately. ‘Dyūtam’ means victory at dice. ‘Kupyam’ is wealth other than gold and silver, such as copper and so forth. Regarding the phrase ‘pakṣatyādi’: ‘pakṣati’ means the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad); the meaning is that the fruit of the lunar days beginning with the first day is auspicious on the new moon (amāvāsyā).
Āpastamba [2.16.6–21].

If it is performed on all the days of the dark fortnight, one gratifies the ancestors. However, for the performer, there is a distinction of results due to the restriction regarding time: if it is performed on the first day, offspring consisting mostly of females is born; on the second, thieves; on the third, those endowed with Vedic luster (*brahmavarcas*); on the fourth, one possessing small livestock; on the fifth, many male children are born, and he does not die childless; on the sixth, one who is habitually traveling or gambling; on the seventh, success in agriculture; on the eighth, prosperity; on the ninth, single-hoofed animals; on the tenth, success in trade; on the eleventh, iron, tin, and lead; on the twelfth, one possessing livestock; on the thirteenth, one with many sons, many friends, and handsome offspring, though they die young; on the fourteenth, success in weaponry; and on the fifteenth, prosperity.
Regarding the section beginning with "One who performs the *śrāddha* constantly attains [the results]," Viṣṇu states [78,36–50]:

On the first lunar day (*pratipad*), beautiful women are obtained in the home; on the second, a maiden who grants boons; on the third, all desires; on the fourth, fame; on the fifth, handsome sons; on the sixth, victory at gambling; on the seventh, agriculture; on the eighth, commerce; on the ninth, cattle; on the tenth, horses; on the eleventh, sons endowed with Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcas*); on the twelfth, gold and silver; on the thirteenth, good fortune (*saubhāgya*); on the fifteenth, all desires. For the *śrāddha* rite of those slain by weapons, the fourteenth day is recommended.

Under the heading "One should perform the *śrāddha*," Hārīta states: one desiring a son [should perform it] on the fifth lunar day; one desiring wealth on the sixth; one desiring cattle on the seventh; one desiring health for those killed by weapons on the eighth; one desiring to conquer an army on the ninth; one desiring food on the tenth; one desiring prosperity on the eleventh; one desiring fortune on the twelfth; one desiring fame on the thirteenth; one desiring power or well-being on the fourteenth; and one desiring all things on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).

Paiṭhīnasi: One desiring a son should sacrifice on the fifth day; one desiring cattle on the sixth; one desiring prosperity on the seventh; one desiring food on the eighth; one desiring spiritual luster on the ninth; one desiring all things on the tenth; one desiring wealth on the eleventh; one desiring land on the twelfth; mastery over women on the thirteenth; [sacrifice for] those killed by weapons on the fourteenth; and one desiring all things on the new moon day.

[27] O Brahmapuṇi, by performing a śrāddha on the full moon day, one obtains the full fruit; on the first lunar day (pratipad) it is for the acquisition of wealth, and the next (the second day) is likewise for wealth.
On the third day, for the sake of obtaining boons, and on another [the fourth], for the destruction of enemies;
on the fifth day, one should diligently perform the Śrāddha for the acquisition of wealth.
On the sixth day, however, for the sake of protecting children; on the seventh, for the prosperity of kinsmen;
likewise on the eighth, for one desiring growth; and on the ninth day, for one desiring a wife.
On the tenth day, one seeking the splendor of Brahman or likewise desiring progeny [should worship];
on the twelfth day, for the sake of victory; and on the thirteenth day, for the sake of prosperity.
It is the settled conclusion that for those who have died by fasting, starvation, weapons, fire, poison, or hanging,
an offering should be made on the fourteenth day for the sake of their satisfaction.
On the new moon day, however, one should satisfy the ancestors with devotion for the sake of attaining heaven.

And in this regard, the diversity of results according to the lunar days (tithi) should be understood as being due to differences among those qualified [to perform the rite]. Furthermore, where a defect of offspring such as theft, youthfulness, or being a murderer is heard of, even there the qualification belongs to one who, being childless, desires offspring merely while accompanied by aversion toward that [defective] offspring.
Manu [3.277]: Performing [the rites] on even days, one enjoys all desires;
but by honoring the ancestors on odd days, one obtains abundant progeny.
Yama says: By performing [rites] during the conjunctions (yoga) and under the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) of the day, one shall obtain all desires;
by worshipping the ancestors during the Gajacchāyā, one obtains abundant progeny.
[28] Yājñavalkya [9.265–268]: For one obtains heaven, offspring, vigor, heroism, a field, strength, as well as a preeminent son, good fortune, prosperity, and auspicious preeminence.
As well as the turning of the wheel [of sovereignty], trade and other such activities,
freedom from disease, fame, freedom from sorrow, and the supreme goal.
He who duly offers a śrāddha shall obtain wealth, knowledge, success in medicine, base metals, cattle, goats and sheep, horses, and long life.
From Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī,
he who is a believer, full of faith, and free from pride and envy, shall obtain these desires.
‘The state of one whose wheel is set in motion’ (pravṛttacakratā) means possessing a command that is always unimpeded.

One who constantly performs the *śrāddha* on Sunday obtains health; on Monday, good fortune; on Tuesday, victory in battle; on Wednesday, all desires; on Thursday, desired knowledge; on Friday, wealth; and on Saturday, long life. In the constellation Kṛttikā, one attains heaven; in Rohiṇī, offspring; in Mṛgaśiras, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). In Ārdrā, there is success in undertakings; in Punarvasu, land; in Puṣya, nourishment; in Āśleṣā, prosperity (*śrī*); in Maghā, all desires; in Pūrvaphalgunī, good fortune; in Uttaraphalgunī, wealth; in Hasta, preeminence among kinsmen; in Citrā, beautiful daughters; in Svātī, success in trade; in Viśākhā, gold; in Anurādhā, friends; in Jyeṣṭhā, sovereignty; in Mūla, agriculture; in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, success in sea-voyages; in Uttarāṣāḍhā, all desires; in Abhijit, preeminence; in Śravaṇa, all [desires]; in Dhaniṣṭhā, salt; in Śatabhiṣaj, health; in Pūrvabhādrapadā, base metals; in Uttarabhādrapadā, a house; in Revatī, cattle; in Aśvinī, horses; and in Bharaṇī, long life.
[29] In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "One who performs the *śrāddha* shall obtain horses under Aśvinī; under Bharaṇī, the highest longevity; and under Kṛttikā, freedom from fever."
Under Prajāpati (Rohiṇī), one gains progeny and nourishment; under Soma (Mṛgaśiras), excellent vigor;
under Ārdrā, success in cruel deeds; and under Punarvasu, beloved sons.
Under Tiṣya one obtains heroic sons; under Āśleṣā, wealth;
under Maghā, preeminence among kinsmen; and under Bhaga, supreme good fortune.
The power of generosity is in the hand of Āryaman; preeminence and great prosperity are in Tvaṣṭṛ;
a meritorious daughter is in Svāti; and excellent trade is in Viśvāvasu.
Under Viśākhā one obtains auspicious sons; under Anurādhā (Maitra), an unsurpassed state;
under Jyeṣṭhā, sovereignty; and under Mūla, supreme health.
Under Āṣāḍhā one gains fame; under Uttarā, freedom from sorrow;
under Śravaṇa, a meritorious rebirth; and under Dhaniṣṭhā, abundant wealth.
Under the constellation Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), there is an increase in agriculture; under Viśākhā, many sheep;
under Uttarā (Phalgunī), many cows; and under Pauṣṇa (Revatī), base metals and a great treasure.
Having reflected thus, he should accomplish whatever [is required] through yoga according to the prescribed rite;
on that day of the śrāddha, he should satisfy the ancestors with devotion.
Now, the places for the Śrāddha rite.
Therein, Viṣṇu [85, 1–67]:

Now, at Puṣkara, the Śrāddha is inexhaustible, as are recitations, burnt offerings, and austerities. By merely bathing at Puṣkara, one becomes purified from all sins. It is exactly the same at Gayāśīrṣa, at the Vaṭa tree, at Amarakaṇṭaka, at Mount Varāha, anywhere on the banks of the Narmadā, on the banks of the Yamunā, and especially at the Gaṅgā; at Kuśāvarta, [Binduka], Bilvaka, Nīlaparvata, Kanakhala, Kubjāmra, Bhṛgutuṅga, Kedāra, Mahālaya, Naḍantikā, Sugandhā, Śākambharī, Phalgutīrtha, Mahāgaṅgā, Taṇḍulikāśrama [Trihalikāśrama], Kumāradhārā, Prabhāsa, and especially anywhere along the Sarasvatī.
On the banks of the Gaṅgā, at Prayāga, and especially on the Sarasvatī;
constantly in the Naimiṣa forest, and especially in Vārāṇasī.

At the hermitage of Agastya; at the hermitage of Kaṇva; on the Kauśikī; on the banks of the Sarayū; at the confluence of the Śoṇa and the Jyotiṣmatī; at Śrīparvata; at Kālodaka; at Uttaramānasa; [at Vaḍavā]; at Mataṅgavāpī; at Saptarṣi; at Viṣṇupada; at Svargamārgapada; on the Godāvarī; [on the Gomatī]; on the Vetravatī; [on the Vipāśā; on the Vitastā]; on the banks of the Śatadru; on the Candrabhāgā; on the Irāvatī; on the banks of the Sindhu; in the southern Pañcanada; at Ausaja—in such and other holy places (tīrtha), in the best of rivers, at all confluences, at sources, on sandbanks, at springs, on mountains, in groves, in forests, in parks, and in houses smeared with cow-dung that are pleasing to the mind—and here there are verses sung by the ancestors:
May that being be born in our family who shall offer us handfuls of water in rivers with abundant waters, especially those that are cool.
"May there arise in our family some supreme among men who,
with a concentrated mind, might perform for us the śrāddha rite at the Banyan Tree of Gayāśīrṣa."
One should desire many sons, so that even one among them might go to Gayā,
or perform the horse sacrifice, or set free a dark-colored bull.

Regarding "at the sources" (*prabhaveṣu*), this refers to the places of origin of rivers; for after introducing them as "in the best of rivers" and "at confluences," they are specifically designated as "at the sources. A "sandbank" (*pulina*) is a region rising from the waters of a river. A "springs" (*prasravaṇa*) is a waterfall or cascade. A "bower" (*nikuñja*) is a place enveloped by creepers and the like. A "grove" (*upavana*) is a domestic garden. "Charming" (*manojña*) means beautiful. Śaṅkha says:
"And that which one staying at Gayā gives at Prabhāsa and at the Puṣkaras..."
At Prayāga and in the Naimiṣa forest, everything is said to be infinite.
[32] On the banks of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, at Payoṣṇī and Amarakaṇṭaka,
and on the banks of the Narmadā and Bāhudā— all these are said to grant infinite merit.
A gift given at Kurukṣetra among the Kurus, on the Bhṛgutuṅga peak, in the Himalayas,
at the Seven Sages’ site, or at Vṛṣṇikūpa is said to be inexhaustible.
Devala said:
The places honored for the performance of the śrāddha rite are Gayā, the Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī,
Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, and the Puṣkara lakes.
The ancestors are gratified by what is given here on riverbanks, at sacred fords, on mountains, on sandbanks, and in secluded places.
"Secluded" means "free from people."
Bṛhaspati [Śrāddha, 66–67, 51]:
Ancestors, fearing a fall into hell, long for sons, thinking:
"Whoever shall go to Gayā, he will deliver us."
He will perform the release of a bull, as well as rites for the gods and ancestors;
in his old age he will protect [the lineage] and offer ancestral oblations every day.
What is given at Gayā, on the Dharmapṛṣṭha, at the lake of Brahmā, at Gayāśīrṣa,
and at the Akṣayavaṭa, becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors.
Having visited Brahmāraṇya, Dharmapṛṣṭha, and Dhenukāraṇya,
and having worshipped the ancestors, one shall uplift twenty generations of one's lineage.
[33] In the *Vāyupurāṇa* [77, 96–99, 101–106, 108–109]: "A *śrāddha* offered at Gayā, on the Dharmapṛṣṭha, likewise at the lake of Brahmā, and at the Gayā-Gṛdhravaṭa, yields great fruit."
In Bharata’s holy hermitage, which is constantly filled with those most meritorious,
the footprint of Mataṅga is seen there by all human beings.
The entire essence of the Dharma has been proclaimed as an illustration for this world;
thus is the meritorious Pañcavana, frequented by those who perform virtuous deeds.
In that place where the Pāṇḍuviśālā Tīrtha is an immediate manifestation,
likewise on the third foot and in the Maṇḍala of Niścīvā.
A śrāddha offered at the great lake of the Kauśikī yields great fruit;
likewise, the wise Mahādeva set foot upon Muṇḍapṛṣṭha.
Having performed difficult austerities at sacred fords for many groups of years,
a man devoted to dharma [attains the same] here in even a short time.
One quickly casts off evil, like a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
By the name Kanakananda, this sacred ford (tīrtha) is renowned throughout the world;
it lies to the north of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha and is frequented by hosts of Brahman-sages.
Having bathed there, a human being goes to heaven in his own body;
furthermore, a śrāddha offering performed there is declared to be eternally inexhaustible.
Having bathed there, the best of men discharges his three debts;
then, having bathed in the Mānasa lake, he should perform the Śrāddha ceremony.
Having gone to Uttaramānasa, one attains unsurpassed success;
there, one should perform the śrāddha rite according to one's capacity and according to one's strength.
He obtains divine desires and the means to liberation in their entirety.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa* (22.10–12):
"Then Nandā and likewise Lalitā, as well as the holy site of Māyāpurī; and then the one named Citrapada, and thereafter the excellent Kedāra."

They say that this auspicious place, the source of the waters of the Śatadru, is the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, containing all sacred fords; likewise, the lake of Brahmā is also a sacred ford.
Likewise [22, 16–18]:
"It is purified, of great merit, and the destroyer of all sins;
for there Nārasiṃha himself, Janārdana, resides."
There is a sacred ford named Ikṣumatī, which is always difficult for the ancestors to attain;
it is there at the confluence that the ancestors always reside by the Gaṅgā.
Likewise: the Yamunā, the Devikā, the Kālī, the Candrabhāgā, the Dṛṣadvatī,
the holy river Dhenumatī, and further the Vetravatī.
Likewise,
O best of the twice-born, there is the sacred ford of the ancestors known as Nīlakuṇḍa,
as well as the meritorious Bhadrasaras and Lake Mānasa.
Likewise, the Mandākinī, the Acchodā, the Vipāśā, and the Sarasvatī;
as well as the holy site of Mitrapada and Vaidyanātha, which yields great fruit.
[35] Priyānandin, Mahākāla, as well as the auspicious Kālañjara,
Vaṃśodbheda, Harodbheda, Gaṅgodbheda, and Mahālaya.
Bhadreśvara, Viṣṇupada, and Narmadādvāra as well.
The great seers have declared that these are equal to the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā.
[Thus] [22,
27–29]: Oṃkāra, Pitṛtīrtha, the Kāverī, the waters of the Kapilā,
the confluence of the Caṇḍavegā, and likewise Amarakaṇṭaka.
Bathing and other rites performed there shall yield a hundred times the merit of Kurukṣetra;
furthermore, Śukratīrtha is renowned, as is the supreme Someśvara Tīrtha.
It removes all diseases, is meritorious, and its fruit exceeds a hundred millionfold.
Likewise [as stated in verses 22.30–76]:
there is the place named Kāyāvarohaṇa and likewise the river Carmaṇvatī.
Likewise, the Gomatī, the Varaṇā, the holy site of Auśanasa, and Bhava.
Bhairava and Bhṛgutuṅga, the unsurpassed Gaurītīrtha,
the holy site named Vaināyaka, and beyond that, Vatseśvara.
Furthermore, the river Tāptī is likewise merit-bestowing and a remover of sins,
as are the Mūla-tāpī, the Payoṣṇī, and the confluence of the Payoṣṇī.
Mahābodhi, Pāṭalā, Nāgatīrtha, Avantikā,
as well as the meritorious river Veṇā, and likewise Mahāśāla.
Mahārudra, Mahāliṅga, and the auspicious river Daśārṇā;
Śatarudrā, Śatāhvā, and likewise the supreme Viṣṇupada.
[36] Likewise, there are the two rivers Aṅgāravāhikā, Śoṇa, and Gharghara; also the meritorious river Kālikā and the auspicious river Vitastā.
These are praised as the sacred sites of the ancestors (pitṛtīrtha) for bathing and giving gifts;
a śrāddha offering made at these places is remembered to yield infinite fruit.
Droṇī, Vāṭanadī, Dhārāsaraḥ, Kṣīranadī,
as well as Dvārakā, Kṛṣṇatīrtha, and Arbuda-Sarasvatī.
The river named Maṇimatī, as well as Girikanyakā,
the sacred ford Dhūtapāpa, and likewise the southern ocean.
Gokarṇa, Gajakarṇa, and likewise Puruṣottama—
in these sacred sites of the ancestors (pitṛtīrtha), a śrāddha offering is said to yield infinite results.
The sacred ford named Meghakara is where Janārdana himself,
Viṣṇu, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, is established in Mekhalā.
Likewise, at the Mandodarī-tīrtha where the auspicious river Campā flows,
as well as at Sāmalanātha and Mahāśālavatī.
Likewise, on the southern bank of the Payoṣṇī, there is Devadeveśvara;
and likewise, O Lord, there is Koṭīśvara in the vicinity of Reṇukā.
Therein are Koṭa and Sākoṭa, as well as the great Jalpeśvara,
Arjuna, Tripureśa, and thereafter Siddheśvara.
Śaileśa, Śrīkara Tīrtha, and beyond that Nārasiṃha;
then Mahendra, which is of great merit, as well as the one known as Śrīraṅga.
[37] One always enjoys infinite fruit by performing a śrāddha even at these [sites];
indeed, even by the mere sight of them, all sins are removed.
The Tuṅgabhadrā river is meritorious, as is the Bhīmarathī stream;
likewise Bhīmeśvara, the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, the Kāverī, and the Vañjulā river.
The river named Godāvarī is a supreme holy ford for the three junctions of the day;
and the holy ford named Tryambaka is indeed saluted by all holy fords.
Where the Lord Janārdana himself, the formidable one, resides.
A śrāddha offered during all of these occasions becomes ten-millionfold in merit;
even by the mere remembrance of them, O twice-born ones, sins are shattered into a hundred pieces.
The Śrīparṇī river is meritorious, as is the unsurpassed Vyāsatīrtha;
likewise the river named Matsya, and similarly the Śivadhārā;
the famous Bhavatīrtha, and likewise the Pampātīrtha.
Likewise, the meritorious Rāmeśvara, as well as Elāpura;
the famous Aṅgārabhūta, Ānartaka, and Alambuṣa;
and likewise Āmrātakeśvara, as well as the supreme Ekāmraka.
Govardhana, Hariścandra, Puraścandra, and Pṛthūdaka.
There is Sahasrākṣa, Hiraṇyākṣa, and likewise the river Kadalī;
there also is Rāmādhivāsa, as well as the one named Saumitri.
Indranīla, Mahānāda, and likewise Priyamelaka—
these too are always highly praised and even more excellent for use in a śrāddha rite.
[38] Since the presence of all the gods is said to reside in these,
a gift given to all of them shall yield a hundredfold more than ten million times its value.
The sacred river Bāhudā, as well as the auspicious Siddhavana;
the holy site named Pāśupata, and likewise Vaṭī and Parpaṭikā.
A śrāddha offered at these places yields a hundred times ten million times ten million-fold merit;
likewise, there is the Pitṛtīrtha where the river Godāvarī flows.
Joined with a thousand liṅgas and carrying water to both its left and right,
that is the tīrtha of Jāmadagnya, the supreme Rāmāyatana.
Where the Godāvarī river was split by fear of Pratīka,
that sacred ford (tīrtha) is the place for offerings to gods and ancestors, frequented by ten thousand apsarases.
There, the performance of fire-sacrifices with faith and the act of giving charity yield merit exceeding a hundred crores;
likewise, there is the thousand Lingas and the supreme Rāghaveśvara.
The river Sendraphenā is holy, where in ancient times Indra was exhausted;
having slain Namuci, Śakra attained heaven through ascetic penance.
A śrāddha offered there by men shall yield infinite fruit;
for that place is the sacred site named Puṣkara, as well as Sālagrāma.
And there is the famous Śoṇapāta, where the abode of Vaiśvānara is located,
as well as the sacred ford named Sārasvata and likewise Svāmitīrtha.
The Mallandara, the holy Kauśikī, the Candrikā,
as well as the Vaidarbhā, the Vegā, and the Payoṣṇī, which flows toward the east.
The Kāverī is meritorious in its northern course, as is the Jālandhara mountain;
at these shrāddha-tīrthas, one’s ancestral offering attains infinity.
Likewise Lohadaṇḍa Tīrtha, Citrakūṭa,
the confluence of the Vindhya with the Gaṅgā, and the auspicious bank of the Nandā.
Likewise, there is the Kubjāmra tīrtha, as well as the Ūrvaśī-pulina;
right there is the Saṃsāramocana tīrtha and the Ṛṇamocana.
By performing a śrāddha at these sacred sites of the ancestors (pitṛtīrtha), one attains infinite merit;
namely, the great tīrtha Aṭṭahāsa and Gautameśvara as well.
Likewise, there is Vasiṣṭhatīrtha, and after that Hārīta;
as well as Brahmāvarta, Kuśāvarta, and likewise Hayatīrtha.
And the famous Piṇḍāraka, as well as Śaṅkoddhāra,
Ghaṇṭeśvara, Bilva, and Nīlaparvata.
And likewise Badarītīrtha and Rāmatīrtha,
as well as Jayanta, Vijaya, and Śukratīrtha.
Likewise, there is the holy site of Śrīpati, as well as the Raivataka Tīrtha;
also the supreme Vaikuṇṭha Tīrtha, and furthermore Bhīmeśvara;
and the famous Aśva Tīrtha, which is infinite in its merit for funeral rites and the giving of gifts.
There is a sacred ford named Vedaśiras, as well as the river Oghavatī;
there is a sacred ford named Vasuprada, and likewise the Chāgaliṅga.
Those who give offerings of faith at these places go to the supreme state;
there is the sacred site named Mātṛgṛha, as well as Karavīrapura.
The Saptagodāvarī-tīrtha is the most excellent among all holy sites;
those desiring infinite fruit should perform a śrāddha ceremony there.
[40] Likewise [22, 81]:
"The *śrāddha* performed at these sacred fords (*tīrtha*) is held to be ten million times more meritorious.
Therefore, one should perform the *śrāddha* at a sacred ford with great effort."
Likewise,
one should always perform the śrāddha rite according to the rules in these places,
having gone toward the south-eastern direction with the desire to fulfill all wishes.

Regarding the specific characteristics of the various sacred fords (tīrtha) mentioned here as locations for ancestral rites (śrāddha), these are to be learned from the inhabitants of those respective regions.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa* [78.21–23]:
"One should avoid the region of Triśaṅku for twelve yojanas on all sides—
north of the Mahānadī and south of Kīkaṭa."
The region named Traiśaṅkava is excluded from the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha),
as are Kāraskara, Kaliṅga, and the region north of the Indus.
And regions where the duties of the stages of life have perished should be avoided with great effort.
Śaṅkha says:
Likewise, [one should not study] in a land of barbarians, at night, and especially during the two twilights.
A wise person should not perform a funeral feast (śrāddha) nor should he go to a land of barbarians (mleccha).
Now, the sacrificial oblations.

In this matter, a specific degree of satisfaction arises from a specific kind of oblation (*havis*). Regarding this, Manu [3.266–272] says: "I shall explain in its entirety that oblation which, when offered to the ancestors according to the rules, conduces to long duration and to infinity."
When sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits are offered according to the prescribed rules,
the ancestors of men are gratified for a month.
For two months one may subsist on fish-meat, for three months on the meat of the deer,
for four months on the meat of sheep, and indeed for five months on the meat of birds.
For six months with the meat of a goat, or for seven with that of a spotted deer;
for eight months with the meat of an antelope, and for nine indeed with the meat of a Ruru deer.
They are satisfied for ten months by the flesh of boar and buffalo;
however, by the flesh of rabbit and tortoise, they are satisfied for exactly eleven months.
By means of cow's milk, or milk-rice,
or by the meat of a vārdhrīṇasa (a type of ox), satisfaction for twelve years is attained for one year.
Black potherbs, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the rhinoceros and red deer, honey,
and all kinds of food fit for ascetics lead to infinite results.

‘Aurabhra’ is the flesh of a sheep; ‘śākuna’ is the flesh of a bird; ‘pṛṣata’ is the spotted deer; ‘eṇa’ is the black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*); ‘ruru’ is the *śambara* deer. [42] The term ‘gavya’ is a qualifier for milk, according to the statement of Uśanas: “A year [is completed] with cow’s milk. The specific nature of the *vārdhrīṇasa* is shown in the Vedic injunction (*nigama*): “The ritualists call that *vārdhrīṇasa* which drinks from three [teats], whose senses are failing, which is white, aged, and lordless (*ajāpati*).”
"The bird with a black neck, red veins, and white wings—every such creature is called a vārdhrīṇasa; such is the Vedic revelation (naigamī śruti)."

‘Mahāśalkāḥ’ are specific types of fish, according to the statement of Yama: “The mahāśalka fish [are permitted]. ‘Munyannāni’ refers to wild grains such as *nīvāra* and the like. Yama says: “The porcupine (*śalyaka*) satisfies [the ancestors] for four months; the *ruru* deer, indeed, for five; the hare (*śaśa*) satisfies them for six months, while the tortoise (*kūrma*) satisfies them for seven.”
The flesh of a boar satisfies for eight months, while that of a ram indeed satisfies for nine;
the flesh of a buffalo for ten months, and that of a gavaya for as many as Rudra (eleven).
Likewise:
"If the meat of a rhinoceros is offered at the Pitṛkṣaya [ancestral site], it becomes an offering for infinity.
Pitṛkṣaya should be known as Gayā; what is given there yields great fruit."
Likewise: "Whatever is joined with honey conduces to infinity;
so too is food prepared according to the rule and consecrated with mantras."

‘Gāvaya’ means the meat of a gavaya. ‘Rudrasammitān’ means those numbering eleven. ‘Upākṛta’ refers to that which has been consecrated with mantras and purified with darbha grass. ‘Annaṃ tathākṛtam’ means food that has likewise been consecrated.
[43] Devala said: They are satisfied with fish for two months; with ruru deer for three months;
with birds for four months; and they are satiated with the flesh of the spotted antelope for five months.
With the flesh of hares, there is satisfaction for six months; with that of tortoises, for seven months.

With the meat of a boar, one is satisfied for eight months; with that of a goat, for nine; and with that of a ruru deer, they are satisfied for ten months. With buffalo meat, they are satisfied for eleven months, and with the flesh of sheep, for twelve.
Kātyāyana says:

Now, regarding satisfaction (*tṛpti*): there is satisfaction for one month with cultivated herbs (or wild herbs); in their absence, they satisfy the ancestors with roots and fruits, or with water mixed with food. They should cook goats, sheep, and rams after they have been sacrificed; as for the remaining animals, one may purchase them, obtain them, or bring back those that died naturally. [With fish, for two months; with the meat of the *hāriṇa* deer, for three months; with the meat of birds, for four months; with the meat of the *raurava* deer, for five months; with goat meat, for six months; with tortoise meat, for seven months; with boar meat, for eight months; with sheep meat, for nine months; with buffalo meat, for ten months; with the meat of the spotted deer (*pārṣata*), for eleven months; [with cow's milk-rice (*pāyasa*) or milk, for a year; and with the meat of the *vārdhrīṇasa* (a white-footed antelope), for twelve years]. There is inexhaustible satisfaction from the rhinoceros, black pot-herbs (*kālaśāka*), the red goat, honey, and large-scaled fish; and likewise when the *śrāddha* is performed during the rains under the asterism Maghā or in the "elephant's shadow" (*hasticchāyā*).
‘Uttarāḥ’ refers to roots, fruits, and so forth; ‘usraḥ’ means a bull; ‘ālabdhāḥ’ means those that have been touched or seized.

[With sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, roots, fruits, vegetables, *śyāmāka* millet, *priyaṅgu*, *nīvāra* millet, mung beans, and wheat, they are gratified for one month. For two months with fish meat; for three months with the meat of the *hariṇa* deer; for four with the meat of the *aurabhra* sheep; for five with the meat of birds; for six with the meat of the goat; for seven with the meat of the *raurava* antelope; for eight with the meat of the *pārṣata* spotted deer; for nine with the meat of the *gavaya* wild ox; for ten with the meat of the buffalo; for eleven with the meat of the hornless goat; and for a year with cow's milk or its derivatives. Regarding this, there are also verses sung by the ancestors (*pitṛgītā gāthā*):
May we obtain black potherbs, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the Vārdhrīṇasa crane,
and rhinoceroses devoid of horns, until the end of time.
A *tūpara* is one that lacks horns even at the time when horns would normally appear.

Paiṭhīnasi says: "One gratifies [the ancestors] for a month with clarified butter; for two months with black pot-herbs (*kālaśāka*); for three months with barley-gruel, cakes, and parched grain; for four months with fish; for five months with goat-meat; for six months with milk-rice (*pāyasa*); for seven months with the meat of birds; for eight months with the meat of the *aiṇeya* deer; for nine months with beef; for eleven months with buffalo-meat; for twelve months with goat-meat; for thirteen months with the meat of the rhinoceros; and with a red-horned goat, [the gratification is] eternal."
With the phrase "they become satisfied" recurring [from the previous rule], Uśanas says:
for four months [one is satisfied] by the meat of the black-spotted antelope; for eight months by that of the boar; for nine by that of the ruru deer; and for ten by that of the sheep.

[45] Āpastamba [2.16.22–26; 2.17.1–3]: 22. "One should not eat food that has been brought by night from a house where the fire is kept, nor from a house where there is no fire, nor from a house where the Veda is not studied. 23. "Nor should one eat food that has been brought by day from a house where the fire is kept, if it has been placed on the ground and covered with a cloth. 24. "Nor should one eat food that has been brought from a house where the Veda is not studied, even if it is pure. 25. "Nor should one eat food that has been brought from a house where the fire is kept, if it has been placed on the ground and covered with a cloth, unless it is offered as a gift. 26. "Nor should one eat food that has been brought from a house where the Veda is not studied, even if it is pure. 1. "Now, regarding the rules for eating: one should eat facing the east, seated on a seat, having first sipped water, and having purified oneself. 2. "He should eat silently, without making a noise, and without scattering the food about. 3. "He should not eat with his head covered, nor with his feet crossed, nor while looking at the sun."

In this regard, the substances are sesame, beans, rice, barley, water, and roots and fruits. However, when the food is oily, the satisfaction of the ancestors is more intense and lasts for a much longer time. Likewise, with wealth acquired through righteous means and offered at a sacred site (*tīrtha*), the satisfaction lasts for a year; with beef, it lasts even longer than that; and with buffalo meat, it lasts even longer still. By this, the sacrificial purity of the meat of domestic and wild animals is explained. With rhinoceros meat served on a rhinoceros-skin mat, the satisfaction lasts for an infinite time; likewise with the meat of the *śatabali* fish and the *vārdhrāṇasa* crane.

‘Snehavati’ means with ghee and the like; in its absence, even with oil and so forth. ‘Tīvratarā’ means exceeding or pre-eminent. ‘Dharmāhṛtena’ means acquired through righteous means. ‘Pratipannena tīrthe’ means by means of wealth obtained during a pilgrimage to a sacred site (tīrthayātrā). ‘Khaḍgopastaraṇena’ refers to a seat made from a tiger skin.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Having acquired wealth through righteous means, one should give it to the ancestors. Śaṅkha says:
At the time of a śrāddha ceremony, one should cause to be offered mangoes, *pālevata* fruits, sugarcane, grapes, *bhavya* fruits, pomegranates, *vidārī* roots, and *bharuṇḍa* fruits.
One should diligently offer parched grain mixed with honey and groats with sugar at a śrāddha; one should also offer water chestnuts, lotus roots, and kebukā.

‘Pālevata’ is a fruit shaped like a citron (*jambīra*), well known in Kashmir as ‘voṭha’. ‘Mṛdvīkā’ is the grape. ‘Bhavya’ is the *karmaraṅga* (wood-apple). [46] ‘Vidārī’ refers to tubers. The author of the *Mañjarī* states that ‘bharuṇḍas’ are specific types of tubers originating in water. ‘Kebuka’ is a specific type of tuber resembling ginger; however, the prohibition regarding *kebuka* applies specifically to wild forest vegetables.
Hārīta says: But that which has been brought by Kṣatriyas according to the rules during a hunt,
and that which has been killed by lions or tigers, they praise at the time of a Śrāddha.
Manu [3.258]: The foods of sages, milk, soma, meat that is unseasoned,
and salt that is not alkaline— these are by their very nature called sacrificial oblations (havis).

‘Anupaskṛtam’ means unaltered; that is to say, not processed. ‘Akṣāralavaṇam’ refers to salt made from saline soil. However, if the negative particle (nañ) were connected after the dvandva compound ‘tat-lavaṇam’, then, because it would apply to both members of the compound, there would be a heaviness of meaning in the compound.
In the Mahābhārata (Anuśāsana-parvan 135.8),
Manu declared that a śrāddha offering in which sesame seeds increase becomes inexhaustible.
Likewise: "He who offers sesame seeds to the ancestors sacrifices with all desired objects;
however, a śrāddha with sesame seeds must never be given by one who lacks desire [to perform it]."
"Vardhamānatila" means abundant with sesame seeds. In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"With *śyāmāka* grains and sugarcane, [an offering] fulfills all desires for the ancestors."
He who performs the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice shall quickly attain success.
Know that those called *śyāmāka* and *hastin*, which have emerged from sacrifices,
as well as *prasātikā* and *priyaṅgu*, are to be accepted in the performance of the *śrāddha* rite.
These too would always be equal in quality to śyāmāka grains;
black beans, sesame seeds, barley, and rice would likewise be excellent.
Large barley, rice, and likewise barley, as well as *madhūlikā*,
black, white, and red [grains] should be taken for the performance of the *śrāddha* rite.
Bilva, āmalaka, mṛdvīkā, panasa, āmrātaka, pomegranate, bhavya, pārāvata, akṣoṭa, dates, and mangoes.
Kaseru, kovidāra, tālakanda, as well as bisa,
tamāla, śatakanda, gandhālū, and śītakandaka.
Kāleya, kālaśāka, suniṣaṇṇaka, suvarcalā, meat, vegetables, curd, milk, cañcu, and the juice of vetrāṅkura.
Kaṭphala, kaṅkaṇī, grapes, lakuca, and mocā; karkandhu, bhīraka, vāra, tiṇḍuka, and that which is called madhūka.
Vaikaṅkata, coconut, śṛṅgāṭaka, parūṣaka, long pepper,
black pepper, paṭola, and the fruit of bṛhatī.
Fragrant fish and meat, all varieties of peas,
and other such items that are savory and sweet.
And in this case, garlic and long radish should indeed be given.

‘Prasātikā’ refers to the grain known as *prasāṭī*, famous in the Middle Country (*Madhyadeśa*). ‘Mahāyavāḥ’ are large barley grains (*vaṇḍayava*). ‘Madhūlikā’ is a specific variety of *yavanāla* (millet); its further specifications are “black, white, and red. ‘Akṣoṭa’ is the fruit of the *pīlu* tree growing on mountains. ‘Kovidāra’ is a specific variety of white *kāñcanāra*. ‘Tālakanda’ is commonly known as *tālamūlī*. ‘Śatakanda’ is *śatāvarī*. ‘Śītakandaka’ is *śālūka* (lotus root). Regarding ‘Kāleya’, Govindarāja states it is a vegetable called *karālā*. ‘Suniṣaṇṇa’ is a water-born vegetable similar to *cāṅgerī*. ‘Suvarcalā’ is *sūryabhaktā*. ‘Cañcu’ is the vegetable commonly known as *ceñcu*. ‘Kaṭphala’ is simply the *kaṭphala* tree itself. ‘Kaṅkaṇī’ is a grape with a sour taste. ‘Moca’ is the fruit of the plantain (*kadalī*). ‘Karkandhu’ is a specific variety of jujube (*badarī*).
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Madhūka, asafoetida (rāmaṭha), camphor, black pepper, jaggery,
rock salt (saindhava), and cucumber (trapusa) are likewise recommended for the performance of śrāddha rites."
*rāmaṭha* is asafoetida (*hiṅgu*).
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* [32.10]:
"Barley, rice, wheat, sesame, mung beans, and mustard seeds..."
The priyaṅgu, kovidāra, and niṣpāva grains are exceedingly beautiful.
*Niṣpāva*s are *valla* beans, resembling pods, well known in the Deccan (*dakṣiṇāpatha*).
According to the *Vāyupurāṇa* (80.42–48):
"Among these foods, there are *karambha*, bricks, and *ghṛtapūraka*s."
Kṛsara, honey, clarified butter, milk, and milk-rice;
He who gives that which is unctuous and warm shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice,
as well as cow's curd mixed with various kinds of foods.
