Having given at a *śrāddha* during the rainy season and under the *Maghā* asterism, one does not grieve;
one should feed the Brahmins with clarified butter and pour clarified butter upon the ground.
Sugars mixed with milk and *pṛthuka* grains shall be eternally inexhaustible;
and for a year, one shall be delighted by fish, sheep, and deer.
One should serve and feed him barley meal, parched grain, cakes, and boiled grains with their condiments—
all prepared with clarified butter and seasoned with curd.
If one should offer those at ancestral rites (śrāddha), the ancestors will gratify him.

‘Karambha’ refers to parched barley flour mixed with curd. ‘One should pour out ghee upon the ground’ means that the vessel should be filled with ghee such that it overflows onto the ground. ‘Pṛthukas’ are flattened grains.
In the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"Whatever is mixed with honey, cow's milk, ghee, and milk-rice—this, when given, is said to be inexhaustible; so declare the ancestors, the deities of old."

Hārīta says: One desiring prosperity should perform the Śrāddha with sesame seeds; one desiring success with cakes; one desiring splendor with ghee, molasses, and sesame; one desiring good fortune or health with *paramānna* (milk-rice); and one desiring all desires with *kṛsara*, meat, curd, and barley-gruel.

In this context, regarding the materials for the *śrāddha*, where there is a connection with a specific fruit (*phala-viśeṣa*), there is an engagement by one who desires that secondary fruit (*guṇa-phala*). Where no such connection with a secondary quality exists, those items are obligatory (*nityavat*) as constituent parts; therefore, in their absence, the constituent parts of the *śrāddha* would simply not be accomplished. Foodstuffs that are fit for consumption, when prescribed in general terms, accomplish the essential nature of the *śrāddha* when prepared according to what is available. In their absence, however, one should take that which is neither prohibited nor specifically enjoined, provided it resembles the enjoined substance. That which is prohibited within the section on *śrāddha* must not be taken even as a substitute. But where there is a connection with a specific fruit, once that substance has accomplished the essential nature of the *śrāddha*, it also brings about its respective particular result. As for that which is prohibited—such as the meat of cows or buffaloes—and yet enjoined for the sake of a specific fruit, it should be taken only by one desiring that fruit, and not by one who does not desire it merely for the sake of accomplishing the essential nature of the *śrāddha*. However, in cases where the prescribed substance that performs the function is unavailable, meat from a buffalo and the like—which is both prescribed and prohibited in this very context—may be taken. Furthermore, the lesser or greater degree of satisfaction of the ancestors (*pitṛ-tṛpti*) resulting from that same substance should be understood as being determined in relation to the particular state of that very substance.
Now, those things to be avoided.
In this regard, Hārīta states:

Now, as for things to be avoided—one should not offer at a *śrāddha* the following: *pālaṅkyā*, *nālikā*, *pātīka*, *śigru*, *sṛmuka*, *vārtāka*, *bhūstṛṇa*, *kapela*, *māṣa*, *masūra*, and prepared salts.

*Śr̥muka* is a water-born vegetable of the *khadira* species. Regarding *bhūstṛṇa* and *kapelū*, the commentator on Hārīta states: "These are two specific types of vegetables, one domestic and the other wild, well-known in Kashmir. The prohibition of *māṣa* (beans) here refers specifically to the *gaura-māṣa* (white bean), because in the Vāyu Purāṇa, under the passage "māṣās tilāś ca," *māṣas* are prescribed as permissible. Viṣṇu [79.17–18]:

One should avoid long pepper (*pippalī*), *sṛmuka*, *bhūstṛṇa*, drumstick tree (*śigru*), mustard (*sarṣapa*), *surasa* [or *sarjaka*, *suvacala*], *kūṣmāṇḍa*, bottle gourd (*alābu*), eggplant (*vārtāka*), *pālaṅkyā* [or *podakī*], *taṇḍulīyaka*, *kusumbha*, *piṇḍāluka*, and buffalo milk. One should also avoid the speech of kings, liquor, food that has stood overnight, and prepared salts.
The *āsurī* is the black mustard seed (*rājasarṣapa*).
[52] Conch: One should avoid bhūstṛṇa, surasa, śigru, pālaṅkyā, sṛmuka, as well as kūṣmāṇḍa, alābu, vārtāka, and kovidāra.
One should avoid long pepper, black pepper, as well as the root of the piṇḍamūlaka plant, all prepared salt, and the tips of bamboo shoots.
One should avoid black gram, lentils, kodrava, koradūṣaka,
and red tree-exudations at the time of the śrāddha rite.
‘Surasa’ is *tulasī*. ‘Vaṃśāgra’ is the tip of a bamboo shoot. ‘Koradūṣaka’ is wild *kodrava* (paspalum scrobiculatum).
In the *Mahābhārata*:
“Grains unfit for ancestral rites (*aśrāddheya*) include *kodrava* as well as chickpeas (*caṇaka*).”
Among all substances, asafoetida, as well as bottle gourd and garlic, [are likewise forbidden].
Onions, saubhāñjanaka, as well as gṛñjanaka and the like,
kukkuṇḍakas, bottle gourds, and black salt;
The flesh of the village pig, that which has not been consecrated with sprinkling (aprokṣita),
black cumin, cumin, and likewise śītapākī;
Likewise, sprouts and the like, as well as water chestnuts, should be avoided here.
One should avoid all types of salt as well as rose-apple fruits;
likewise, one should avoid food that has been called out for or over which someone has wept during Śrāddha rites.

[53] ‘Kukkuṇḍakas’ are mushrooms—substances similar in nature to *chatrākas*, resembling small balls. ‘Black salt’ (*kṛṣṇa-lavaṇa*) is *sauvarcala*. ‘Black-born’ (*kṛṣṇāja*) is black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīraka*). ‘*Śītapākī*’ is *kākajaṅghā*. Regarding the phrase “among substances, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) is not to be offered,” the meaning is that asafoetida is prohibited when given in its own form. As for the prescription in the *Ādityapurāṇa* stating “*madhūka* and *rāmaṭha* (asafoetida),” that is because they serve as flavoring agents for other substances. The same applies to black pepper (*marīca*) and so forth.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "O best of the twice-born, one should avoid all kinds of grain for which the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice has not been performed, as well as kidney beans, *aṇu* grains, and lentils."
Hārīta says: Meat killed by means of poison or a disguise, that which is killed by a hunter or a beast of prey,
and that which is devoid of mantras— these they do not commend for a śrāddha rite.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "I shall now describe those things that must always be avoided in the rite of Śrāddha:
karambha and whatever else has its flavor or fragrance destroyed."
Resins not mentioned in the Vedas, salts from saline soil,
that which is foul-smelling or frothy, and likewise water from a stagnant pool.
Wherever a cow finds satisfaction at night, and whatever is collected at night—
including the milk of sheep, goats, camels, and all one-hoofed animals,
as well as that of buffaloes and yaks— all such milk should be avoided by the wise.
[54] ‘Palvala’ means a small pond.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa [32.18, 16–17]:
"Having said, 'Give this to me for the sake of the ancestors,' that which is offered—
even if it be milk— should always be avoided by the virtuous in the performance of the śrāddha rite."
Water that is foul-smelling, frothy, or from a small spring; that which has been discarded for all purposes, and that which comes from a reservoir unfit for consumption.
Therefore, dear one, that water must always be avoided in rites for the ancestors.
"Born from unfit food or drink" refers to water from a pond or similar body of water that has been used by those who have fallen [from their caste] or others of such status.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
lentils, hemp, peas, kidney beans, and horse gram;
The lotus (*padma*), *bilva*, *kadhattūra*, *pāribhadra*,

and *āḍharūṣaka* are not to be offered in rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*), nor is the milk of goats and sheep. Likewise, *kodrava*, *hāravara*, *ṭakka*, *kapittha*, *madhuka*, and *kākāsī* [are forbidden].
These too should not be given to the ancestors by one who desires their welfare.
‘Pāribhadra’ is well known as *pharahadda*. In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"That which has been twice cooked, thoroughly burnt, and likewise licked from the edge..."
And that which is defiled by gravel, insects, stones, and hair.
Oil-cake, buttermilk, as well as anything excessively salty, prepared foods, and snacks seasoned with salt before one's eyes; these are forbidden.
Those defiled by foul speech, as well as those struck down by the wicked,
and garments shaken off [by the wind], are to be avoided in the rite of Śrāddha.
One should avoid curd, vegetables, and solid foods that have turned sour, as well as those prepared without medicinal herbs;
likewise, one should avoid all fermented liquors.

‘Agrāvalehitam’ means that the first portion has been tasted. Regarding the phrase ‘siddhāḥ kṛtāś ca’ and so forth, the meaning is this: those prepared dishes in which salt was added subsequently, after they had already been cooked.
Now follows the examination of the brahmins.
Regarding this, Manu and Śātātapa state in the second [chapter]:
"In that regard, I shall declare in their entirety those best of the twice-born who are to be fed, those who are to be avoided, how many there are, and with what kinds of food."
One should examine from afar a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas;
he is considered a worthy recipient for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*, and he is remembered as a guest.
For where thousands upon thousands of those ignorant of the Ṛgveda may dine,
a single man who knows the mantras, being pleased, is worth all of them according to dharma.
The *kavyas* and *havis* offerings should be given to one who is preeminent in knowledge;
for hands smeared with blood are not purified by blood alone.

"Examination from afar" (*dūrātparīkṣā*) means an examination of one's ancestry, such as that of one's father and grandfather. "A sacred ford" (*tīrtha*) means, in this context, a cause for the attainment of results. "In giving, he is a guest": in this act of giving, he is to be honored like a guest. Yama says:
One should first examine the Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas.
Those who are purified of the defects arising from the body and have fulfilled their vows.
One should examine from afar those Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas,
whether they be liked or disliked, and bring them there at that time.

The word "previously" implies "prior to the invitation. Here, "desirable" and "undesirable" refer, for the time being, to objects of pleasure and displeasure; this is because of the prohibition against [inviting] both enemy and friend, as in the rule: "neither an enemy nor a friend.
Manu [3.149] states: "One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brāhmaṇa at a rite dedicated to the gods."
When a rite for the ancestors has arrived, one should examine [the recipient] with great care.
Having introduced the topic with the statement, "One should feed those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and so forth, and one should not feed those such as the *durvāla*," Gautama [states]:
"And likewise regarding sacrificial offerings (*havis*); in the case of a *śrāddha*, each of these [categories], beginning with the *durvāla*, [is excluded]."
"In *haviḥṣu*," meaning among the sacrificial offerings (*havya*), specifically those intended for the gods; as Manu [3.118] states:
"Sacrificial offerings (*havya*) and ancestral oblations (*kavya*) must be given by donors only to one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*)."
What is given to that brahmin who has attained arhatship yields great fruit.
Vasiṣṭha [3.8]:
That which is given to one who is not learned in the Vedas reaches neither the ancestors nor the deities.
Manu and Śātātapa state in the second [chapter]:
"A sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) given according to the rules to learned men makes both the givers and the recipients partakers of the fruit, both in this world and after death. (Manu 3.133, 135, 136)
One should diligently feed at the śrāddha a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Veda,
or an Adhvaryu who has reached the end of his branch, or a Chandoga who has completed his study.
If any one of these, being duly honored, should eat at someone's *śrāddha*,
the satisfaction of that person's ancestors shall be eternal, extending through seven generations.
‘Samāptigam’ refers to one who has studied all the Vedic branches (*śākhā*). Yama states:
“Either a Bahvṛca (Rigvedin) who knows the *Trisauparṇa*, or a Chandoga (Sāmavedin) who sings the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*.”
Whether he be a practitioner of the five fires, a knower of the four Vedas, or one who has offered the "head of Brahmā" sacrifice;
One who knows the self, one who knows the constituent parts, and likewise the son of a woman wedded according to the Brahma rite—
all these would be [eligible], whether they possess all [the qualities] as prescribed or even just a single portion thereof.
Three ancestors and three descendants, with oneself as the seventh among them—
all these seven persons together consume that food.

The *triṣauparṇa* is characterized by the three verses beginning with "suparṇa" and "the fourfold young woman, well-formed. A *jyeṣṭhasāmaga* is one who studies the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*. A *pañcāgni* is one who studies the mantras that illuminate the five fires. A *brahmaśīrṣaka* is one who studies the *Atharvaśiras*. A *brahmadeyā* is a woman married according to the *Brāhma* rite of marriage.
Bṛhaspati says: If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, one should feed a Chāndoga there;
for the threefold collection—the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda—is contained within him.
One might wander the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves,
searching for one who contemplates the syllables of the *sāmans* for the sake of the ancestors.

The father is satisfied by the *ṛc* verse, the grandfather by the *yajus* formula, and the great-grandfather by the *sāman* chant; the master of the *chandas* (the Sāmavedin) is even more superior than that.
[59] Yama and Śātātapa state: One should feed a Chandoga at a Śrāddha and a Vaiśvadeva rite;
an Adhvaryu at a rite for prosperity (puṣṭikarma); and an Atharvaṇa at a rite for pacification (śāntikarma).
Śātātapa says:
"Whoever feeds one learned in the Atharva Veda at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors, his reward is indeed infinite and imperishable; such is the sacred revelation."
But he who feeds another at a śrāddha while Atharvan priests are present—
his deities, together with the ancestors, depart disappointed.
Therefore, with every effort, one should feed an Atharvavedin at the time of a śrāddha during offerings to the gods and ancestors; that [offering] for the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.

Manu [3.124–125]: "Some twice-born men are devoted to knowledge, others likewise are devoted to austerity; some are devoted to the study of the Vedas and knowledge, and others are devoted to ritual action."
Offerings to the ancestors (kavya) should be diligently established among those devoted to knowledge,
while offerings to the gods (havya) should be presented according to the śrāddha rites even among these same four classes.
If the father is unlearned in the Vedas but his son has mastered the Vedas—
or if the son is unlearned in the Vedas but the father has mastered them—
one should know that the one whose father is learned in the Vedas is the superior of the two.
But for the sake of honoring the mantra, the other person deserves hospitality.
[60] Yājñavalkya [1.219, 221]: One who is foremost in all the Vedas, a learned scholar (*śrotriya*), a knower of Brahman, young,
a knower of the meaning of the Vedas, a master of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, and one who knows the *Trimadhu* and *Trisuparṇa* [hymns].

Those Brahmins who are devoted to ritual action, devoted to austerity, those who maintain the five fires, lifelong students, and those dedicated to their fathers and mothers, are the perfection of the Śrāddha.

"Foremost" means excellent. "The *trimadhu*" refers to a specific portion of the *Ṛgveda* and its associated vow; because of that connection, the person who practices it is also so designated. Regarding the instruction "one should feed [them]," Gautama [15.9–11] states:
"Those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) who are endowed with eloquence, beauty, age, and good character; among these, gifts should first be given to the young."
Some say it is like that of a father.

"Versed in the Vedas" (*śrotriyān*) means those who have studied the *chandas*. "Endowed with speech" (*vāksaṃpannān*) means those who speak refined Sanskrit. "Endowed with beauty" (*rūpasaṃpannān*) means those of pleasing form. "Endowed with age" (*vayaḥsaṃpannān*) means those who are not children. "Endowed with character" (*śīlasaṃpannān*) means those whose mind, speech, and body are rightly disciplined. Even among those endowed with age, "giving to the young" (*yuvabhyo dānam*) is "first," meaning primary; for this is the first rule, namely that giving should be to the young—this is the sense. "Some [say] like the father": some hold the view that one should feed those of the same age as one's deceased father and other ancestors.
Vasiṣṭha [11.16–17]:

One should offer to the ancestors during the dark fortnight after the fourth day. Having assembled on the previous day Brahmans who are ascetics, householders, or virtuous men of middle age, who do not engage in improper acts, who are learned in the Vedas, and who are neither pupils nor resident disciples.

"Having assembled" means having brought together. "The virtuous" (sādhu) refers to those whose defects have been exhausted. "Others residing in the stages of life" (āśramastha) who are "not engaged in improper acts" (avikarmastha), meaning those whose actions are not censurable. "Non-disciples" (aśiṣya) refers to resident pupils (antevāsinaḥ) who, having completed their studies, have returned from the presence of their teacher.

Kātyāyana says: On that day, one should invite Brāhmaṇas; or on the preceding day. Some say [one should invite] Snātakas; others, ascetics (yatins), householders, or virtuous men; specifically those learned in the Vedas (śrotriyas) who are blameless and established in their own duties. In the absence of such, even students of good conduct may be invited.

Āpastamba [2.17.10]: "Among those of equal qualities, one who is advanced in age is more distinguished; and among those of equal qualities, one who is destitute of wealth and desires [the materials for the rite] is more distinguished. The meaning is that, among those of equal qualities, a poor man seeking the materials for the Śrāddha is more distinguished.

Manu [4.31]: One should honor with offerings to the gods and the ancestors those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) who have completed their Vedic studies and vows and have come to one's house; however, one should avoid those who are the opposite.

Yama said: Those who have completed their studies with the Vedas, the sciences, and vows; who are learned in the Vedas and have mastered them; who are devoted to their own duties, patient, observant of ritual acts, and ascetic.
To them, when they are tranquil, offerings to the gods (havya) and offerings to the ancestors (kavya) are presented;
not to those who sell the Vedas or who look for flaws in the duties of others.
Āpastamba [2.15.11].
In all ritual acts, one should feed those who are pure and learned in the mantras.
Paiṭhīnasi states:
"To one who is self-restrained and pure, the *havya* and *kavya* offerings should be given in all circumstances; therefore, one is known as 'pure'."

In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "One who is omniscient, eloquent in speech, a performer of sacrifices, endowed with knowledge, learning, and noble lineage; a knower of the Purāṇas, a knower of dharma, wise, and devoted to the study of the Vedas."
A devotee of Śiva, devoted to his ancestors, a devotee of the Sun, or a Vaiṣṇava;
a Brāhmaṇa who is a knower of Yoga, peaceful, self-conquered, and possessed of virtuous conduct.
One should also diligently feed one's daughter's son, one's father-in-law, one's guru, the husband of one's sister,
one's maternal uncle, a kinsman, a sacrificial priest, a preceptor, and those who have drunk the soma juice.
‘Viṭpatiḥ’ means the son-in-law.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "One who is free from greed is superior to those endowed with noble lineage and Vedic learning;
and even over those two types of Brahmins, one who has resided there for a long time is superior."
Yama says: That which is eaten by those Brahmins who do not specify the lunar mansion, the lunar day, the auspicious day, the muhūrta, or the auspicious omens, becomes indeed inexhaustible.
Those who purify the company at a meal.
Devala says: One should avoid those among the Brahmins who are unworthy of the company at a row (apāṅkteya) when it comes to offerings to the gods and ancestors (havya-kavya).
Having examined the Brahmins in many ways, one should invite those who purify the company (paṅktipāvana).
In this regard, Manu (3.173–176) says:
"Learn in their entirety those foremost of the twice-born, the purifiers of the row, by whom a row defiled by one unworthy of the company is purified."
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions,
and who are born of a lineage of Vedic scholars, should be known as the purifiers of the assembly.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisauparṇa hymns, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one born of a lineage that has maintained the Brahma-gift, one who knows the Dharma, and one who chants the Jyeṣṭha-sāman.
One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a reciter, a celibate student, one who bestows a thousand [cows],
and one who has reached a hundred years of age— these Brāhmaṇas are to be known as purifiers of the assembly.
The *triṇāciketa* is a portion of the Adhvaryu Veda and its associated vow; because of his connection with that, the person is also so designated.
[64] Yama said: Those who drink the Soma juice, who are free from passion, who know the Dharma, whose intellects are tranquil,
who observe vows, who abide by their restraints, and who approach their wives only during the proper season;
Even one who maintains the five fires is indeed a knower of the Yajurveda if he is a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Trisauparṇa or the Trimadhu.
One who has performed the Triṇāciketa sacrifice, one who is free from passion, a singer of the Chandas, a chanter of the Jyeṣṭhasāman,
and one who studies the Atharvaśiras— these are all purifiers of the assembly.
Even a child who maintains the sacred fire, one who knows the Nyāya system, one who knows the six Vedāṅgas,
one who knows the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, and whoever else is a reciter of the Dharma;
The Ṛṣivratin, the Ṛṣīka, likewise the Dvādaśavārṣika,
the son of a Brahmadeya woman, the Garbhaśuddha, and the Sahasrada;
He was one who observed the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, a speaker of truth, a knower of the Purāṇas,
proficient in all branches of learning, tranquil, and free from sin.
Devoted to the worship of the guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, intent upon knowledge,
liberated from all things, steadfast, and become one with Brahman— he is the best of the twice-born.
One who has no enemies and no friends, who is friendly and a knower of the Self,
who is a *snātaka*, devoted to silent recitation, and always a giver of flowers and fruit.
He was upright, compassionate, patient, self-controlled, tranquil, devoted to truth, pure, a knower of the Vedas,
a knower of all the scriptures, and dedicated to fasting.
A householder, a celibate student, and one who knows the four Vedas;
Brāhmaṇas who have completed their Vedic studies and vows—these are the purifiers of the assembly.
Those twice-born who are devoted to the practices of celibacy, though emaciated and of meager means, have transcended all unrighteousness; they are the purifiers of the assembly.
Those Brahmins who are engaged in sacrificial sessions, established in their observances, and well-versed in the Vedas;
And those twice-born ones who have desisted from harming living beings are purifiers of the assembly;
they are devoted to the fire-sacrifice, tranquil, compassionate, and free from envy.
Those twice-born ones who are free from attachment to receiving gifts,
who are truthful, steadfast, and always devoted to giving, are purifiers of the assembly.
And those twice-born ones who are endowed with auspicious conduct are purifiers of the assembly;
indeed, they were created by the gods of old as gods upon the surface of the earth.
Whatever is given to these [brahmins] for the sake of the ancestors or the gods becomes inexhaustible;
one should examine brahmins who have observed their vows from afar alone.
Whether they be elders, ascetics, self-controlled, or experts in other [fields],
one should feed all of them at the śrāddha and invite them with kindness.
Likewise: "The learned, those of good vows, the peaceful Brāhmaṇas who purify the company—what they eat causes [the offering] to go to the gods; what they eat causes it to go to the ancestors."

"An *ṛṣīka* is one who is slightly inferior to a *ṛṣi*. A *dvādaśavārṣika* is one who has observed the Vedic vows for twelve years. According to Medhātithi, a *sahasrada* is a giver of a thousand cows. 'Released from all [debts]'—the word 'debts' (*ṛṇa*) is to be understood as the remainder. 'Without enemies' means free from foes. 'Nor a friendless man' means not being an enemy to anyone. 'Friendly' means possessing friendliness. 'Compassionate' means merciful. Śaṅkha says: 'One whose lineage is the gift of Brahman' means one who does not withhold the gift of Brahman."
The lord of a gift of land made to Brahmins, and those Brahmins who purify the assembly;
Those Brahmins who have mastered the Yajus, those who have mastered the Samans,
and those who study the Atharvaśiras are purifiers of the assembly.

O Brahmins, those who are constantly devoted to sacrifice, who regard a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, and who are wise ascetics established in meditation— these are the purifiers of the assembly.
Hārīta says:

Stability, unbroken knowledge of the Vedas, non-confusion of the *yoni* (lineage), and possession of Vedic ancestry (*ārṣeya*)—these are the qualities of family (*kulaguṇa*). The Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, Dharma, the inner self (*adhyātma*), specialized knowledge (*vijñāna*), and stability—this is the sixfold sacred learning (*śruta*). Reverence for Brahmins, devotion to gods and ancestors, equanimity, gentleness, non-injuring others, absence of envy, mildness, lack of harshness, friendliness, pleasant speech, gratitude, providing refuge, and tranquility—this is the thirteenfold conduct (*śīla*). Forbearance, self-restraint, compassion, charity, non-violence, worship of gurus, purity, bathing, recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), austerity (*tapas*), study of one’s own branch of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), truthfulness, contentment, and firmness in vows—this is the sixteenfold observance (*vṛtta*). Those who are of noble birth, learned, virtuous, established in their vows, truthful, free from physical defects, and worthy of the *pāṅkta* (invited to a feast)—these are the qualified guests. Those who are learned in both branches of the Veda (*ubhayataḥ-śrotriya*) on twelve points; those who have mastered the *Nāciketa*, *Madhu*, *Suparṇa*, and *Triśīrṣa* hymns; those who sing the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*; those who maintain the five fires (*pañcāgni*); those who know the six Vedāṅgas; those who mutter the *Rudra* hymns; those who are celibate (*ūrdhvaretas*); those who approach their wife only during her season (*ṛtukālābhigāmin*); and those who know the reality (*tattvavit*)—these are the sanctifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*). Now, they cite an illustration here: [The text continues with the illustrative verses.]
He in whose house there are the five fires— the pacana and the pācana, along with the tretā—
and which blaze forth every evening and morning, that brahmin is a purifier of the assembly.
[68] They say that one who possesses the aforementioned qualities is equal to a thousand *snātakas*;
one endowed with qualities such as maintaining the five fires (*pañcāgni*) is said to be equal to a hundred thousand.
Whether it be a single verse or even an entire row extending for a *yojana*,
a Brahmin learned in the Vedas who is appointed to the head of the row purifies it all.

The twelve [persons] to be mentioned below, beginning with the *śrotriya*, are [qualified] on both sides. "The cooking fire" (*pacana*) is the *āvasathya* fire; "the digestion fire" (*pācana*) is the *sabhya* fire. "Endowed with the aforementioned qualities" means possessed of the qualities previously described. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Now, those worthy of the *pāṅkta* [feast] are: one who knows the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*), one who maintains the five fires (*pañcāgni*), a learned reciter (*anūcāna*), one engaged in legal affairs, a *śrotriya*, one who has thrice kindled the *Nāciketa* fire, one who knows the three *Madhu* verses, one who knows the three *Sāuparṇa* verses, a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, one who performs the twilight ablutions (*sandhyā-snāyin*), one devoted to the Veda, one who constantly maintains the sacred fires, one who serves his mother and father, and one who knows the *Dharmaśāstra*."

An *anūcāna* is one who has studied the Vedic recitation along with its supplements (*prāsaṅga*). A *vyavahārī* is one whose habit is the practice of the scriptures. A *sadāgnika* is one whose daily obligatory rites (*nityakṛtya*) have not been interrupted. (Vasiṣṭha 3.19)

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa, one who has performed the four Medha sacrifices, a follower of the Vājasaneyi school, one learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one in the direct line of descent from a Brahmin who received a gift of knowledge, a Chāndoga, a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāman, one who knows both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas, and one who studies his own specific duties; furthermore, those whose maternal and paternal lineages extend ten generations back and are known to be learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), wise, and *snātaka*s—they are the purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*).
"Caturmedhī" refers to one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; for in that [sacrifice], four "medhas"—namely the Vaiśvadeva and the others—are performed.

Uśanas says: In that regard, those who purify the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*) are as follows: a Brāhmaṇa who has completed his studies and vows (*vedavidyāvratasnātaka*), whose conduct and moral boundaries have remained unbroken through five generations; one who has performed the *triṇāciketa*, *trimadhu*, and *trisuparṇa* rites; one learned in the Vedic meters (*chandovid*); a singer of the *jyeṣṭhasāman*; one who is a hundred years old and has not neglected the study of the Dharma; one devoted to the recitation and teaching of the *mantra-prabhṛti-jāpyas*; one who approaches his wife only during her fertile period (*ṛtukāla*); and one who is pure for ten generations on both paternal and maternal sides—such a person is a *snātaka*. These are the purifiers of the assembly.

Now, those who sanctify the company (*paṅktipāvana*): one who has performed the *triṇāciketa* rite; one who maintains the five fires (*pañcāgni*); one who chants the *jyeṣṭhasāman*; one who has mastered the Vedas (*vedapāraga*); one who has mastered even a single auxiliary of the Veda (*vedāṅga*); one who has mastered the *Purāṇas*, *Itihāsas*, and grammar; [one who has mastered even a single treatise on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*)]; one purified by sacred fords (*tīrtha*); one purified by sacrifice (*yajña*); [one purified by austerity (*tapas*)]; one purified by truth (*satya*); one purified by charity (*dāna*); one purified by mantras (*mantra*); one devoted to the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*; one in the lineage of those to whom a Brahmanic gift was given (*brahmadeyānusaṃtāna*); one who knows the *Trisauparṇī* hymns; a son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*); and a daughter’s son (*dauhitra*)—these are worthy recipients (*pātra*). And especially so are the practitioners of Yoga (*yogin*). On this subject, there is a verse sung by the ancestors (*pitṛgītā*):
Perhaps there may be someone in our family who would diligently feed a yogi— a brahmin at a śrāddha— by which we ourselves might be satisfied.

In the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "He who expounds the sacred word, he who investigates the sacrifice, and he who knows the rules for the melodies of the Sāman— these are the purifiers of those who purify the assembly."
A girl who is given in marriage at eight years of age to one endowed with learning and virtuous conduct is Gaurī; her son is Gaura, the purifier of those who purify the assembly.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "But the ascetic (yati) shall be the first to eat among all brahmins;
he who is the best of the twice-born should recite the Vedas, with the Itihāsas as the fifth."
Immediately thereafter, he who is striving should be appointed by one who knows; after him, a knower of the three Vedas; after him, a knower of two Vedas;
after that, a knower of one Veda; and after that, one who is constantly engaged in study.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "A knower of the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), a practitioner of the yoga of knowledge, one who knows the true nature of sacrifice,
a Brahmin who seeks no unsolicited gifts, or one who knows the ritual procedure for the *śrāddha*."
One who has mastered even a single one of the eighteen branches of knowledge,
who is purified in three ways, who knows the Trisauparṇa hymns, who maintains the five sacred fires, and who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman;
[71] He who has been purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa or Parāka penances and observances,
and who knows the treatise on statecraft (nītiśāstra) of Bṛhaspati as well as the science of grammar (śabdavidyā);
And he who is always purified by the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
Even while performing what ought not to be done, he is superior to a hundred purifiers;
what need is there for much speaking here? He is a knower of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
In former times, both of them were students of the Atharvaśiras;
having performed austerities, they became renowned for their ancestral rites through the power of yoga.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "A single yogin excels over a thousand householders, a hundred forest-dwellers, and a thousand students."
Whether one is an atheist, one who performs forbidden acts, one of mixed caste, or even a thief—
Prajāpati has declared that there is no other qualification for giving to yogis.
The ancestors of that man are gratified, just as farmers are by a timely rain,
if he feeds one who meditates, whether it be a son or even a grandson.
"This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*;
but this secondary rule (*anukalpa*) should be known as that which is always practiced by the virtuous."

One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, one's own father-in-law, a preceptor, a daughter’s son, the husband of a sister, a kinsman, as well as the officiating priest and the person for whom one performs sacrifices.
[72] Immediately after those who purify the company—Baudhāyana [2.14.3–4]:

In their absence, one who knows the secret doctrines (rahasyavid). The greatness of the Śrāddha consists of the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants. Therefore, one should feed even a Sapiṇḍa who possesses such knowledge.
Āpastamba [2.17.4–6]:

One should feed Brāhmaṇas who know the Veda, provided they are not related by birth, lineage, mantra, or pupilage. However, if others possess deficient qualities, even a uterine brother who is endowed with good qualities should be fed. By this, pupils are also explained.

In continuation of the phrase "he should not feed [them]," Gautama [Dharmasūtra 15.19–21] states: "Some say he may feed his pupils and those of the same lineage (sagotra). He should feed at least three; [he may also feed] one who possesses excellent qualities."
Vasiṣṭha [11.18]:
One should also feed disciples who possess good qualities.

[73] *Mahābhārata* [Anuśāsana-parvan 61.24–25, 30–31]: "O King, even those who are farmers, provided they have observed their vows, are endowed with virtues, know the *Sāvitrī*, and perform the prescribed rites— they are worthy of being invited."
One may indeed appoint a twice-born man of noble birth who follows the dharma of the warrior class as a representative in battle;
but one should never, my dear, designate a merchant for the śrāddha rites.
Even one who is vowless, a gambler, a thief, or a seller of living beings,
if he has subsequently drunk the Soma juice, he too is worthy of the sacrificial feast.
Having acquired abundant wealth through harsh agricultural labors, one may later become a host to all guests; such a person, O King, is worthy of being invited.
Now, those who are to be avoided.
Regarding this, Manu [3.138–141] states:
"One should not feed a friend at a śrāddha; his acquisition should be made through wealth. One should feed at the śrāddha that twice-born man whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend."
He whose funeral offerings and oblations are primarily for the sake of friends.
For him, there is no fruit after death, neither in the ancestral rites (śrāddha) nor in the sacrificial oblations (havis).
That lowest of the twice-born who, out of delusion, forms friendships with those who perform śrāddha, falls from heaven and from the world— being a friend to śrāddha [only for gain].
That which is called a communal feast is declared by the twice-born to be a Piśāca-like sacrificial gift;
it remains right here in this world like a blind cow in a single house.
*Saṃbhojanī*: that by which one eats together.
"One may, at will, honor a friend at a *śrāddha*, but never an enemy, even if he be worthy."
For an oblation consumed by one who harbors hatred becomes fruitless after death.
Manu and Yama state in the first [section]:
"For a Brahmin who has not studied the Veda is extinguished like a fire of straw;
one should not offer an oblation to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes."
Just as a sower who has sown seed in barren soil does not obtain fruit,
so too a donor who gives an oblation to one ignorant of the Ṛgveda does not obtain fruit.
[75] Vasiṣṭha [3.12]: Those Śrāddhas which the ignorant eat when they ought to be eaten by the learned— those bring about drought, or a great danger arises.
Manu, Yama, and Śātātapa state:
"As many morsels as one who is ignorant of the mantras swallows during offerings to the gods and ancestors,
so many glowing spikes, spears, and iron balls shall he swallow after death."
Hārīta says:
Even those who are endowed with learning and noble lineage, if they are of base conduct, are the lowest of men;
indeed, because their bodies are difficult to obtain, they are remembered as being evil-minded.
Those who are constantly devoted to honey are proclaimed as Yātudhānas;
thus do these lowest of men always go because of their many sins.
Those who kill birds, fish, and deer, those who slay snakes and tortoises,
and those who are addicted to the slaughter of various living beings— these indeed are declared to be wicked Brahmins.
Likewise:
"A servant of a Śūdra, one maintained by the king, a Vṛṣala who officiates for a village,
and one who lives by killing or imprisoning— these six are kinsmen of Brāhmaṇas in name only."
"Kṣaudra" refers to base actions, such as the killing of living beings and the like. "Of the body" means of the human body. "Brahmabāndhavas" are the lowest of the twice-born.
Yama says:
He whose Veda and sacrificial altar have been lost for three generations is indeed called a "degraded Brahmin," as is he who is the husband of a *vṛṣalī*.

[76] Uśanas: Manu has declared that those who have fallen from their status due to a specific cause have been designated; for these are sellers of the Veda, and one should never feed them at *śrāddha* rites.
"Taught according to the truth" means teaching [the texts] as they actually are.
Likewise,
Manu has declared those who perform sacrifices for unworthy persons, those who sell the Vedas, and those born of women previously married to others to be outcasts.
"Those who teach the unrefined and those who teach for a fee enter into terrible darkness," so said Vaivasvata.
"Unrefined" means "not brought [into the assembly] here. Following the word "should invite," Kātyāyana states:
"Twice, excluding those who are naked, white, moist, black-toothed, pierced [in the genitals], diseased, deformed, leprous, afflicted with skin disease, or having deformed nails."

"Double-naked" means one who lacks the religious observances (*vidharma*). "White" means excessively fair-skinned. "Wet-skin" means afflicted with scabies or similar skin diseases. "With pierced generative organ" refers to a specific deformity of the penis well known in the South.

Gautama [15.15–19]: "Because there is no contradiction with the Veda, because it is not seen that there is any other means of knowledge for this, because there is no difference from the case of the Veda, and because it is accepted by all, the Smṛti is authoritative. [15.16] "If it were argued that it is not authoritative because it contradicts the Veda, we say: no, because there is no contradiction. For the Smṛti is authoritative when it does not contradict the Veda. [15.17] "If it were argued that there is contradiction because the Smṛti prescribes actions that are impossible to perform, we say: no, because those actions are indeed possible to perform. For instance, the Smṛti prescribes the performance of the *Aṣṭakā* and other rites; these are certainly possible to perform. [15.18] "Furthermore, since there is no other means of knowledge for this [the Dharma], and since there is no difference from the case of the Veda, and since it is accepted by all, the Smṛti is authoritative. Just as the Veda is authoritative because it is not seen that there is any other means of knowledge for it, so too is the Smṛti. [15.19] "And because it is accepted by all—by all those who are learned in the tradition and free from passion—the Smṛti is authoritative."

One should not feed a thief, a eunuch, one who has fallen from his caste, an atheist, one who lives by such [forbidden] means, one who has killed a hero, one whose younger brother marries before him (*agredidhiṣū*), one whose elder brother’s wife marries him (*didhiṣūpati*), one who sacrifices for a village, a non-reciter (*ajapāla*), one who has abandoned the sacred fires, a drinker of intoxicants, a rogue, a false witness, a usurer, one who has a paramour, one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*, a seller of Soma, an arsonist, a poisoner, one who has broken the vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), a servant of a group, one who approaches a woman who should not be approached, a violent man, an elder brother whose younger brother marries before him (*parivitti*), a younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*), one for whom the marriage rites are performed in reverse order (*paryāhita*), one who performs them in reverse order for another (*paryādhātṛ*), one who has abandoned himself, one who is weak, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, the son of a remarried woman, a gambler, one defeated in a lawsuit, a servant of a king, a counterfeit-maker, the husband of a Śūdra woman, one who has renounced the Vedas (*nirākṛti*), one suffering from leprosy, a usurer, a merchant, one who lives by crafts, and those habitually addicted to gambling, instrumental music, clapping, dancing, and singing. Nor should one feed those divided against their father’s will, nor—according to some—the disciples of the same lineage (*sagotra*).

‘One who lives by that’ (tadvṛttiḥ) is one who subsists on the wealth of those who have fallen [from their caste]. ‘A priest for women or a village-priest’ (strī-grāma-yājakaḥ) is one who performs sacrifices for women or for a multitude of people without distinction. ‘A drinker of intoxicants’ (madyapaḥ) is a consumer of intoxicants other than *surā* (distilled liquor), since the drinker of *surā* is already included under the term “fallen” (*patita*). ‘A rogue’ (kucaraḥ) is one of reprehensible conduct. ‘A juggler’ (prātihārikaḥ): *pratihāra* means a magical trick; one who lives by that is a juggler. Regarding the phrase “and he whose”: it means “he who has a paramour,” that is, he whose wife is unchaste. ‘One who commits suicide’ (ātmatyāgī) is a reckless person. ‘The weak’ (*durbala*) here refers to a eunuch. ‘One who does not mutter prayers’ (*ajapaḥ*) is one devoid of the recitation of mantras. ‘A counterfeit dealer’ (*prātirūpikaḥ*) is a seller of adulterated goods. ‘A leper’ (*kilāsī*) is one afflicted with *sidhma* (scrofula). ‘One addicted to weapons’ (*jyāśīlaḥ*) is one devoted to the practice of arms.

Yājñavalkya [1.222–224]: One who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is blind in one eye, one born of a remarried woman, one who has broken his vow of chastity, a *kuṇḍa* or a *golaka*, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth; The *kuṇḍa* is the son born to a woman while her husband is still living, by another man; the *golaka* is the son born to a widow by another man. A *kunakha* is one whose nails are deformed. A *śyāvadantaka* is one whose teeth are black. These are excluded from the *sapiṇḍa* relationship. Those who are excluded from the *sapiṇḍa* relationship are not entitled to inherit property. However, they should be supported by the family out of compassion. If they are not supported, they become outcasts (*patita*). Thus says Yājñavalkya.
One who teaches for hire, a eunuch, one who defiles a maiden, one who is accused of a grave crime,
a betrayer of friends, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, and one who reviles others.

One who abandons his mother, father, or teacher; one who eats food from a *kuṇḍa* (an illegitimate son born of adultery); the son of a *vṛṣala* (a low-caste man); the husband of a woman previously married to another—these and others whose actions are corrupt are censured.
Yama said: The gods do not eat the food of a slanderer, nor do they eat that of one who speaks untruth;
they do not eat the food of one conquered by his wife, nor of one in whose house lives a paramour.
The ancestors do not partake of the sacrificial offering from one who has grown coarse hair, nor from one wearing a red undergarment, nor from one whose ears extend beyond two finger-breadths.
One should designate those who possess these characteristics as unfit for the company;
however, one should employ those who are free from these inauspicious defects.
Devala said:

Those who kill a cow, their master, one who trusts them, an ascetic, or a friend; those who abandon their mother, father, son, wife, or the sacred fire; those who destroy a sacrifice; the husband of a *vṛṣalī*; a seller of Soma; an apostate (*vrātya*); and one who neglects his religious duties—these are the fallen (*patita*). The paramour and his wife’s lover; one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* or *golaka*; the husband of a woman whose husband is living or of a younger sister married before the elder; one who teaches for wages; one who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to offer them; a sacrificer; a seller of the Veda, of dharma, or of impure goods; a miser; one who causes the confusion of castes; an ignoble man; one who has fallen away from purity; one who is unfortunate; a temple-priest (*devalaka*); a usurer; a divider of the lineage; the younger brother who marries before the elder (*parivitti*); the elder brother whose younger brother marries first (*parivettṛ*); one who is black-backed; a professional soldier; one who lives off others; one who has violated his vow of chastity; a barbarian; an inferior person; one who performs rituals for hire; one who sets fire to forests or houses; the six kinds of eunuchs (*klība*); and these are the secondary sinners (*upapātakin*). Those who have no offspring; a false witness; one who destroys virility; one conquered by women; a destroyer of bridges; a musician; one who lives by the stage; a reciter of heterodox scriptures; a fraudulent performer of penances; a rogue; a violent man; a hunter; a gambler; an atheist; a slanderer; a rogue; a merchant; a bard; the son of a remarried woman; one who lives off himself; a shell-blower; one who travels by sea; one habituated to malevolent magic; a member of a secret society; one who rides a dog; a physician; a hired servant; a defiler of maidens; an ungrateful person; a cruel man; a magician; one who betrays friends; one who squanders what has been given; a breaker of agreements; one harsh in speech or punishment; a carpenter; an artisan; an elephant-rider; and horse-grooms—these are to be avoided as those who cause a fall (*pātanīyaka*). Those afflicted by the eight foul diseases, those with impaired senses, and those with missing or extra limbs are defilers of the assembly line (*paṅktidūṣaka*). The eight foul diseases are: insanity, skin disease, consumption, asthma, diabetes, fistula, abdominal dropsy, and dysentery. Those with impaired senses are the mentally dull, the blind, the one-eyed, the deaf, and the one with a withered arm. Malformed wounds result from both types of discharge and moisture. These are the most sinful of all.
These five types of lowest of men have been declared as those to be avoided;
they possess their own specific characteristics, and the distinction among them will be stated here.
All these have been declared in succession as "bad Brahmins," who are contemptible due to their actions, their birth, and the defects of their bodies.
Those lowest of men who have fallen due to the fault of their actions go to terrible hells,
abandoned even here by the virtuous.
Those who are afflicted by defects of the womb, as well as those with defects born of the body—
even if they are innocent— should be avoided right here in this world.
The ungrateful, the slanderer, the cruel, the nihilist, the deceiver, the rogue,
and the betrayer of friends— all these, by their very nature, have hell as their abode.
Furthermore, all such persons shall be unfit for food and unworthy of participating in ritual acts;
they are excluded from the state of Brahman, being subject to the power of their sinful faults.

A *tālāvacaraṇa* is one who lives by playing cymbals. A *vidharmapāṭhaka* is a reciter of practices not ordained by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*; he is a *puṣkasa*. A *melaka* is one who lives by killing deer. A *śvayuk* is a dog-fancier. A *dattāpavyayī* is one who squanders what has been given. One who is harsh in speech and punishment (*vāgdaṇḍaparuṣaḥ*) is fierce in both word and rod. An *aśvabandha* is one who ties up horses for the purpose of selling them. A *kuṇi* is one with a defective hand. Furthermore, others such as the king’s domestic priest (*purohita*) and so forth have already been defined by the authors of the *Smṛtis*; we shall mention them later.
Thus are those to be avoided.
Now, those who are unworthy of the company at a meal (apāṅkteya).
In that regard, Yama says: "Listen as I declare those other twice-born men who are excluded from the company at meals;
gifts given to them do not perform their function for the gods or the ancestors."
The one-eyed, the pot-bellied, the eunuchs, the ungrateful, those who violate the teacher’s bed,
the slayers of Brahmins, the drinkers of liquor, thieves, the killers of cows, and physicians;
Those who desire sovereignty, as well as the insane, those who sell animals,
those who use false measures and false scales, artisans, and village priests;
Guilds and royal sacrificers who have been corrupted by low-caste women;
and the king’s servants who are blind, deaf, mute, bald, and lame.
Likewise those who live by the arts, as well as those who sell the Veda;
those Brahmins who carry the staff and banner [of office], and those who perform the village rituals.
House-burners, poison-givers, forest-setters,
those who eat from sacrificial vessels, temple-priests [who subsist on offerings], and those who violate the wives of others;
Those with black teeth, those with deformed nails, those afflicted with leprosy, artisans, merchants, those who kill bees, and Brahmins who are trainers of elephants and horses;
Those who defile maidens, those who revile Brahmins,
informers, those who rear animals for slaughter, gamblers, and actors;
Those who break their vows, those who create obstacles to giving,
those who keep goats and sheep, those who keep buffaloes, those who sell all kinds of goods,
those who are attached to the Vaiṣṇava women, and likewise those who do not give parched grain as an offering— [these are excluded].
A maker of bows, one who lives by gambling, a betrayer of friends, and a rogue as well.

Likewise, one who makes arrows, he who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is still unmarried, one afflicted with jaundice, one with scrofula, one suffering from consumption, and likewise one with epilepsy, should be avoided.
An informer, a false witness, one who suffers from a chronic disease, one whose efforts are in vain,
one who has returned from the life of a wandering mendicant, and one who has entered the religious order in vain;
[83] And he who is born of one who has gone forth, and he who has settled in the state of going forth— Yama, the son of Vivasvat, says that both of these are *brahmacāṇḍālas*.
One who serves as a messenger for a king, one who belongs to a village or a city,
one who travels by sea, one who eats what has been vomited, and those who sell human hair— [these are excluded].

One who has spilled his semen, one who harms the body, one who kills a teacher, one who reviles his father, a seller of cows, a person of wicked conduct, and one who performs sacrifices for a multitude;
A drunkard, a miser, one who quarrels with his father, a magistrate,
the husband of an unchaste woman, one who has abandoned himself, and a defiler of women.
One whose conduct is censured by the virtuous, one who has abandoned his own duties,
one who has been superseded in marriage by a younger brother, one who marries before his elder brother, a teacher for hire, and one who has rejected the Vedas;

One who teaches a Śūdra, one who teaches his own daughter, one who has a Śūdra as a pupil, an atheist, a corrupt person, one who teaches his own children, one who is arrogant, and likewise an oil-presser;
Thieves, usurers, the wicked, those who destroy the property of others,
and those outside the four stages of life— all these are defilers of the assembly.
One should not appoint those twice-born men who are endowed with these characteristics.

‘Paṇḍo’ here means a eunuch. ‘Cikitsakaḥ’ is one who lives by the practice of medicine. ‘Rāṣṭrakāmāḥ’ are those who desire sovereignty over a kingdom. ‘Mānakūṭāḥ’ are those who deal with false measures. ‘Śreṇī’ is a group of people belonging to the same class. ‘Khalvāṭaḥ’ is one who is bald. ‘Daṇḍadhvajaḥ’ is one who has been marked with the sign of punishment by the king for acts of violence and the like. ‘Poṣakāḥ’ refers to those who keep birds; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. ‘Vaiṣṇavī’ is a Śūdra woman. ‘Alājādāhinaḥ’ means those devoid of the burning of parched grain (lāja), which signifies marriage; they are to be understood as those who have performed the rite of returning home after their studies (samāvartana). ‘Śaṭhaḥ’ is a deceitful person. ‘Bhrāmarī’ is one suffering from epilepsy. ‘Durvālaḥ’ here means one with red hair, since he is mentioned separately from the bald and the one with a goitre. ‘Pūgaḥ’ is a multitude or assembly. ‘Dārakāḥ’ are those who have not yet undergone the initiation ceremony (anupanīta). ‘Tailikaḥ’ is one who subsists on the sale of oil.
Manu (3.150–167): "Those who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, and those who follow the lifestyle of nihilists—
Manu has declared that such men are unworthy of being invited as Brahmins for offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya)."
One should not feed at a śrāddha those who wear matted hair but do not study the Vedas, nor those with shaggy hair, gamblers, nor those who officiate as priests for large groups.
Physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers,
and those who live by trade— these should be avoided at offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
A servant of a village or of a king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth,
one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer;

One afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, a younger brother who marries before his elder, one who has been expelled from his caste, a hater of the Veda, an elder brother whose younger brother has married before him, and one who belongs to a religious guild— these are unfit to be invited.

One who is immoral, one who has broken his vows, the husband of a low-caste woman, the son of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house lives a paramour; [these are those with whom one should not eat].
One who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught by a teacher for a fee,
one whose pupil is a Śūdra, one whose teacher is a Śūdra, one who is foul-mouthed, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka.
Having abandoned his mother, father, and teacher without cause,
and having entered into association with outcasts through Brahmanical or matrimonial connections;
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats from a vessel [belonging to another], a seller of Soma,
one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger;
One who quarrels with his father, one who squints, a drunkard,
one afflicted by a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids (or flavors).
One who makes bows and arrows, and one who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried;

One who betrays a friend, one whose livelihood is gambling, likewise one who is a teacher of his own son, one who suffers from vertigo, one with scrofulous swellings, one with leprosy, and likewise a slanderer.
The insane, the blind, and those who revile the Vedas should be avoided, as well as trainers of elephants, cattle, horses, and camels, and one who lives by means of the lunar mansions.
One who is a breeder of birds, likewise one who is a teacher of combat,
one who diverts streams of water, and one who delights in obstructing them.
A messenger who enters houses, one who plants trees,
a dog-keeper, one who lives by falcons, and a defiler of maidens;
One who is violent, the son of a Śūdra, a priest for communal sacrifices,
devoid of proper conduct, impotent, and likewise one who is constantly begging;
One who lives by agriculture, one with elephantiasis, and one censured by the virtuous;
likewise, a shepherd, a buffalo-breeder, and the husband of a woman previously married to another.
And those who carry out the dead for the hungry ghosts must be avoided with great effort;
these lowest of men, whose conduct is censurable, are unworthy of sitting in the row for a meal.
The learned best of the twice-born should avoid both.

A *jaṭila* is a religious student (*brahmacārī*). Here, "one who has not studied" refers to one who has merely been initiated (*upanīta*) but has not yet been instructed in the Vedic vows. That which was stated regarding the sanctity of the assembly (*paṅktipāvanatva*) in the case of the "religious student who bestows a thousand," should be understood as applying to one engaged in study. A *durvāla* is one who is bald (*khalati*), not one with skin disease (*duścarmā*), because the latter is mentioned separately by its own term. An *pratiroddhā* is one who obstructs his teacher. A *gaṇābhyantara* is a common member of a group. In the case of "those who plant trees, those who construct houses, and messengers," those who live by wages (*bhṛtijīvinaḥ*) are to be understood.
Śaṅkha says:
Those Brāhmaṇas who are engaged in improper occupations, those who act like cats,
as well as those with missing limbs or extra limbs, should be known as defilers of the row.
One with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one with a skin disease, the husband of a Śūdra woman,
one afflicted with leprosy, and one suffering from pulmonary consumption— these, O Brāhmaṇas, are defilers of the row at a meal.
Those who act in opposition to their gurus, those who extinguish the Vedas and the sacred fires,
those who abandon their gurus, and such Brahmins are defilers of the assembly.
Those Brāhmaṇas who study during forbidden times, who are devoid of purity and proper conduct,
and whose limbs are nourished by the food and essence of Śūdras, are defilers of the assembly.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"One who speaks untruth, a thief, a royal servant, one whose livelihood is planting trees, a poisoner, an arsonist, a Śūdra who acts as a teacher, a bard, a bell-ringer, a temple-priest, a domestic chaplain, one who makes his living by predicting the positions of the stars, a Brahmin’s servant, a drinker of liquor, a seller of the Veda, a gambler, a forger, and those who sell human beings as cattle—these are excluded from the company at a meal."
Hārīta says:

One should exclude from rites for the gods and the ancestors those who practice medicine, those who serve Śūdras, servants, artisans, gamblers, those who live by training dogs, those who live by birds, fishermen, those who subsist on the killing of fish, prostitutes, usurers, snake-charmers, those who have fallen from their caste, hired teachers, oil-pressers, informers, jailers, actors, and the like. Furthermore, those who are atheists, eunuchs, misers, those who consort with harlots, liars, those who neglect their prayers, fire-sacrifices, twilight devotions, and purification; those who are impure due to sexual intercourse, the use of weapons, or the mouth; those who are of mixed or confused origin; those who are unholy; those who subsist by seizing the livelihood of Brāhmaṇas, by slaughter, or by imprisonment; the husband of a Śūdra woman, those who perform sacrifices for Śūdras, thieves, arsonists, poisoners, sellers of Soma, singers, dancers, makers of bows and arrows, the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* sons, those who praise men, followers of Kapila, temple-attendants, those who live by astrology, those who travel to the great ocean, those afflicted with chronic diseases, long-distance travelers, the outcasted, and those who act as priests for the outcasted—these, if they do not desist, are defilers of the row (*paṅkti*).

A *vṛṣalapreṣya* is one who carries out the commands of a Śūdra. A *śakunijīvana* is one who lives by means of hawks. A *mīnaghātakaceṣṭita*—a *mīnaghātaka* is a heron; he whose conduct or livelihood is like that of such a bird is so called, meaning one who follows the "heron's way" (*bakavṛtti*). An *āhituṇḍika* is one who lives by playing with snakes. A *niyāmaka* is a boatman, or one who, having received wages, directs others. A *kuśīlava* is a wandering actor or bard. An *ākrīḍī* is one whose nature is to constantly play. An *anṛtavādī* is one whose habit is to speak falsehoods. A *narāśaṃsa* is one whose habit is to praise men. A *dhanuḥśarayojaka* is a maker of bows and a maker of arrows. A *kapila* is a contemptible tawny person, meaning one whose physical form is excessively tawny. A *dīrghamahāpathika* is one who has made an effort toward death on a long journey. Those who are *anivartamāna* are those who take delight in that very state.

One should avoid those with missing or extra limbs; those engaged in improper occupations; those who act like cats (hypocrites); those who wear religious marks in vain; those who subsist on astrology; temple-priests; physicians; sons of unmarried women; and the sons of such sons; those who officiate at sacrifices for many people; village priests; priests for Śūdras; [and those who officiate for those unfit to sacrifice]; outcasts (vrātyas); those who perform sacrifices for false purposes; carpenters; informers; [those who teach for a fee]; those taught by those who teach for a fee; those nourished by the food of Śūdras; those who associate with the fallen; those who do not study; those who have neglected their twilight devotions; royal servants; the naked; those quarreling with their fathers; and those who have abandoned their father, mother, guru, sacred fire, or Vedic study.
For these are declared to be the outcasts among Brahmins, defilers of the sacrificial row;
a wise man should avoid them with effort during the performance of a śrāddha rite.
[90] ‘Parvakāraḥ’ means an arrow-maker. ‘Ugraḥ’ here refers to one whose anger is directed toward the senses. Āpastamba [2.17.21]:

“A leper, a *śipiviṣṭa*, one who approaches the bed of another’s wife, the son of a soldier, and one born of a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother—these, while eating, are defilers of the row (*paṅktidūṣaṇāḥ*).”

*Śvitrī* means one with leprosy (*duścarmā*). *Āyudhīyaputraḥ* is the son of one who lives by weapons. Regarding *śudrotpanno brāhmaṇyām*, Kapardin explains that when one has taken a wife of a different caste, this refers to a son produced by a Śūdra father upon a Brāhmaṇa mother, after having failed to produce a son upon the Brāhmaṇa wife.
Sumantu said:

Thieves, gamblers, keepers of gambling houses, courtesans, Śūdras, servants, those who approach women who should not be approached, one who marries before his elder brother (*parivettṛ*), the elder brother so superseded (*parivitti*), one whose younger brother has married before him (*paryāhita*), the one so superseded (*paryādhātṛ*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the blind, the deaf, professional bards (*cāraṇa*), eunuchs, those who have broken their vows of celibacy (*avakīrṇin*), usurers, poisoners, false witnesses, atheists, the husband of a Śūdra woman, those who abandon the sacred fires, those who sell Soma, those who eat from a vessel belonging to an outcaste (*kuṇḍāśin*), those born of adultery (*kuṇḍagolaka*), makers of machines, those who live by weapons (*kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*), those with diseased skin, the impotent (*ṣaṇḍa*), the fierce (*caṇḍa*), those whose penis has been pierced (*viddhaśiśna*), temple-priests (*devalaka*), those who have mounted upon their own necks (*kaṇṭhārūḍha*), those fallen from their caste and risen again (*prāyotthita*), those with deformed nails, those suffering from leprosy, those with black teeth, merchants, artisans, those who live by music, dance, and song, astrologers, long-distance travelers, stone-crushers, those with missing limbs, those with redundant limbs, and those wearing discolored garments—these are excluded from the assembly.

The term *preṣya* (servant) is to be connected individually with each of the following terms, beginning with *gaṇa*. "A maker of machines" (*yantrakāraka*) refers to one who operates a machine for pressing sugarcane. "One who has risen prematurely" (*prāyotthita*) refers to one who has failed in his vow of fasting. "One who lives by the annual fee" (*mūlyasāṃvatsarika*) refers to one who tells [the positions of] the constellations and so forth for a fee; that is, an astrologer.

Paiṭhīnasi: Those with deformed nails, ringworm, or black teeth; one who quarrels with his father; one who is dominated by women; a leper, a eunuch, a gambler, one of weak character, one of evil conduct, one who has drunk liquor from a vessel, one whose generative organ is perforated, an outcast, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, a seller of sacrifices or the Vedas, a merchant, a village priest, one falsely accused, one born of a Śūdra woman, an elder brother whose younger brother marries before him, a younger brother who marries before his elder, the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried, the son of a remarried woman, those born of a cow, a jar, a goat, or a sheep, a thief, a professional soldier, and a servant—these are excluded from the row. One should not feed these at a Śrāddha, nor at a sacrificial rite.
"Surāgarbhaḥ": one in whose womb liquor was present—that is, one who was conceived while his mother was drinking liquor. [92] Uśanas says:

"They become excluded from the company at meals (apāṅkteya). For example: the mentally dull, the deaf, those born blind, the leper, the white-spotted, the one afflicted with skin disease, the one with deformed nails, the one with black teeth, the usurer, the temple-priest, the merchant, the rogue, those belonging to a guild, the physician, the son of a remarried woman, the one-eyed, those who live by their craft, the outcaste, the associate of outcasts, the gambler, the liar, the hypocrite, those corrupted by others, and so forth."
‘Kuṇiḥ’ means one with a deformed hand. ‘Paraparibhāvitaḥ’ means examined as an enemy—that is, scrutinized as an adversary.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"He who subsists on air while remaining outside the four stages of life (āśrama),
and the ascetic who propounds liberation— both of these are defilers of the assembly."
One who is engaged in fierce austerity, a speaker of various doctrines, or one of great learning—
such a Brahmin who does not belong to a specific stage of life (anāśramin) should not be invited for the theft of penance.
The Śākya who denies rebirth, the nihilist, the reviler of the Vedas,
and those who revile meditators— all of them are defilers of the sacrificial feast.
One should avoid those who wear shaven heads in vain, those with matted hair, and all such mendicants; as well as those who are merciless, those of broken conduct, and those who eat everything.
[93] He who has become the Veda himself, he who lives off the Veda,
and likewise the husband of a daughter— both of these are unworthy of the *śrāddha*.
A twice-born man who approaches his wife in vain, one who officiates at sacrifices performed in vain,
and likewise an atheist— these two are not worthy of the śrāddha offering.
He who cooks food for his own sake, and not for the sake of the gods or guests, does not deserve to partake in the *śrāddha*; he is fallen and becomes a *brahmarākṣasa*.
One should not feed at śrāddha ceremonies those who wear red garments, those who delight in slandering others, and those who are devoted to wealth and sensual pleasure.
There are some who, considering themselves wise, act in contradiction to the Vedas;
being non-sacrificers by name, they consume [the results of their actions] like dust.

One should carefully avoid those with shaven heads, those with matted hair, and those wearing saffron robes at a *śrāddha* ceremony; instead, one should offer [the gifts] to those who wear tufts of hair, those whose garments are dyed with mineral pigments, and those who carry the triple staff.

*Ayatiḥ* means one who is unrestrained. *Aupapattiḥ* refers to one who deals with mere logical reasoning; the meaning is a sophist (*haituka*). *Śākyaḥ* here refers to one devoted to the Śākya doctrine. *Vṛthāmuṇḍāḥ* are those who practice forbidden tonsure. *Vṛthājaṭilāḥ* are those who wear matted hair not sanctioned by the scriptures. *Kāpaṭikāḥ* are those who deal in rags. *Nirghṛṇāḥ* means merciless. *Bhinnavṛttāḥ* means those who have abandoned proper conduct. Regarding the phrase "he who, being hired as a bearer of the Vedas, recites the Vedas" (*vedān vedabhṛt prāha*), the meaning is one who, having been employed for the purpose of Vedic study, recites the Vedas. *Putrikāpatiḥ* is the husband of a woman designated as a "son's daughter" (*putrikā*). "And he who approaches wives in vain" means sexual pleasure with women apart from the desire for offspring. The repetition of the term "atheist" (*nāstika*) is for the sake of emphasizing the censure. "Women in red garments" refers to menstruating women. "Devoted to wealth and pleasure" means those devoted to wealth and pleasure apart from virtue (*dharma*) and liberation (*mokṣa*). In the expression "those who do not preside over sacrifices" (*ayajñapatayaḥ*), the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) is intended to indicate all duties prescribed for the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*). Here, *muṇḍāḥ* refers to those whose topknots (*śikhā*) have been shorn. The mention of the "one with matted hair" (*jaṭila*) again is for the sake of emphasizing the censure.
In the Mahābhārata [Anuśāsana Parvan, 61.18, 20, 21]:
"O King, even a Brāhmaṇa who was formerly made a leader and who has accepted the company of those of lower castes, though he be learned in all branches of knowledge, does not deserve an invitation."
O Bhārata, those who have not previously been known, those who were formerly members of a group,
and those who were formerly the sons of appointed daughters, do not deserve an invitation to a śrāddha.
O King, he who incurs debt, the twice-born usurer, and he whose livelihood consists of the sale of living beings— such a person, O King, does not deserve an invitation to a funeral feast.

Regarding the term *agraṇīḥ*: the meaning is that one who was previously honored as a leader by the learned, yet later enters into association with those of inferior caste, is to be excluded from the *śrāddha*. *Ketana* means an invitation. *Aparijñātapūrvāḥ* refers to those whose ancestors, such as their fathers and so forth, were previously unknown. *Gaṇapūrvāḥ* are those who have become leaders within a corporate body (*saṅgha*). *Putrikāputrapūrvāḥ* are those born of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). *Ṛṇakartā* here refers to one who, having taken a loan, does not wish to repay the creditor. *Prāṇavikrayavṛttiḥ* is one who lives by performing actions that bring about a danger to life.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "Likewise, [one should avoid] ungrateful people, atheists, those dwelling in the lands of the Mlecchas,
the Triśakus, the Barbaras, the Āndhras, the Ṭaṅkas, the Draviḍas, and the Koṅkaṇas."
Likewise, one should avoid the Karṇāṭakas, the Kīras, and the Kaliṅgas.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Those whose minds are afflicted by wretchedness do not deserve to eat at *śrāddha* ceremonies:
the eunuch, the mute, the one with deformed nails, the bald man, and the one suffering from dental disease."
One with black teeth, a putrid nose, a missing limb, or an extra finger;
one suffering from throat disease, scrofula, cracked limbs, or fever.
Some were lame, others had shaven heads, and likewise others were long-term invalids;
they were born in vain, devoid of passion, and tormented by the burden of disease.

‘Tūvara’ refers to one who is devoid of a beard even at the time when a beard should grow. ‘Vṛthājātāḥ’ means those who are averse to dharma. ‘Viraktāḥ’ here refers to those other than ascetics (yatis). Now, Manu [3.170, 180–182]:
“That which is eaten by twice-born men who have not undergone initiation, as well as by those such as a ‘parivettṛ’ (one who marries before his elder brother), and so forth...”
Whatever is eaten by others who are unworthy of the company at a meal, that indeed one feeds to the Rākṣasas.
To a seller of Soma, it becomes excrement; to a physician, pus and blood;
to a usurer, it is without foundation; and to a temple-priest, it is lost.
But that which is given to a trader brings no fruit either in this world or the next;
it is like an oblation poured into ashes, so too when given to a twice-born man who is the son of a remarried woman.
But regarding other unworthy persons who have been specified as unfit for the company at a meal,
the wise declare that their food is equivalent to fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone.
Yama said: Those who have strayed from their own duties are proclaimed to be thieves;
for him who gives the ancestral offering (kavya) to them, that gift perishes after death.
But those of little intelligence who give to them with prior knowledge,
O observer of good vows, eat nothing but excrement for a hundred years.
Likewise: "One should not give sacrificial oblations (havis) in rites for the gods or the ancestors to a drinker of intoxicants;
what is given to him perishes, just like an offering poured into ashes."
The hand of the giver is cut off and the tongue of the eater is split asunder;
he swallows flaming morsels—that śrāddha becomes false.
"As many worthy guests as one who is unworthy of the company sees while they are eating,
for so many of them the foolish giver receives no fruit there."
Likewise:
"As many Brahmins as one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs,
for that many [gifts] the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the meritorious gift."
A blind man, upon seeing [the gift], destroys the fruit of ninety [gifts]; one who is one-eyed, that of sixty; one with white leprosy, that of a hundred;
but one afflicted by a foul disease destroys the fruit of a thousand for the donor.
Yama says: A one-eyed man sees sixty, a eunuch a hundred, and a leper as many as he looks upon;
likewise, one afflicted with white leprosy sees a hundred, and an outcast a thousand.

[97] Vasiṣṭha [11.20]: "In this regard, Yama has declared that even if one is joined with those who defile the assembly by means of their bodies, provided he is not himself defiled, he is indeed a purifier of the assembly."
"By means of bodies" means by means of defects such as being one-eyed that arise from the body, but not by means of qualities such as being a thief which are produced independently.
Now Devala says:
A man who, out of delusion, approaches another's wife is called a *jāra*;
he who constantly dwells in her house is to be known as an *upapati*.
One born from an adulterer while the husband is alive is a *kuṇḍa*; one born when the husband is dead is a *golaka*.
He who eats the food of these two is called a *kuṇḍāśin*.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "A vessel made of sixty-four pure palas shall have a capacity of four prasthas;
he who swallows such a vessel falls downward."
Yama says:
He who, while observing a vow, approaches a woman is called an *avakīrṇin*. But he who is the husband of a woman whose husband has died is indeed the *didhiṣūpati*.
Devala says:
One who approaches the wife of his elder brother out of lust is a *didhiṣūpati*.
Manu [3.173]: He who, out of lust, would lust after the wife of a deceased brother— even though she has been formally appointed according to dharma— is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*.
Laukāxi says: If a younger sister is married while the elder sister remains unmarried,
she is to be known as an *agredidhiṣū*, whereas the elder sister is remembered as a *didhiṣū*.
Yama says: A woman who is called a "mahiṣī" (a chief wife) but is indeed unchaste— he who tolerates that fault is known as a *māhiṣika*.
Devala says:
He whose practice of austerity is corrupt is designated by the name "Gūḍha";
likewise, he who teaches for a fee and he who has been taught for a fee.
Both those two Brahmins have fallen from their status due to the buying and selling of the Veda:
he who, for the sake of wealth, performs sacrifices for Śūdras or even for outcasts.

Furthermore, Manu has declared that a Brahmin who, having been commissioned by those two [a Śūdra and a Vaiśya], performs sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice, becomes an outcast, as does one who accepts gifts for the sake of wealth after being questioned about them.
For these sellers of the Veda are excluded from the Soma sacrifices and other rites;
whatever sacrifice (iṣṭa), charitable work (pūrta), study, or austerity they have performed for themselves—[all such merit perishes].
He who sells his dharma for the sake of wealth gives it to others;
likewise, that twice-born man who is a seller of dairy products or a seller of cows.
[99] A seller of molasses, salt, and sesame seeds is a dishonest trader;
he causes suffering to himself, to his religious duties, and to his children and wife.
He who accumulates wealth out of greed is established as a miser;
