he who is unrestrained toward those of low, high, or middle castes is likewise so defined.
But he who practices the conduct of others is a defiler of the social orders;
one who possesses a hundred cows but has not established the sacred fires, and one who possesses a thousand cows but has not performed a sacrifice.
And those twice-born who subsist on the livelihood of a Śūdra do not deserve the guest-offerings.
A Brahmin living for a year in a village where there is water only sufficient for a well [should likewise not receive them].
Through the total abandonment of purity and proper conduct, one is deprived of Brahminhood—
those who do not regularly perform the twilight devotions and who eat without having bathed.
Those who have fallen away from purity fall [to lower states], for according to dharma they are equal to Śūdras;
he who remains alone, even when overcome by calamity, is called "blessed" by the wise.
And one who lives off the treasury of the gods shall be known by the name Devalaka.
‘Anavagrahaḥ’ means one who has abandoned the restrictive rules of the scriptures; ‘aparācāram’ means conduct appropriate for the lowest caste.
Yama says:
He who, having acquired goods at a low price, sells them at a high price,
is indeed called a usurer, as is he who employs interest.
Likewise: "He who, while living, censures another and praises his own qualities,
is indeed called a usurer, and is despised among those who discourse on Brahman."
"Jīvan" means for the sake of living. Likewise:
"He who extinguishes the sacred fires is called a slayer of heroes (vīrahā)."
[100] Devala says: A Brāhmaṇa who has married a woman of the same lineage becomes a "breaker of the lineage" (gotrabhid);
the husband of a Vaiśya woman becomes a "black-backed" (kṛṣṇapṛṣṭha) man, and he is a "man with a staff on his back" (kāṇḍapṛṣṭha).
Immediately after the occupations of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, Nārada [4.60] states:
"And that Brāhmaṇa who takes delight in that very occupation out of passion— he is fallen from the path, known as a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, and is declared unfit to sit in the row for meals (*apāṅkteya*)."
Hārīta says:
Sons born of Śūdra women, those who have given themselves [as sons], and those sons who have been purchased—
all these are declared by Maitriṇa to be *kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas*, without a doubt.
The "stalk" (kāṇḍa) is said to be the name of their family, while the "joints" (parvan) are the ages (yugas).
He who protects that [family] according to the rule is remembered as one of noble birth (kulīna).
He who, having cast his own family behind him, goes instead to another's family, becomes a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* by that evil conduct; of this there is no doubt.
Yama says: "One who has fallen into calamity, one who has surrendered [to another], and one who is the son of a Vaiṣṇava—
all these three are declared by Manu to be remembered as *kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas*."
The family is known as the "kāṇḍa," and therefore they call its sections "parvans";
because that which is the eldest therein is indeed designated as the "kāṇḍa."
He who, having cast his own family behind him, goes instead to another's family,
is known as a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* because of that evil conduct.

[101] Devala says: A Brahmin who constantly performs service for the king is declared to be "deformed" (vikṛta). A Brahmin who has forgotten the Veda he studied becomes one who is "excluded" (nirākṛti).
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* states:
"He who possesses the sacred study and the sacred fires, yet has not worshipped the gods and others with these [fires],
and who rejects the gods and others— he is to be known as a *nirākṛti*."
‘[One should not worship] the gods and others with these’—this refers to [the omission of] necessary duties by way of sacrifices such as the Darśa and Paurṇamāsa. Devala says:
“One who conceals his gender, one who has broken his vow, and likewise one who has violated his celibacy (avakīrṇin),” and so forth.
He who knows the distinction between dharma and adharma is firmly established in the teaching of the Vedas.
One who possesses compassion, modesty, patience, and intelligence is noble; one who lacks these is a barbarian.
He who, having eaten the food of a second father, has been transformed into a twice-born is [noble].
One who lives by the dharma of a Śūdra should be known as an *avareḍha*;
he may also be designated as a *kāraṇa* and shall be involved in all legal transactions.
He should be known as a burner of houses who has indeed burned many deceased persons;
and he too would be a burner of houses who sets fire to a dwelling out of malice.
Those who burn fields, crops, and forests are "forest-burners.
A *ṣaṇḍaka* is one born impotent; a *ṣaṇḍa*, a *ṣaṇḍa*, a *klība*, and a *napuṃsaka* are all terms for a eunuch or one lacking virility.
And the *kīlaka*; this sixfold classification of eunuchs has been explained.
Among them, one who possesses speech and gestures similar to a woman and exhibits female characteristics is a *ṣaṇḍaka*.
[102] Having become a man, one should likewise later sever one's own male characteristics;
or a woman, having attained the state of a man, possesses qualities consistent with the conduct of a man.
A *ṣaṇḍa* may be known by the name *vātaja*, or it may be named *strīṣaṇḍa*;
a *ṣaṇḍa* may also be one who lacks sexual organs, while a *ṣaṇḍa* is characterized by a withered penis.
He who, out of impotence, first unites his wife with another man and afterwards enjoys her himself is called a *kīlaka*.
In the Skanda Purāṇa,
Īśvara said:
"The Vedic revelation states that a śrāddha should be given only after [the recipient] has been examined."
And through examination, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, straightforwardness is seen to be the superior quality.
But he who, abiding in sincerity, gives a śrāddha without examining [the recipient], his ancestors and the deities are satisfied; of this there is no doubt.
Now, the invitation and the rules for those who have been invited.
Regarding this, Devala says:
"Free from anger, composed, self-abiding, full of faith, unhurried, pure,
with a concentrated mind, one should always and repeatedly apply oneself to that ritual action."
Having thus resolved, "I shall perform it tomorrow," the donor should invite the Brahmins once,
after having declared that there will be no meat in the house while all the people have already eaten.
If it is impossible [to perform the rite on that day], he should invite those Brahmins on the following day—
persons who are not his agnates, who do not share his *ṛṣi* lineage, and who are an odd number, according to his own capacity.

"Secluded" (*nibhṛta*) here means staying in a solitary place. "With a concentrated mind" (*samāhitamanāḥ*) refers to [the state regarding] the food and other items. This is the meaning: "Repeatedly" (*asakṛt*), that is, again and again, one should act at the *śrāddha* in such a way that the mind does not become uncontrolled. "Having eaten meatless food once" is common to both invitations on the previous day and on the following day. "When all the people have eaten" means that in which all the people have finished eating. "In the event of impossibility" (*asaṃbhave*) means when, due to some cause, the invitation on the previous day cannot be fulfilled. "The *ārṣas*" are the ancestral lineages (*pravara*).
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
He should invite Brahmins endowed with the characteristics of birth, body, and qualities, [informing them] that he will perform the Śrāddha "tomorrow" or "today."
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa [31.30, 33, 34]:
One should invite on the previous day the best of the twice-born mentioned above,
or on that very day if they are unavailable, excluding those addicted to women.
Or, when self-controlled ascetics come at the proper time seeking alms,
he should feed them, having propitiated them with prostrations and other gestures, while maintaining a restrained mind.
‘Non-attainment’ here means impossibility.
Manu [3.187]: When the Śrāddha rite is about to take place, on either the previous day or the following day,
one should properly invite at least three Brahmins who possess the qualities previously described.
Uśanas says: Having cleansed the ground with cow-dung and water and purified the vessels, one should invite at least four Brahmins, saying, "I shall perform [the rite] tomorrow."
"Four at least": two for the gods, and one each for the groups of paternal ancestors and maternal ancestors.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: One who knows, "I shall perform [the rite] tomorrow," should attend to the purification of his garments and other preparations;
having smeared the ground and prepared the site, he should invite a Brahmin.
The student, being pure, should cast away the tooth-stick;
having prepared the ground, which possesses qualities such as sloping toward the south, he should "cast it away," meaning he should give it to the Brahmins.

[105] Āpastamba [2.17.11–17]: On the previous day is the announcement; on the following day is the second [announcement]; the third is the formal invitation. Some teachers prescribe that the Śrāddha rite should consist of three attempts. As the first is performed, so are the second and the third.

To all the Brahmins, he should announce: "Tomorrow a *śrāddha* must be performed by me; you, honored sirs, are to be invited there. He should urge the Brahmins [to accept] in the morning, and invite them at the time of the meal.
In the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "Having touched his right knee, [the wise man] should invite him with these words: 'You are invited by me here.
Having thus invited him, the wise man should announce the ancestral observances (*niyama*)."
He says to them:
"In this śrāddha rite, you as well as I must remain free from anger, devoted to purity, and constantly observant of celibacy."
Yama says: One should invite virtuous people.
Having heard that the time for the śrāddha has arrived, those ancestors,
having reflected upon one another in their minds, descend with the speed of thought.
Likewise:
"For the ancestors dwelling in the intermediate space eat together with the Brahmins;
having become like the wind, they are not seen, and having eaten, they go to the supreme goal."

The phrase "one should invite virtuous men" is used when one is unable to invite them oneself; for Yama and Śātātapa state that inviting oneself is the primary method, as indicated by the expression: "You and I must both be present here at this *śrāddha* rite. Furthermore, they state: "The food of a Brāhmaṇa is not to be eaten if he has been invited by a *vṛṣala* (outcaste), and likewise, the food of a *vṛṣala* is not to be eaten if he has been invited by a Brāhmaṇa."
Yājñavalkya [1.225]: On the day before [the ceremony], the self-possessed and pure host should invite the Brāhmaṇas;
they too must remain restrained in their thoughts, words, and physical actions.
Regarding the rules for the *śrāddha*, Āpastamba [2.17.24] states:
"Once it has begun, there shall be no eating until its completion."
The Rules for Those Who Have Been Invited.
Yama says:
When the time for the śrāddha has arrived, those invited Brahmins should remain restrained in their diet and devoted to celibacy.
Yama says:
A twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors should always remain self-restrained;
he should not recite the Vedas, and that [rite] shall be his Śrāddha.
Hārīta says: On the previous day, the ancestors indeed enter into the Brahmins for whom the rites have been consecrated;
therefore, they and the sacrificer should remain there that night, self-restrained.
Kātyāyana [Śrāddhakalpa 1.23–25]:

On that day, he should be pure, free from anger, prompt, vigilant, and truthful; he should avoid travel, sexual intercourse, fatigue, and Vedic recitation. He should remain silent from the invocation (*āvāhana*) until the ritual sipping of water (*upasparśana*). Those who have been invited should likewise observe these rules.
[107] ‘From the ritual sipping of water’ means up to the final sipping of water by the eaters.
Yama says: Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and the act of staying far away [from the funeral site].
Patience is the non-bearing of burdens; for one endowed with faith, it is the method of non-appropriation.
Kātyāyana [Śrāddhakalpa 1.12–13]: When invited by one who is blameless, one should not decline; once formally invited, one should not accept food from another.
Yama and Manu state in the first [section] (Manu 3.190):
"A Brāhmaṇa who has been duly invited for the offerings to the gods and the ancestors,
if he somehow fails to attend, that sinner shall go to the state of a pig."
Having personally performed the rite for a Brahmin together with the gods and ancestors,
one should not transgress the food that they consume.
If a twice-born man, having caused a memorial monument (ketana) to be built, should cause it to be destroyed,
he incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin and is born into the womb of a Śūdra.
Likewise: "But that evil-minded man who, having been invited to a *śrāddha*, grants his time to another, loses the merit he has accumulated over a year."
[108] Likewise: "But he who, having invited a brahmin, does not honor him according to the rule,
is born among the terrible animal wombs that are most difficult to endure."
"He makes a moment for another" means that he accepts the invitation of another.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "A Brahmin who has been invited should never, at any time, delay for long [in accepting],
whether it be for the sake of the deities, the ancestors, a donor, or anyone else."
One who acts slowly becomes a betrayer and is cooked by the fire of hell;
"one who acts slowly" means one who delays action.
(Mahābhārata, Anuśāsana-parvan, 61.54).
Whether it be a rite for the gods or one for the ancestors, whoever should eat among the Brāhmaṇas and others [without having first offered], [is at fault].
Hārīta says:
If one invites a Brāhmaṇa for a rite for the gods or for the ancestors,
but does not satisfy him according to the rule, he shall take away the fruit of that [offering].
Knowing that it was forgotten through negligence, one should diligently propitiate him and offer him special libations; thus, one shall obtain the full fruit of that [negligence].
Devala says:
If a Brahmin invited to a Śrāddha ceremony has sexual intercourse with a Vṛṣalī,
he instantly incurs the entire sin of the donor.
[109] If one who has been previously invited by another should accept the invitation of another,
or if he eats when his own meal has already been consumed, his merit perishes.
Therefore, having abandoned these and those other faults,
a capable person, being a celibate student and pure, should partake of the śrāddha feast.
A donor who has restrained himself should feed exactly three persons after having eaten his own meal;
that is, he should feed exactly three invited Brāhmaṇas. "Restrained" (yantrita) means self-controlled; "after having eaten his meal" (bhuktāhāreṇa) means having finished his eating.
In this regard, Yama and Uśanas state in the first three verses:
"If a twice-born man who has been invited to a śrāddha goes on a journey,
his ancestors shall subsist on dust for that entire month."
But when a twice-born man who has been invited to a śrāddha ceremony bears a burden [of resentment],
his ancestors will have to subsist on sweat for that entire month.
If a twice-born man, having been invited to a śrāddha, commits an act of violence,
his ancestors shall subsist on blood for that entire month.
But if a twice-born man, having been invited to a śrāddha, causes distress,
his ancestors remain dissatisfied for that entire month.
But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha, rejoices with a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī),
his ancestors shall subsist on white food for that entire month.
If a twice-born man, having been invited to a *śrāddha*, engages in quarreling,
his ancestors shall subsist on impure food for that entire month.
Therefore, a twice-born man invited to a *śrāddha* should remain self-restrained; he should be free from anger, devoted to purity, truthful in speech, and a master of his senses.
Śaṅkha says:
"But that twice-born man who, having been invited to a śrāddha, engages in sexual intercourse—
whether after giving or after eating at the śrāddha— is joined with great sin."
Manu [3.192–201]: Free from anger, devoted to purity, constantly practicing celibacy,
having laid down their weapons, the highly fortunate Pitṛs are the ancient deities.
Since the origin of all these [castes] has been explained in its entirety,
learn now those rules by which they are to be designated according to their respective occupations.
The sons of all those sages— Marīci and the others— who were the offspring of Manu Hiraṇyagarbha, are recorded as the Pitṛ-gaṇas (the classes of ancestors).
The sons of Virāṭ, known as the Somasads, are remembered as the ancestors of the Sādhyas;
and the Agniṣvāttas, renowned throughout the world, are the ancestors of the gods, the offspring of Marīci.
The Barhiṣads, born of Atri, are traditionally held to be the progenitors of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, Suparṇas, and Kinnaras.
Among the Brahmins they are named Somapas; among the Kshatriyas, Havirbhujs; among the Vaishyas, Ajyapas; and among the Shudras, Sukalins.
The Somapas were the sons of Kavi; the Haviṣmants were the sons of Aṅgiras; those named Ājyapas were the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins were the sons of Vasiṣṭha.
One should designate the Agnidagdhas, the Anagnidagdhas, the Kavyas, the Barhiṣads,
as well as the Agniṣvāttas and the Saumyas, as belonging exclusively to the Brahmins.
Furthermore, regarding these principal groups of ancestors that have been proclaimed,
it should be understood that their sons and grandsons here are infinite.
From the sages were born the ancestors; from the ancestors, gods and humans;
and from the gods, the entire world—both moving and stationary—in due order.
Hārīta states: Soma, Yama, and Aṅgiras, as well as the Somapās, the Agniṣvāttas, the Barhiṣads, and the Hutādas— this is the sixfold class of Pitṛs.
The moon, the seasons, the fire that burns the dead,
those invited by Soma, those who have drunk Soma, and Brahmins who have not performed sacrifices.
This group of six is also the consumer of the unoffered oblation (*ahutāda*).
On this point there is a Vedic citation:
"Those ancestors who were slain there in battle became threefold."
Whatever is offered as an oblation in the ancestral sacrifices, that sacrificial food goes to them.

And this is the essential meaning of all this: just as at the time of invocation, deceased ancestors and others are to be meditated upon by the Brāhmaṇa and other castes in the form of Agniṣvātta and the rest.
Thus ends the invitation and the rules for those who have been invited.
The ritual procedure for the śrāddha prior to the invocation.
The procedure for the *śrāddha* prior to the invocation of the ancestors (*agrāvāhana*). Regarding this, Hārīta states under the heading "On the previous day, one should invite the Brāhmaṇas":

"Then, when the next day has dawned, having gone toward the southern direction, one should fetch southward-pointing *darbha* grass along with its roots, as well as water that has not been previously appropriated.
[Yama]
The darbha grass used in the ancestral śrāddha rite should have its roots;
by means of the root, one conquers the worlds of the high-souled Śakra.

The *barhis* grass for the gods consists of *kuśa* blades cut with the tips facing away from the roots. For the ancestors, they are cut near the roots. In the absence of these, all kinds of grass may be used, with the exception of *śūka*, *tṛṇa*, *śara*, *śīrya*, *balbaja*, *mutava*, *nala*, and *śuṇṭha*.

*Śūkatṛṇaṃ* means grass with awns. *Śara*, *śīrya*, and *balvaja* are specific species of grass produced by the intense rays [of the sun], well-known in their respective regions. As stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"The [grass] should be green, along with its roots, glossy, lush, and well-arranged."
Kuśa grass blades, the thickness of a cow’s ear, cut once and including their roots,
as well as dūrvā grass and śyāmāka grain, should be offered with the *pitṛ-tīrtha*.
So too should kāśa, balbaja, and other sharp-hairy grasses.
The muñja grass and the śādvala grass are proclaimed to be the six types of darbha.
In a śrāddha ceremony, one should carefully avoid those who have flat feet, those with hairy calves, and those with hairy ankles.

In the absence of *kuśa* grass, there is a rule for using *dūrvā*, *śyāmāka*, and *kāśa* and so forth. "Pinjūla" means a purifier (*pavitra*). "Samāhitāḥ" means faultless. "Gokarṇamātrāḥ" means the size of a span (*prādeśa*), that is to say, with tips. "Ulapa" is a specific kind of grass resembling *kuśa*.

In the Vāyupurāṇa: "The best kuśa grass for the purpose of a sacrificial seat (prastara) is praised when it is one span (aratni) in length, consecrated according to the rite of the ancestors (pitṛtīrtha), and cut near the base."
Likewise: "In a *śrāddha*, one must always avoid *gundrā*, *kṣīrakuśa*, *balvaja*, *gandhakī*, as well as *vīraṇa*, *colapa*, and *lambā*."

"Prepared" (*saṃskṛtāḥ*) means mixed together. "Grass-bundle" (*prastaraḥ*) here refers to a layering of clods of earth. "Gundra" is *bhadramustaka*. "Milk-kuśa" (*kṣīrakuśaḥ*) is that which has recently sprouted. "Gandhakī" refers to fragrant grasses. "Lambāḥ" are simply long kuśa blades exceeding the stated measurement.
Manu and Bṛhaspati state first:
"One should smear a pure and secluded place with cow dung,
and one should diligently ensure that it slopes toward the south."
In open spaces, in clean places, at the banks of waters,
and indeed in secluded spots, the ancestors are always satisfied by what is offered.
"In open and clean places" means in delightful locations; "in secluded places" means in solitary areas such as forests and the like.
Yama says:
One should avoid for the performance of a śrāddha rite a place that is rough, infested with worms, damp, crowded, foul-smelling, or characterized by unpleasant sounds.
Having examined a pure site that slopes toward the south, is smooth, secluded, and possesses auspicious characteristics, one should then smear it with cow dung.
In secluded dwellings, at sacred fords, by rivers,
and in solitary regions, the ancestors are always gratified.
If one performs the ancestral rite (śrāddha) on land belonging to another,
that śrāddha act is obstructed by the ancestors of the owner of that land.
Therefore, śrāddha offerings should be given with diligence at sacred sites,
on the banks of rivers, at holy fords, and on one's own land.
In secluded places, on slopes, as well as on mountain ridges,
and in solitary dwellings smeared with cow dung.
‘Klinnam’ means muddy; ‘upahvaram’ here refers to the edge of a mountain.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"If a fool offers libations to his own ancestors in the house of another,
the ancestors forcibly seize them from the owner of that land."
Then one should give them the first portion and the price for their livelihood;
here, "the first portion" refers to the substance intended for the śrāddha, and "to them" means to the ancestors who are the owners of that land.
— Yama.
Forests, mountains, sacred rivers, and whatever holy fords there may be—
all these are said to be without owners, for there is no private possession over them.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Formerly, Viṣṇu slew the two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
then Mahendra slew Vṛtra; thereafter the earth was covered by their fat."
For this reason, that ground is known as "Medinī" by people in the world;
therefore, at a *śrāddha* ceremony, it should be smeared with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and likewise purified with firebrands.
Devala says: [The ground] should be covered with white clay and strewn with sesame and mustard seeds;
likewise, the donor, having bathed in the morning along with his garments, should remain self-restrained.
One should begin the meal with new vessels and commence the eating of food together with one's kinsmen.
[117] One should scatter sesame seeds there and bind goats on all sides;
everything defiled by an *asura* is purified by sesame seeds and by a goat.
Then, one should prepare food that is well-prepared, consisting of various condiments and edibles, and abundant in things to be sucked and drunk, according to one's ability.
Then, when midday has not yet passed, he should approach the twice-born whose hair and nails have been trimmed and provide them with a tooth-stick according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer oil for anointing, bathing water, and various kinds of bath-powders with vessels made of udumbara wood, preceded by offerings to the Viśvedevas.
Then, having bathed and returned, he should rise to meet them with palms joined in reverence and offer water for the feet and water for sipping in the proper sequence.
"Annārambhaḥ" refers to the commencement of cooking. "Udumbara" means copper.
At the time of the Śrāddha, one should adorn those invited twice-born men with the work of shaving, bathing the head, fumigation, anointing, and applying collyrium.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "One should bring the water-vessel, the bronze bowl, the stirring-spoon, the sacrificial fuel, and the kuśa grass—
all with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), slowly, toward the south."
Having thus obtained all of that, on the ground in front of the house,
one should prepare a mandala smeared with cow dung and cow urine.
Having worshipped him with unbroken grains and flowers while keeping the sacred thread over the right shoulder,
one should wash the feet of the Brahmins after saluting them again and again.

The "water-pot" (*udapātra*) is for the purpose of washing and so forth; the "bell-metal vessel" (*kāṃsya*) is for the purpose of pouring the sacrificial porridge (*caru*). Now, the mention of the *mekṣaṇa* (stirring-ladle) and other implements belonging to the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* in the ritual manual for the *śrāddha* is intended to show that the *śrāddha* and the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* share a single ritual procedure (*ekatantra*). This is because the *Matsyapurāṇa*, having introduced the single ritual procedure of the *śrāddha* and the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, presents the materials for the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* immediately after the removal of the sacrificial porridge (*carūdvāsana*).
One should offer a seat made of kutapa wool or another pure material;
one should personally wash his feet with humility.
He should say to them, "Be seated," while touching the seats;
they should sit with their right sides toward the center and should not touch one another.
And they should engage in "brahmodya" discussions; this is desired by the ancestors.
"Brahmodyas" are explanations of the Veda, such as "Who indeed wanders alone? and so forth.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

Being self-restrained, pure, dressed in white garments, and standing upon *darbha* grass in the afternoon, he should say, "Welcome. Having offered water for the feet, the guest-offering (*arghya*), and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and having touched the seats, he should cause the Brahmins to sit down after they have grasped them.
In the Brahma Purāṇa:
"There, seats should be provided along with cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass;
and upon each individual seat, lamps with sesame oil should be placed."
[119] Likewise, they should be given without interruption, and they must indeed be protected by the twice-born.
"In the seats" means in the vicinity of the seats; "uninterrupted" means remaining until the completion of the śrāddha.
[Devala and Kūrma Purāṇas: Furthermore, those Brahmins who have previously been invited here for the ancestral rite (pitrya) for the gods—
seats for them should be placed facing east and provided with two blades of darbha grass.
The seats for the ancestors, however, should be arranged facing south,
with a single blade of darbha grass pointing toward the south and sprinkled with water mixed with sesame seeds.
"Facing south" means having their tips pointing toward the south; and "tip-ness" is in relation to the part of the wood that was at the base.
On the new moon day, the highly wise one, having summoned and honored the Brahmins, himself arranged all the grass seats (bṛsī) so that they turned toward the south.
Then, darbha grass with its tips pointing southward was placed upon the seats for the feet of the brahmins who were partaking of the food.
Thus, from the statement in the *Bhārata* (Anuśāsana-parvan, 138.12–14): "Those who turn toward the south" means those whose heads are directed toward the southern direction.
Yājñavalkya [1.226–228]:
Having honored those who have arrived with a welcome in the afternoon,
and having offered them water for sipping (ācamana), he, with purifiers (pavitra) in his hand, should seat them upon their seats.

[120] At a rite for the gods, one should offer an even number of guests according to one's ability, and likewise an odd number at a rite for the ancestors; this should be done in a secluded, pure place that slopes toward the south.
Two [seats] are for the gods, facing east; three for the ancestors, facing north; or even one for each.
The same applies to the maternal grandfathers, or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed as a single common procedure (tantra) for all.
"In an enclosed" means in a screened place. "Facing east" means with faces turned toward the east. Viṣṇu [73.2]:

On the second day, in the forenoon during the bright fortnight or in the afternoon during the dark fortnight, he should cause the Brahmins—who have bathed well and sipped water—to sit down upon seats covered with *kuśa* grass, arranged according to their seniority in learning.

"On the second day" means with reference to the day of the invitation. "According as their learning is greater" means without exceeding those who possess much knowledge, proceeding in order, beginning with the gods. Śātātapa says:
"One should seat two Brāhmaṇas learned in the Atharvaveda facing east for the rite to the gods."
But at the rite for the ancestors, the Rigvedic priest should seat three—namely the Adhvaryu and the Sāmaga priests—facing north.
Manu, Baudhāyana, and Śātātapa state in the first [chapter]:
"One who is well-off should feed two for the gods and three for the ancestral rites, or one for each of both; he should not be overly attached to a large company."
Hospitality, proper time and place, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should not seek prolixity.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "Due to the absence of place, time, or wealth, one may feed either one person at each [of the two rites] or both at each;
the remaining [guests] should be fed in another house according to one's means."
Because of the great number of Brahmins, many faults would arise:
the ruin of the *śrāddha*, the ruin of the silence, and the forgetting of the ritual procedure of the *śrāddha*.
Touching those who have been defiled by food remnants, censuring the giver or those who eat the food, caviling, derision, and various kinds of idle chatter— these are the different [faults].
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa [3.15.17–18]:
One should feed the Brahmins representing the gods facing east;
and one should also feed those representing the ancestors and maternal grandfathers facing north.
Regarding these two, some wise ones say that the performance of the *śrāddha* should be separate;
other great sages declare it should be done together with a single cooking.
Baudhāyana [2.17.12]: The ancestors are situated on his chest; the grandfathers on his left side;
the great-grandfathers on the right; and the funeral cakes are behind him.

‘Those residing in the chest’ (*uraḥsthāḥ*) and so forth refers to the view of a single Brāhmaṇa. ‘Those who desire the *piṇḍa* and the *tarka*’ (*piṇḍatarkakāḥ*) means those who long for the *piṇḍa* offerings and the ritual remains (*lepāḥ*).
Gautama [15.7–8]:
One should feed at least nine [guests]; or an odd number, according to one's ability.

[122] Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra [4.7.1–4]: Now, therefore, regarding the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, the optional (*kāmya*), the *ābhyudayika*, or the *ekoddiṣṭa*: having invited Brahmins endowed with learning, good character, and proper conduct—either individually or all at once—at the proper time; having had them bathe, perform their purificatory rites, and sipping water (*ācamana*); and having seated them facing north as if they were the ancestors; he should seat two, two, or three for each [ancestor], or three for each in the case of an increase, for the sake of greater fruit; but never only one for all. At the first [type of śrāddha], it is optional. This is explained by the rules for the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*).

"By one" means that when these [qualities], such as learning and so forth, are not possible to be possessed collectively, they may be endowed with even any one of them. "Having performed the purification" means having washed their feet; first, having seated the Brāhmaṇas for the Viśvedevas. "Like for the ancestors" means in the order beginning with the father. "Two by two" refers to the subject of the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* (prosperity rite), because other Smṛtis prescribe an odd number of Brāhmaṇas for the *pārvaṇa* and other rites; this is because it is stated at the very beginning of this [text]: "Now, therefore, regarding the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, the optional (*kāmya*), and the *ābhyudayika*. "'Explained by the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*)' means that just as there is a rice-ball for each individual among many ancestors, so too is there a Brāhmaṇa for each individual. 'In the non-initial'—here, the 'initial' is the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa-śrāddha*, which is the beginning of the duties pertaining to the *pārvaṇa*; in a *śrāddha* other than that, whether optional or otherwise, there is one Brāhmaṇa for the ancestors. Regarding 'in the non-initial,' some say that even if there is a lack of edible substances, even a single person should be fed."

Paiṭhīnasi says: Having made the formal resolve, "I shall perform the Śrāddha tomorrow," and having invited seven or five Brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas, being pure himself, he should smear with cow-dung a pure place—either a cow-pen or a fire-sanctuary—and having arranged an offering of flowers, he should seat the Viśvedevas facing east. It is stated in the Śrāddhakalpa that the ancestors are to be seated on seats provided with *barhis* grass toward the south-east.

Baudhāyana says: On the previous day, having invited at the very dawn those who possess good conduct, are learned in the Vedas, are pure, possess the sacred formulas, and are not related by birth, lineage, or mantra—being an odd number, at least three—he should cause them to sit on seats prepared with Darbha grass, facing either east or north.

‘Those possessing conduct’ refers to those established within their own Vedic branch (*śākhā*). ‘Those unconnected with mantras’ refers to those other than disciples and teachers. ‘Those possessing mantras’ refers to those engaged in the study of mantras.

Hārīta [A. 12]: Having completed the preparations for the house, the participants—including women, children, and the elderly—having bathed with fragrant substances, being pure and wearing clean garments, should feed the Brāhmaṇas who have been purified by sipping water (*ācamana*). They should be seated on pure *darbha* grass with the tips pointing south, facing east; some say they should face north. Maitrāyaṇi says that one should not face north because of the previous instruction to face east, for those facing [north] are cruel and become harmful. Therefore, one should feed them facing east. However, in the Vaiśvadeva rite, they should face north, for they thus protect the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

The phrase "they should be dressed in clean clothes" is the ellipsis to be supplied. "Or not" means one should not feed them while they face north. Regarding the phrase "because of the prior direction":

since these [twice-born ones] were previously designated for the sake of the ancestors—being invited through an invitation arranged for that purpose—and because the ancestors attend upon those invited twice-born ones, following them like the wind, they sit near them as they are seated.

Thus, because they are presided over by the ancestors (pitṛs), these [beings] are cruel. Therefore, for a sacrificer performing a śrāddha while facing south, these harmful beings would indeed face him. For that reason, he should himself face south and feed those who are facing east. "Dakṣiṇās" means situated in the southern direction. And this rule regarding the seating of the Brāhmaṇas representing the ancestors, facing east, is established for the followers of the Maitrāyaṇīya school.
Vasiṣṭha [11.29–31]:
Or alternatively, one may feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
who is endowed with learning and good character, and who is free from all inauspicious marks.
If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how should the rite for the gods (daiva) be performed?
Having set aside a portion of all the food prepared, it should be placed in a vessel.
Having performed the *śrāddha* in a temple of the gods, one should proceed accordingly;
one should either cast that food into the fire or give it to a celibate student (*brahmacārin*).
"Devoid of characteristics" refers to leprosy and other such conditions. Śaṅkha says:
"Or else, one may feed a single Brāhmaṇa who purifies the company."
Having first presented the food offering (naivedya) to the deity, one should afterwards offer it to him.
"In the *divya* [rite]" means in the place of the Viśvedevas. "Food offering" (*naivedya*) is that prepared for the sake of the gods. Bṛhaspati [Śrāddhakalpa 86, 88]:
"If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha because the prescribed rite is too small..."
Having set aside small portions from each of those, one should present the food to them.

"Prakṛtam" means the substance appropriate for the *śrāddha*. "Having set aside small portions" means that one should designate the food for the ancestors and others by dividing it into a single vessel; this is the meaning. Thus says Hārīta.
If one who is unworthy should occupy the seat of honor while Arhats are present,
he takes upon himself the entire sin of that row and is deprived of his life-span.
A Brahmin who creates obstacles takes away the misdeeds of four people.
Of food, of the Lord of Food, of the row [of guests], and likewise of those desiring a meal.
[Sumantu: Indeed, for those preeminent in learning and austerity, the foremost seat is prescribed. [126] Yama says:
Generally, a fool who lacks learning and sacred mantras takes the seat of honor due to his own foolishness; he,
being dull-witted, perceives no other danger.
Upon the destruction of the body, there is most terrible hell.
He who, though learned, is neither a student of sacred knowledge nor established in a stage of life, and is not purified by mantras,
yet partakes of sacrificial oblations while standing at the yoke.
Thus he consumes the impurities and sins of the row.
After [the discussion on] those who purify the row (*paṅktipāvana*), Paiṭhīnasi states:

"Each one of them, when appointed at the head of the row, purifies even those defiled by thousands [of sins]. Therefore, one should not go to the seat of honor unless appointed; if he goes, he takes away the evil deeds of the row."
Now, the excellences of the Śrāddha.

In this regard, the causes for the perfection of the Brahmins have been shown by the statement of Yājñavalkya: "The foremost among all those learned in the Vedas," and so forth. Manu also states another [set of requirements] at [3.255–256]: "The afternoon, sesame seeds, *darbha* grass, as well as the preparation of the site, abundance, refinement, and eminent twice-born men—these are the perfections in the rites of *śrāddha*."
Darbha grass, the purifier, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial food (haviṣya),
as well as whatever purifying means were mentioned previously— these should be known as the perfections of the oblation.

‘Vāstu’ here refers to the site for the *śrāddha* ceremony; its ‘preparation’ (*vāstusaṃpādana*) consists of making it slope toward the south, leveling it, smearing it with cow-dung, and so forth. ‘Emission’ (*sṛṣṭi*) means giving away; it is the distribution of food, condiments, and other items without stinginess. [128] ‘Refinement’ (*mṛṣṭi*) is the preparation of the food and such for deliciousness. ‘Prosperities’ (*sampadaḥ*) are riches. ‘Purifier’ (*pavitra*) refers to the mantras. ‘Purifier’ also means that which purifies, such as pure conduct and the like. ‘Previously mentioned’ refers to the preparation of the site and so forth. ‘Havya’ here denotes the rite pertaining to the gods. — Devala.

Darbha grass, sesame seeds, the shadow of an elephant, a daughter’s son, honey and clarified butter, the Kutapa period, and the blue-necked deity (Śiva)— these are the purifiers in rites for the ancestors.
The "blue-throated" one is a blue bull; it is mentioned here in connection with the rites for the ancestors. Yama says:
"One should diligently feed at the *śrāddha* a daughter's son who is observing vows, even if he is a child."
Having offered a seat made of kutapa grass and having scattered sesame seeds over it.

"Even a child"—this refers to Paiṭhīnasi. He states that sesame seeds, a daughter's son, and kutapa wool are purifiers at a śrāddha ceremony; and that they praise truth, the absence of anger, purity, and proper conduct.

Viṣṇu [79.16]: One should offer [the following] as purifying and demon-destroying substances: bird feathers, cow-dung, black antelope skin, sesame seeds, white mustard seeds, and unbroken grains. [129] In the Vāyupurāṇa:
The proximity to, the sight of, and the gift of a black antelope skin destroy demons,
bestow Vedic luster, and grant cattle and sons.
Hārīta says:
Even that which is given silently with *darbha* grass, water, and sesame seeds reaches heaven;
however, when offered according to the prescribed rules in their proper sequence, it is ordained to be inexhaustible.
Offered with darbha grass and other materials according to the mantras upon gold and other substances,
these offerings reach the ancestors inexhaustibly, becoming nectar through great waves.

"Silently" means devoid of the *śrāddha* mantras. This is a praise of the darbha grass and other items when used in their prescribed sequence. "In vessels such as gold," the word "vessels" is to be supplied. "Offered," the phrase "in times of distress" is to be supplied.
Yama says: "The darbha grass protects against the *asuras*; the sesame seeds protect against the *rākṣasas*."
A knower of the Vedas protects food given to an ascetic, making it inexhaustible.
Hārīta says: Sesame seeds protect against the Daityas; Darbha grass protects against the Rākṣasas;
those learned in the Vedas protect the assembly; and what is given to a Snātaka is inexhaustible.
Viṣṇu [18.4]: One should drive away the Yātudhānas with sesame seeds or mustard seeds.
[130] Uśanas said: Kuśas are known as darbhas, and likewise kutapas and vṛsīs;
and those who are the sons of a daughter are proclaimed to be dauhitras.
'Bṛsī' is a specific type of seat; it is a round seat made of grass.
Śātātapa says:
"That which is born on the forehead of a daughter's son like the horn of a rhinoceros—
the vessel for that horn they know as 'dauhitra' (the daughter's-son's portion)."
In the eighth part of the day, the sun becomes mild;
that time is called *kutapa*, and what is given to the ancestors at that time becomes inexhaustible.
Paiṭhīnasi says:
"If a Śrotriya is seen from anywhere at the time of a Śrāddha, he purifies the Śrāddha; therefore, he is designated as a Kutapa."
And in this regard, since the words *kūpa* and *dauhitra* each have multiple meanings, it should be understood that the success of the *śrāddha* rite occurs even when only one of them is employed.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "An ascetic with three staffs, compassion, a silver vessel,
a daughter's son, the *kutapa* time, a goat, and likewise a black antelope skin."
[131] White, black, and likewise wild—these three kinds of sesame seeds were created by Brahmā himself for the satisfaction of the ancestors; these ten [types of offerings] were ordained by him.

Rākṣasas carry off that which is offered without *darbha* grass, mantras, sesame seeds, gold, or silver, even if water is present; therefore, one should not give [an offering] consisting of water alone.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Likewise, a sword, its sheath, a Nepalese blanket,
gold, darbha grass, sesame seeds, cows, and the daughter's son is remembered as the eighth."
They say that "pāpa" is indeed contemptible because it causes torment;
since these eight possess that quality, they are therefore renowned as "kutapa."
Now follows the rite for guests.
In this regard, Yama says: "A mendicant and a celibate student who have arrived seeking food—
if they arrive after others are already seated, one may certainly feed them as well."
If a *yati* does not eat before the sacrificer,
the host of *rakṣasas* seizes what was intended for sacrifice and what has been offered.
The ascetic who, knowing the true nature of the qualities of primordial matter (prakṛti), eats the sacrificial oblation—
indeed, he excels a thousand knowers of the Vedas.
Therefore, a self-controlled ascetic, or a Vedic scholar, or a celibate student, should be fed at the principal seat by the sacrificer; by that, the sacrifice is not impaired.
Where a thousand times a thousand Snātakas eat,
a single knower of Yoga, being pleased, rightfully deserves all of them.

"Has arrived" means as a guest; this is the ellipsis. "Of the sacrificer" refers to one performing a *śrāddha*. Regarding "undesirable": since the host of *rakṣas* seizes both what is sacrificed (*iṣṭa*) and what is offered (*huta*), therefore that which is not sacrificed (*ahuta*) becomes undesirable; such is the meaning. "One who knows the reality of the qualities of *prakṛti*": here *prakṛti* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), as seen in the *Bādarāyaṇa-sūtra*: "And [the Self is] *prakṛti*, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. Its qualities are consciousness, bliss, and so forth. Their "reality" (*tattva*) is their non-difference from its own nature; "one who knows that" is the meaning. "On the foremost seat" means at the head of that very row. "He deserves" means he accepts it for himself.
[133] Chāgaleya said:
One should honor an ascetic who is a fellow student even at the time of a śrāddha rite;
such a person delivers from sin not only the brahmins, but also the hosts of one’s ancestors and maternal kin.
Wherever ascetics and celibate students eat,
there the ancestors and gods receive [the offering], and he too attains the supreme goal.
And they deliver the donor—likewise his sons, his wife, and his ancestors.
Therefore, with every effort, one should honor a guest who has arrived at one's hermitage.
If monks who practice meditation cannot be found, one should feed a celibate student;
if even he is unavailable, one should feed a layperson who is indifferent to worldly affairs.
A single ascetic (yati) excels over thousands of celibate students (brahmacārins), hundreds of forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas), and thousands of householders (gṛhasthas).
One should honor the ascetic, who brings satisfaction to the ancestors, at a śrāddha ceremony with perfumes, garlands, fruits, and foods prepared with milk.
A celibate student and an ascetic are indeed always worthy of honor;
whatever merit they perform, one shall receive a sixth part of that from them.
Since recitation, yoga, and sacrifice are derived from him, he is remembered as the triad;
salutation and worship offered to him become inexhaustible.
A student, as well as a forest-dweller or an ascetic, may go to the householder’s hermitage;
there he should offer himself, as well as food, drink, fruit, and flowers.
What is given to ascetics who are constantly engaged in yoga, who have abandoned passion, who are practitioners of austerity,
and who have desisted from all undertakings, is inexhaustible.
Food that is offered with great reverence to an ascetic who is free from passion does not perish,
even after hundreds of millions of eons, through the power of that faith.
Both the student and the ascetic are the rightful owners of cooked food;
those who cook for themselves fall, and the ascetic falls even more so.
If one should bypass a yogi and instead feed a householder, [the merit is lost].
One does not obtain that fruit; rather, one causes the entire lineage to fall.
Having bypassed the yogi, they honor one another;
both the giver and the enjoyer go to hell along with their kinsmen.
The course of worldly life does not proceed through the giving of one to another according to the Dharma;
therefore, one should give with effort, otherwise one will fall.

"Along with fellow religious practitioners" means accompanied by those practicing the holy life (*brahmacārin*). The phrase "in the absence [of others]" is intended to indicate that even when meditators (*dhyānabhikṣu*) and others arrive together, each preceding one is superior. "Ascetic" (*tapasvin*) refers to a renunciant (*yati*). "He should inform" means he should announce it. "Lineage" (*gotra*) means family. "He would cause to fall" implies that the renunciant has transgressed; this is the ellipsis. "Mutual gifts" means gifts to one another should not be made. For "that is worldly conduct, not according to the Dharma"—here the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is used in the sense of a simple prohibition (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), as in the case of "one who does not eat at a funeral feast" (*aśrāddhabhojī*). The suffix *-tasi* is added to the nominative form "according to the Dharma" (*dharmataḥ*). "Otherwise" means by means of mutual giving.
Manu [3.283]: A Brahmin who has arrived for the purpose of begging food should be honored according to one's ability, with the permission of the other Brahmins.
[135] Śātātapa says: That *śrāddha* in which a guest does not eat is not praised;
nor is that which is eaten by those devoid of Vedic learning and vows, or by those who are not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*).
In another work by Śātātapa:
"Those ignorant twice-born who eat at a śrāddha ceremony devoid of hospitality for guests,
they go to the womb of a crow through that food and drink prepared in vain."
Now, those who are to be avoided.
In this regard, Manu [3.239–241] states: "A Caṇḍāla, a pig, and likewise a cock, a woman in her menses, and a eunuch— these must not look upon twice-born men while they are eating."
Whatever is looked upon by these [outcastes] during the giving of a house, at a meal,
or in rites for the gods and the ancestors, that becomes ineffective.
The boar kills by means of its smell, and the cock by the wind from its wings.
A dog [is purified] by the falling of a glance, and one born of a low caste by touch.

‘Ayathātatham’ means the opposite of that for which [the act] is performed. The phrase ‘a cock by the wind of its wings,’ and so forth, is a qualification of proximity intended for exclusion; the meaning is that they should be removed from whatever area the wind of the wings of cocks and other such birds might be expected to reach. ‘Avaravarṇajaḥ’ refers to a Śūdra.
Yama said: A cock, a village pig, a crow, a dog, and a cat;
the husband of a low-caste woman, a low-caste man, a eunuch, and a menstruating woman—these are [impure].
These should always be avoided at the times of the śrāddha rite;
for a cock, by the wind of its wings, destroys an unenclosed śrāddha.
The village pig [is repelled] by the sense of smell, the crow by its cry,
the dog by the casting of a glance, and the cat by the sound of hearing.
The husband of a *vṛṣalī* destroys [merit] with his gift; likewise, the *vṛṣala* with his eyes;
the eunuch with his shadow; and the menstruating woman with her touch.
Lame, one-eyed, with a withered arm, or afflicted with leprosy, he shall become the servant of the donor;
moreover, one who has missing limbs or redundant limbs shall quickly lead him [to the king] from there.
Devala says: One with missing limbs, an outcast, a leper, one with ulcers, a Pulkasa, an atheist,
a cock, a pig, and a dog— these should be avoided from afar at Śrāddha ceremonies.
One should avoid that which is loathsome, impure, naked, intoxicated, deceitful, or a woman in her menses; likewise, one should avoid those wearing blue or saffron robes, and those with severed ears.
One should avoid weapons, iron, lead, and those dressed in soiled garments; likewise, one should avoid stale food when visiting shrines.
‘Bībhatsa’ refers to a distorted object that causes agitation. One who wears soiled garments is ‘malināmbaravāsāḥ’.

In the Mahābhārata: "A woman who is menstruating, as well as one who is deformed in her ears, should not stand by at the funeral offering; nor should she be accepted [as a wife] if she is born of another lineage."

"In the *nirvāpa*," that is, in the śrāddha rite beginning from the commencement of the cooking; "born of another lineage" means not connected to the lineages of one's mother or father; "should not be accepted" means she should not be employed [in the ritual].

[138] Viṣṇu [81,5–10]: One should not perform a *śrāddha* in an enclosed space. One should not look at a woman in her menses, nor a dog, nor a village pig, nor a village cock. One should, with great care, allow a goat to look upon the *śrāddha*.
Furthermore, Viṣṇu [81,15–17]:
Those with missing or extra limbs must not see the śrāddha; nor Śūdras; nor outcasts;
nor those afflicted with major diseases.
Uśanas says:
A village pig, a cat, a cock, a mongoose, a Śūdra, a menstruating woman, and the husband of a Śūdra woman must be removed to a distance.
Bṛhaspati [Śrāddhakāṇḍa, 48–50]: Outcastes, eunuchs, calumniators, dogs, cocks, pigs, women in their courses, and Cāṇḍālas must not be allowed to see the Śrāddha ceremony.
One should give [the food] in an enclosed space, or one should scatter the ground with sesame seeds;
then, seated there, the purifier of the row (paṅktipāvana) should pour out that defect.
A *śvapāka* is a specific class of the lowest caste (*antyajāti*). Hārīta states:
"Whether at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors, if one who has drunk liquor should touch [the food or the vessel]," [it becomes unfit].
For a woman who is menstruating or unchaste indeed consorts with a Rakshasa.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "Naked mendicants and others should not see the śrāddha; this is the established rule. For if they see it, [the offerings] do not reach the fathers or the grandfathers."
The triple Veda is remembered as the covering for all beings;
those who abandon it out of delusion are indeed people such as the naked ones.
The Buddhist Śrāvakas, the Nirgranthas, the Śākyas, the Jīvakas, and the Kāpilas—
those who follow such doctrines are indeed people such as the naked ones and others.
The man who wears matted hair in vain, who is shaven-headed in vain, and who is naked in vain—
those people, such as the naked ones, are indeed equal to those who have committed the great sins (mahāpātakin).
Those who pride themselves on their lineage yet are like corpses, hunters, and those who strike with their fists—
these, resorting to evil deeds, are proclaimed to be those on the wrong path.
One who has shaken off [impurities] by these means is seen to go to the Dānavas;
likewise, those who delight in sinful speech toward the deities and the ṛṣis are seen to go to the Asuras and the Yātudhānas.
A eunuch, one who has been cast off, a hen, and a village pig.
A dog indeed destroys all *śrāddha* offerings by its mere sight;
so too does a place defiled by a dog, a jackal, or a pig, as well as by those suffering from chronic diseases.
It must never be seen by those who are outcasted or impure;
whatever food these might see would not be fit for offerings to the gods or the ancestors.
The principal substance must be discarded; however, purification is prescribed in times of distress.
For substances consecrated with oblation-material, purification must indeed be performed first.
Sprinkling with water mixed with clay is prescribed;
and scattering with white mustard seeds and black sesame seeds should likewise be performed.

Or, one should diligently seek a vision of the Guru, the Sun, or Fire. "Bauddha-śrāvaṇakas and others" refers to specific heretics (*pākhaṇḍas*). "Those who pride themselves on their lineage" (*kulatvamāninaḥ*) are those who have abandoned proper conduct out of an obsession with their family status. "Śāvas" are those who carry the dead. "Muṣṭika" is a wrestler. "For the sake of the principal purpose" means for the sake of the *śrāddha* rite. "It should be discarded" means that it must not be employed in the *śrāddha*. However, in the event of unavailability, after performing the purificatory rites beginning with sprinkling using water mixed with clay, up to the point of showing a goat, it may be employed; this is the collective meaning.
Now, the General Explanations of the Ritual Procedure.
Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"The daily *śrāddha* should be without a deity (*adaiva*), and likewise the *ekoddiṣṭa*;
however, the *śrāddha* for the mother should be performed separately with an even number [of Brahmins], without a deity, and facing the east."
One should diligently perform other Śrāddhas preceded by the deities;
likewise, one should always offer the Śrāddha in this manner and cause it to proceed with those [deities] at its head.
Otherwise, however, the asuras and rākṣasas always plunder it.
"Preceded by that" means preceded by the gods;
as stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"In a *śrāddha* for the ancestors or likewise for the gods, one should not touch anything that has not been sprinkled with water."
One should take [the fire] from the north of the altar and dismiss it to the south.
"Vedi" here refers to the place for the śrāddha ceremony, such as ground sloping toward the south. "Daive" means in the śrāddha for the gods.
Manu [3.203–205]: For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors is more distinguished than the rite for the gods.
For it is traditionally taught that the rite for the gods is the primary means of strengthening the rite for the ancestors.
One should first employ a deity as their protector;
for the *rakṣasas* plunder a *śrāddha* that is devoid of protection.
One should pursue that which begins and ends with the divine; it should not begin and end with the ancestors.
For one who pursues that which begins and ends with the ancestors perishes swiftly, along with his lineage.

‘Āpyāyana’ is that which brings about the prosperity of the principal rite of the ancestral śrāddha, being its subsidiary (aṅga) rather than being itself a primary rite. ‘Ārakṣabhūta’ means that which provides protection on all sides. ‘Daivādyanta’ means that which has the deities at its beginning and end. By this it is meant that the invitations should be performed starting with the deities, while the dismissal (visarjana) should be done in the reverse order.
Devala says: Whatever rite is performed for the ancestors with respect to the Brahmins,
all of that must be performed preceded by the Vaiśvadeva offering.
Bṛhaspati [Śrāddhakāṇḍa, 91–94]:
Ṛtu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Satya, Kāla, and likewise Kāma; Dhuri and Rocana, and also Purūravas.
These ten, including Mārdrava, are proclaimed as the Viśvedevas:
Dakṣa is for the performer of an *iṣṭi* sacrifice, Satya for the *śrāddha*, and Vasu for the *nāndīmukha*.
Naimittika and Kālakāma are prescribed for the occasional rite (naimittika), while Dhuri and Rocana are for the optional rite (kāmya); Purūravas and Mārdrava are declared for the Pārvaṇa śrāddha.
Those twice-born ones who do not know the origin and the names of these [sacred sites] should recite this verse with full faith:
May the illustrious Viśvedevas, the bestowers of boons, come;
may they who have been appointed to this śrāddha rite remain attentive.

[143] *Iṣṭiśrāddha* is a voluntary *śrāddha*. *Naimittika* is the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) rite. *Ekoddiṣṭa* is that which is performed for one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) and others, in the manner of the *pārvaṇa* rite; this is because the Viśvedevas are not present therein. Śātātapa says:
"One should face north toward the gods, but face south toward the ancestors."
One should offer [the food] at the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha according to the rule, preceded by the deities.

Kātyāyana, in the *Śrāddhakalpa* [1.1.24–25; 1.2.1–5], states: From the invitation (*āvāhana*) until the ritual sipping of water (*upasparśana*), one should remain silent. Those who have been invited are likewise [to remain silent]. For the *śrāddha* begins with the deities (*daiva*). The procedure for the ancestral rite (*pitrya*) is like that of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. However, the *darbha* grasses used should be doubled. One should offer everything while seated, with the *pavitra* blades held in hand. Regarding questions, he asks the head of the row (*paṅktimūrdhanya*).

Because of the statement, "Or [the rites] for the ancestors are all [performed with doubled grass]," they perform even the libations and other such acts for the ancestors using doubled *kuśa* blades, and not with straight ones alone.
Manu [3.289]: Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the offering properly made counter-clockwise, unwearied,
and holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should perform the ancestral rite according to the rules until its conclusion.
‘Apasavyam’ means on the left side. ‘Atandriṇā’ means by one who is not lazy. ‘Ānidhanāt’ means until the completion.
Kātyāyana states in the Chandogapariśiṣṭa [1.23]:
“One should always keep the right knee bent when attending upon the gods.”
One should always keep the other knee on the ground while attending upon the ancestors.
Thus ends the section on the Vedic injunctions and traditional expositions (*vidhibhāṣā*) in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmīdhara.
Now follows the procedure for the seat for recitation and so forth.
Now, the procedures for the seat, the offering, the invocation, and the presentation of the *arghya* and *pādya* waters.
Regarding this, the *Brahma Purāṇa* states:
"Having sat down, the wise man should recite the *Gāyatrī* with her permission."
Likewise: "I shall therefore proclaim the mantra fashioned by Brahmā, which removes sin, is purifying, yields the fruit of the horse sacrifice, and is like nectar."
"May there be constant salutation to the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis; may there be *svadhā* and *svāhā* forever."
At the beginning and at the end of the Śrāddha, it should always be performed three times;
for this yields the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice when one is honored and worshipped by the twice-born.
Or, while offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), one should recite this with a concentrated mind;
for when the time for the śrāddha ceremony has arrived, one should listen to this as it is being recited.
The ancestors arrive quickly and the Rākṣasas flee.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
Having first offered a seat, one should worship the Viśvedevas with barley and flowers.
One should fill a pair of vessels after placing them upon *darbha* grass purifiers.

Yājñavalkya [1.220–235]: Having given water for washing the hands and also *kuśa* grass for the seats, he should, being authorized, invoke the Viśvedevas with the verse beginning "O Viśvedevas... (*viśvedevāsaḥ*).
Then, having scattered barley grains into a vessel containing a *pavitra* grass ring,
he should pour water with the verse "śanno devīr" and likewise scatter barley grains with the formula "yavo 'si."
With the mantra "yā divyā," one should pour the *arghya* water into their hands;
having offered water, one should then present perfumes, incense, garlands, and lamps.
Likewise, he should give a cloth for covering and water for the purpose of washing the hands;
then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), he should perform the circumambulation of the ancestors in a counter-clockwise direction.
Having folded the kuśa grass twofold and having invoked the ancestors with the verse "uśantas tvā," he should, being authorized by them, recite the mantra "āyantu naḥ."
[Having scattered sesame seeds all around with the words "apahatāḥ,"] one should perform the functions of barley using sesame seeds, and offer the *arghya* and other rites as before.
Having given the remnants to them and placed them in the vessel according to the rule,
he then turns the vessel face down on the ground with the words, "Thou art the station of the ancestors."

‘Pāṇiprakṣālanaṃ’ (hand-washing): that by which one washes is ‘prakṣālanaṃ’, namely water. ‘Viṣṭarārtham’: for the purpose of a seat. ‘Anujñātaḥ’: permitted. From the very word ‘permitted,’ the question beginning with ‘I shall invoke the Viśve Devas’ is to be understood as having occurred previously by implication. ‘Yavair anvavakīrya’: having scattered barley after the invocation for the sake of a seat. ‘Yavo ’sīti’: with the mantra beginning ‘Thou art barley, the king of grains. ‘Āyantu na’ iti: the mantra beginning ‘May our ancestors come. ‘Yavārthāḥ’: the purposes of the barley, such as scattering and so forth. [146] ‘Saṃsravāḥ’: the drops of water flowing together when the *arghya* offering is being given. ‘Teṣāṃ’: of those *arghya* waters. ‘Nyubjaṃ’: face downwards. ‘Adhaḥ’: on the ground.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "Having offered the *arghya* with the verse beginning 'yā divyā,' one should then give the perfumes and other offerings;
having given the upper garment and so forth in due order, as well as the remnants of the water-offering (*saṃsravaṇa*) and the rest."
Then, having set down the vessel for the ancestors, one should place it face-down to the north.

"Vastrottaram" means that in which the gift of clothing is the "uttaram," that is, the final [gift] among the offerings of perfumes and so forth; it is thus. "Anupūrvam" means in due order. "Saṃsravaṇam" refers to the water of the residue. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of sesame seeds, flowers, and purifiers (pavitra). "Uttarataḥ" means in the northern direction from the seated Brāhmaṇa.
Kātyāyana in the Śrāddhakalpa [2.5–14]:

Having spread *darbha* grass upon the seats, he asks, "Shall I invoke the Viśvedevas? Being permitted with the words, "Invoke them," he invokes them with the verse, "O Viśvedevas, come hither! Having scattered [the grass], he mutters, "O Viśvedevas, hear this! He then asks, "Shall I invoke the ancestors? Being permitted with the words, "Invoke them," he invokes them with the verse, "Desiring you... Having scattered [the grass], he mutters, "May they come to us... Into each of the sacrificial wooden cups (*camasa*) containing a *pavitra* filter, he pours water with the verse, "The divine waters... Into each one, he scatters sesame seeds with the formula: "Thou art sesame, belonging to the ancestors as deities; thou art the cow-sacrifice (*gosava*), created by the gods. Mixed with ancient waters and the *svadhā* offering, do thou gratify the worlds of our ancestors, svāhā! In vessels made of gold, silver, copper, rhinoceros horn, or precious stones—or in whatever other vessels are available, or even in leaf-cups—he gives [water] to each guest using one vessel at a time, while their hands hold the *pavitra* filters, with the formula: "The celestial waters which have arisen together with the milk, those which are in the atmosphere and those which are on earth—those golden-colored, worthy of sacrifice, auspicious waters, may they be propitious, pleasant, and easy to invoke for us. Then he says, "O So-and-so, this is your *argha* (offering). Having poured the remnants from all the vessels into the first vessel, he places that vessel face down with the formula, "Thou art the place for the ancestors. At this point, there is the presentation of perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.
The word ‘asau’ (this one), ending in the vocative case, is an elliptical expression for the name of the father or others. ‘Attra’ (here) means at this time.
[Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 4.7.5–14].

Having offered water, having offered a seat made of *darbha* grass folded double, and having offered water again; then, having poured water into three vessels—made of metal, stone, or clay, or into one vessel of the same material—over which *darbha* grass has been placed, he consecrates them with the verse, "The divine waters for our aid," and pours sesame seeds into them with the formula: "Thou art sesame, whose deity is Soma; created by the gods at the Gosava sacrifice; offered by the ancients, do thou, through the *svadhā* offering, gratify these Pitṛs and these worlds for us: *svadhā*! Homage! [He does this] with the palm turned toward the left (the *prasavya* manner). With his right hand, assisted by the left, using the space between the thumb and forefinger because he is wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītin*), he offers the *arghya* water, saying: "O Father, this is your *arghya*; O Grandfather, this is your *arghya*. This is done without repetition. When he is about to have them accept the water, he says once for each: "The *arghyas*, *svadhā*! When they have released their hands from the vessels, he should consecrate the water with the verse: "The celestial waters that have come together upon the earth, those that are in the atmosphere and those that are on the earth—those waters, golden-hued and worthy of sacrifice, may they be auspicious and pleasant for us. Having collected the overflow water (the remains) together, he anoints his face with that water if he desires a son.
One should not lift up first the vessel from which the *arghya* was offered to the ancestors;
Śaunaka has declared that the ancestors remain there, enveloped [by the water].
If a Brāhmaṇa weak in knowledge should lift up that vessel,
that Śrāddha becomes unfit to be eaten by the hosts of ancestors who have departed in anger.
At this time, there is the offering of perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and coverings.

"Having provided *darbha* grass as a seat" means having offered *darbha* grass to serve as the seating. "In vessels made of metal, stone, or clay" refers to those fashioned from these three materials respectively for the ancestors and others. "In vessels made of a single material" means, in the event that the three materials are unavailable, those made of a single kind of substance such as clay and so forth. "With the left hand" (*prasavyena*) means with the left hand; moreover, not merely with the left alone, but "between the thumb and [other fingers] of the other hand," that is, by means of the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part between the thumb and forefinger) of the other, namely the right hand. By this, the following is stated: holding the *arghya* vessel with the left hand and touching the *pitṛ-tīrtha* with the right hand, the water should be given in such a way that it falls into the hands of the Brahmins.
Then, having taken the cups in sequence with the left hand,
one should pour that water with the right hand using the *pitṛ-tīrtha*.

This is according to the statement in the *Brahma Purāṇa*. The reason for this very point is given as "because it is the sacred thread (*upavīta*). Just as one becomes an *upavītī* (one wearing the sacred thread) while performing a rite with the right hand by means of the sacrificial thread resting on the left shoulder, so too one becomes an *upavītī* while performing a rite with the left hand by means of the sacrificial thread resting on the right shoulder. "One should offer the *arghya* waters with the right hand, or with the right hand supported by the left" means that one should give the *arghya* waters with the right hand alone, or with the right hand grasped by the left. "When the waters have been poured out" means when the water has been offered. "One should not lift up the vessel first" means before the previously mentioned time for lifting [the vessel].
The Baijavāpa-gṛhya.

Having prepared the food and seated the even-numbered Brāhmaṇas—who are blameless and learned in the Vedas—in accordance with their rank, he, wearing the *prācīnāvīta* cord, places vessels filled with water, along with *darbha* grass and sesame seeds, to the west of the fire upon *darbha* grass. Standing, he announces, "I shall invoke the ancestors," and having invoked the father and grandfather of the sacrificer by name with the verse "May they come to us" (*uśantas tvā*), he recites "May our fathers come" (*āyantu naḥ pitaraḥ*) and then assigns the vessels [to them]. Having poured the contents of the vessels into the joined palms of the Brāhmaṇas, saying, "O Father, this is your *arghya*; O Grandfather, this is your *arghya*; O Great-grandfather, this is your *arghya*," he pours the remainder over the *darbha* grass, saying, "May there be inexhaustibility for the ancestors."

"Having given the remainder of the *arghya*," meaning the remaining *arghya* still contained in the vessel; "upon the *darbha* grasses," which have been prepared for the purpose of supporting the *arghya* vessel.
Śāṅkhāyanagṛhyasūtra 4.1.2–4:

Having seated an odd number of Brāhmaṇas who are knowers of the Veda—at least three—as representatives of the ancestors, he should scatter sesame seeds into an odd number of water-vessels and, having assigned them by saying, "O [Name], this is for you," he should pour [the water] into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas.
‘Tryavarārghyāḥ’: those among the Brāhmaṇas in whom there are three or fewer as the minimum number;
thus says the Nigama.

Day after day, having honored [the guests] with a barber’s service, oil massage, rubbing, bathing, and the cleaning of teeth, and having welcomed those who have arrived and bathed by offering water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-offering (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), *darbha* grass seats, ointments, incense, and flowers, he asks: "Shall I invite the ancestors and others? He prepares double-folded *darbha* blades for each of the paternal ancestors, as well as for the maternal grandfather and the maternal great-grandfather, in case of an increase in the number of guests; having placed these on the seats and drawn other lines from the feet, he makes them upon the southern line. He fills four metal bowls (*camasa*)—mixed with sacrificial rice, sesame, milk, curd, honey, and ghee—with water using the *Mahāvyāhṛtis*, the verse *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, and the verse *śanno devīḥ*. Having offered these by pouring them out crosswise like the portions of oblation (*avadāna*), he sprinkles water into their hands while pronouncing the names, and for the maternal grandfather and others, he uses the fourth [name].

"Day after day" (*śvaḥśvaḥ*) means on the second day following the day of invitation. "Worship of the barber" (*nāpitābhyarcanam*) refers to the grooming of the nails and so forth. "In the repetition on account of prosperity" (*vṛddhāvabhyāse*) means that when there is a "repetition" (*abhyāse*) of the *śrāddha* due to a cause of prosperity (*vṛddhinimittake*), the invocation and other rites must be performed for each deity individually, such as the mother, maternal grandfather, and others. "Other metal vessels" (*anyān lauhān*) refers to those made of copper and similar materials. "Four" (*catura*) means three vessels for the ancestors beginning with the father, and one for those beginning with the maternal grandfather, because it is stated that "the fourth is for the maternal grandfather and others. "Garland" (*srak*) refers to strung flowers. "Having interlaced" (*vyatiṣaṅgam*) "with them"—that is, with the water—is the ellipsis to be supplied. "Like the portioning" (*avadānavat*) means according to the ritual rule for the *avadāna* (cutting of portions). 1.151.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: Having placed the garment and the sacrificial thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), having scattered sesame seeds, and having poured water mixed with fragrant sesame seeds into the vessels, he should request permission from the Brāhmaṇas with the mantra "śaṃ no devīḥ. Then, saying "I shall invoke the ancestors," and having invoked them with "uśantas tvā," he should pour water into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas, which have been separated by purifiers (pavitra).
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "I shall invoke the gods," he says; and while they are being invoked, having taken hold of the thumb of the Brahmin, he should summon the Viśvedevas.
Then, observing silence, one should mutter the mantra: "O Viśvedevas, come hither!
And for a second time, one should mutter the mantra: "O Viśvedevas, listen!"
One should recite the third mantra, which is ancient and increases merit:
"Oṃ, may the highly fortunate Viśvedevas, the bestowers of boons, come hither."
May those who have been invited to this *śrāddha* be attentive.
Here is for you water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), flowers, incense, and unguent.
"This lamp-light is offered to the Viśvedevas;
I shall now invoke the ancestors," he should then say to the remaining Brahmins.
When told by them, "Invoke [the deity]," he should say, "Be attentive," and then offer this water for the feet (*pādya*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*), using the name in the dative case.
I shall worship the fathers,
the grandfathers, and all the great-grandfathers, as well as their fathers, in due order with food.
Then, while muttering the mantra "uśantas tvā," he should invoke the ancestors:
those who partake of Soma, those who sit on the sacrificial grass (barhiṣad), and those others who are consumed by fire (agniṣvātta).
"May all our ancestors, meritorious and illustrious, come to us"—
having said this, he should then scatter sesame seeds in that house in a counter-clockwise direction.
Endowed with supreme faith, one should recite the mantra "apahatās tv" (the spirits are driven away).
Then, [he should place the offerings] in vessels made of sacrificial wood, accompanied by kuśa grass.
Having taken up the purifiers (*pavitra*) while reciting the *śanno devī* mantra, one should cast them [into the fire];
and upon them, one should scatter sesame seeds while reciting the sequence beginning with *tilo ’si*.
Having worshipped them according to the scriptures with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and perfumes,
one should then take up the cups in sequence with the left hand.
With the sacred thread over the right shoulder (pitṛtīrtha), he should offer that water with his right hand,
having placed darbha grass and water in their hands, to each of the brahmins individually.
While reciting the mantra "yā divyā āpaḥ," one should then offer [the water], saying:
"O [Name], of the [Name] lineage, may this water with sesame seeds be for you."
Having said, "This is the *arghya* for you," he should then give it to them eightfold:
water, milk, curd, ghee, sesame seeds, rice, and mustard seeds.
Having given auspicious tips of *kuśa* grass and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) himself,
he should then offer beautiful fragrant substances, saying, "This is your fragrance."
Having said, "And this is the flower," one should offer the flowers;
then, having said, "This is the incense for you," one should burn it before them.
Having said, "This is your lamp," one should present a pleasing lamp;
and according to one's means, a pair of fine garments that are not worn out and are auspicious.
Having said, "This garment is for you," he should offer the triad;
or, having said, "This garland is for you," he should give a most beautiful garland.
One should offer white sandalwood, camphor, auspicious flowers,
