and whatever else is pleasing to the ancestors, for the purpose of anointing.

‘Maunī’ means one who has ceased from uttering speech other than that which is prescribed. The third mantra, beginning with ‘āgacchantu’, is to be understood as pertaining to the origin, names, and specific seats of the Viśvedevas, in accordance with the statement of Bṛhaspati: “Their origin and name... and so forth. ‘Caturthyantaṃ’ means in the form: “O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, this is for you. ‘Sakuśeṣu’ means accompanied by kuśa grass in the form of *pavitra* strainers. ‘Śāstravat’ means with the prescribed perfumes, flowers, and so on. ‘Aṣṭadhā’ refers here to the eightfold nature based on the eight types of substances. ‘And whatever else is dear to the ancestors,’ such as silver and so forth, or whatever is desired by the living ancestors and others.
Likewise, he who desires a son should look into those vessels for the remnants filled with water; facing the east, he should recite the mantra.
And [he recites]: "May the worlds, the abodes of the ancestors, be purified; you are the abode of the ancestors."

Then, one should worship those ancestors with water for the feet, respectful offerings, flowers, and so forth, beginning with the paternal ancestors, while those offering vessels remain covered with lids.
Likewise:
Vessels that have leaked should be avoided in rites for the ancestors or the gods;
in ancient times, the Earth was milked by the ancestors using a vessel made of silver.
Therefore, the *svadhā* mantra is always more dear to them than that;
for this reason, one should cause the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings to be prepared in a silver vessel, even when the occasion is minor.
Having given [a gift] in a vessel made of gold, that man shall become handsome;
having given in a vessel made of jewels, he shall become the lord of all jewels;
in a vessel made of *pālāśa* wood he becomes endowed with the splendor of Brahman, and in one of *aśvattha* wood he shall obtain a kingdom.
By giving a vessel made of udumbara wood, one becomes the lord of all beings;
by giving a vessel made of nyagrodha wood, however, one obtains progeny, contentment, and prosperity.
By giving [an offering] in a vessel made of *kāśmarī* wood to one who destroys demons, one obtains merit and fame;
furthermore, by giving it in a vessel made of *mādhūka* or *phalgu* wood, one obtains good fortune and prosperity.
By offering [food] in a vessel made of white Arka and Mandāra wood, one becomes wise;
by using a Bilva leaf-vessel, one obtains wealth, intelligence, and a long life.
Then, having placed it in a lotus-petal vessel, one becomes beloved by the sages;
or likewise, it may be sprinkled with honey and ghee, or simply as available.
"Srastabhāṇḍam" means broken vessels. "Phalgupātram" refers to a vessel made of wood or udumbara.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa it is said:
"Likewise, among the arghya, piṇḍas, and food offerings for the ancestors, silver is best."
One should diligently avoid inauspicious things during rites dedicated to the gods.

Regarding the injunction "one should avoid," Viṣṇu states: [79.5–11] One should avoid flowers that have a pungent odor, those that are odorless, those produced from thorny plants, and those that are red. One may offer white flowers that are fragrant, even if they are produced from thorny plants; likewise, one may offer water-born flowers, even if they are red. One should not offer fat, marrow, or similar substances for the purpose of a lamp. And nothing derived from living beings should be used for incense. One should offer oil and clarified butter. One should offer guggulu resin mixed with honey and clarified butter. Sandalwood, saffron, camphor, agallochum, and padmaka wood are for the purpose of anointing.

In the phrase "fat, marrow, and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (ādi), it is understood that other such substances originating from living beings are likewise to be avoided. Regarding "one should give oil and ghee," the words "for the purpose of a lamp" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Śaṅkha says: "Those produced in water should be given, especially those that are red."
A woolen thread, or else a new one made of cotton, should be provided.
A wise person should avoid [garments] that have reached their tenth stage, even if they are made of new cloth,
as well as those with a pungent odor, those that are odorless, and those produced from trees at a shrine (caitya).
Flowers that are red in color should be avoided;
furthermore, a lamp should be offered with either ghee or sesame oil.
For the purpose of incense, one should offer guggulu mixed with ghee and abundant honey.
[156] In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: White *sumanas* flowers are best, as are lotuses and water-lilies.
And those others which have arisen as scent and form in their entirety.
The *japā* flower, the *bhāṇḍī*, the *ruṣikā*, and the *kuraṇṭaka*—
these flowers are always to be avoided in the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*).
From the words *japā* and so forth, such red flowers are indicated. *Bhāṇḍī* is *mañjiṣṭhā*. *Rūṣikā* is the flower of the *arka* plant. *Kuruṇṭaka* is the yellow flower of the *amlātaka*.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"One should avoid those that have a pungent odor, those that are odorless, and those that are defective."
Both sandalwood and agallochum, as well as ushira and padmaka;
One should burn turuṣka and guggulu together, smeared with clarified butter;
one should not offer clarified butter alone, nor spoiled grass-guggulu.
"Turuṣka" is the resin of the *siṃhaka* tree; "tṛṇaguggulu" is *sarjarasa*. In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Everything that is most excellent in the world, and whatever is dear to oneself..."
Everything should be given to the ancestors by one who desires that very gift to become inexhaustible.
The giver of food obtains an imperishable, divine celestial mansion made of Jāmbūnada gold, resembling the sun and filled with divine apsarases.
But he who gives a new, unwashed garment at the time of the Śrāddha rite obtains long life, the fulfillment of desires, sovereignty, and auspicious beauty.
He who, knowing the Dharma, gives a sacred thread at the time of a śrāddha ceremony,
obtains the fruit of a gift of the Veda, which is the purifier of all brāhmaṇas.
If a brahmin should give a water-pot at the time of a śrāddha rite,
a cow that flows with honey and milk follows after the donor.
He who gives a water-pot with a wheel-engraved handle at the time of a śrāddha ceremony obtains a divine cow that yields milk simply by being placed upon a jar.
He who gives sandals filled with cotton during the performance of a śrāddha rite obtains a beautiful vehicle and happiness for his feet.
One should give a fan and a palm-leaf whisk, honored with respect, to a Brahmin;
[thereby] one shall obtain things that are pleasant to the touch, fragrant, and soft.
At ancestral rites, a wise man should always give sandals to the Brahmins;
he thereby obtains divine vision as well as chariots yoked with horses.
Whoever should give an excellent parasol adorned with flower garlands,
that supreme palace indeed follows after him as he goes.
Having given a refuge filled with jewels, along with beds, seats, and food,
to the ancestors during a *śrāddha* ceremony, one is glorified in the vault of heaven.
Pearls, lapis lazuli, garments, and various kinds of jewels;
as well as ten thousand and hundreds of millions of preeminent vehicles.
He certainly obtains a divine celestial chariot that resembles a great blazing fire, is endowed with all objects of desire, and possesses the radiance of the moon and sun.
Surrounded by Apsarases, traveling at will and with the speed of thought,
he indeed dwells at the forefront of the celestial chariot while being praised by the best of the gods.
There, the Gandharvas and Apsarases sprinkle divine flowers, or indeed rain them down in full showers, while singing and playing musical instruments.
They are constantly awakened by the charming and melodious sounds of the laughter and ornaments of maidens, young women, and those of middle age.
A lodging for yogins is superior to the gift of a thousand horses, a hundred chariots,
and indeed a thousand elephants.
That man who offers a radiant sacred thread (*pavitra*) to yogis in the water obtains the fruit of a thousand *niṣkas*.
Indeed, no other gift excels the gift of life;
therefore, with every effort, one should grant protection to living beings.
Non-violence is sacred to all deities, purifying, and bestowing everything;
for the wise say that the gift of life is indeed the supreme among all gifts.
One should cause vessels made of gold to be given at a śrāddha by means of salt;
thus flavors, foodstuffs, and good fortune attend upon him.
One should respectfully offer sesame seeds, sugarcane, and food at a śrāddha;
thus one obtains friends in this world as well as good fortune among women.
One should indeed give a beautiful metallic vessel for the Śrāddha meal;
such a vessel becomes a source of all desires, as well as of knowledge and wealth.
The man who gives silver and gold in śrāddha ceremonies obtains,
through that gift, the fulfillment of his desires as well as wealth.
He who gives a cow that has calved for the first time and yields a jar of milk at the ancestral rites (śrāddha),
the cows attend upon him, as does the prosperity of cattle.
He who diligently provides a fire with abundant fuel during the cold season shall attain the radiance of the bodily fire, the power of mastery, good fortune, and beauty.
He who gives fuel to the twice-born at the onset of the cold season always conquers in battle and, endowed with prosperity, shines resplendently.
Having filled vessels with fragrant bathing waters and likewise with perfumes, one should respectfully cause them to be given at the śrāddha.
Fragrant breezes, great rivers, various pleasures,
and chaste young women attend upon the giver.
He who gives beds, seats, vehicles, grounds,
or mounts at a śrāddha ceremony shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
[159] By giving a forest endowed with flowers and fruits, one enjoys the Gosava sacrifice; as do those who give wells, groves, tanks, fields, cow-pens, and houses.
Having given those, one rejoices in heaven eternally as long as the moon and stars exist;
likewise, by giving a well-spread bed adorned with jewels at a śrāddha ceremony.
His ancestors are satisfied with this, and he enjoys infinite happiness;
dwelling in this world, he shall rejoice in chariots together with their mounts.
He is honored by kings, and he prospers with wealth and grain;
likewise, he possesses dyed silks, woolens, and blankets.
Having given these— a deerskin, linen cloth, silk, and a woolen rug— to the Brahmins, and having fed them according to the prescribed rule;
But the one who has faith obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice:
learning, beautiful women, sons, servants, and attendants.
In this world, living beings abide under one's control;
likewise, there is freedom from disease through garments made of linen, silk, cotton, or fine dukūla cloth that has not been washed.
For he who should give these at a *śrāddha* obtains unsurpassed desires;
he quickly destroys misfortune, just as the rising sun dispels darkness.
It shines at the forefront of the celestial chariot like the moon among the stars;
for this garment is sacred to all the gods and is extolled by all the deities.
In the absence of clothing, there is no ritual action—neither sacrifices, nor the Vedas, nor ascetic penances.
Therefore, garments should be given, especially at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony.

‘Prākāmya’ is a particular kind of sovereignty. ‘Gṛṣṭi’ is a cow that has calved for the first time. ‘Varṇakauśeya’ is silk cloth of yellow or other colors. ‘Prāvārakambala’ is a fine woolen blanket suitable for covering. ‘Ajina’ refers to a waist-belt. ‘Kṣaumaja’ is well known as leather made from an extremely fine woven fabric. ‘Praveṇī’ is a woolen rug used as a bed-covering for elephants.
Likewise: "A vessel made of silver or coated with silver is said to belong to the ancestors;
even a conversation about silver, the sight of it, or its gift [brings great merit]."
The gift of silver is said to result in infinite and inexhaustible heaven.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"The mandalas should be prepared with auspicious flour made from wild rice (*nīvāra*),
or with white clay, or with consecrated ashes."
One should avoid striking it there if it is mixed with stone dust.
Now follows the offering of food into the fire (annaukaraṇa).
In this regard, Yājñavalkya [1.236–238] states:
"Intending to offer it into the fire, he takes up food soaked in ghee and asks, 'Shall I perform? Having been authorized with the reply, 'Do so,' he offers it into the fire as in the Pitṛyajña."
With a concentrated mind, one should offer the remains of the oblation into vessels as they are available,
and especially into those made of silver.

He asks, "I shall offer in the fire. The grammatical connection is: "having taken food soaked in clarified butter. "Like the sacrifice to the ancestors" (pitṛyajñavat) means by whatever procedure exists for the *homa* that constitutes a subsidiary part of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. "In whichever [vessels] are available" means in any one of those prescribed [vessels].

Āśvalāyana [Gṛhya Sūtra 4.9.2–9]: Having taken up food smeared with ghee, he asks for permission, saying: "I shall perform the offering in the fire" (*agnau kariṣye*), or "I will perform it" (*karavai*), or "I am performing it" (*karavāṇi*). The response of permission is: "Do so" (*kriyatām*), "Perform it" (*kuruṣva*), or "Perform it" (*kurv*). Then he offers into the fire as previously stated. Or, when permission has been granted, he may offer into the hands themselves; for the Brāhmaṇa says: "The gods have the fire as their mouth; the ancestors have the hand as their mouth. If he offers other food into the hands after they have sipped water (*ācānta*), he says over the food: "Food upon food! Released! Given! Prosperous!"

[162] Regarding the three questions beginning with "I shall do" (*kariṣye*) and the three answers beginning with "Let it be done" (*kriyatām*), there is a rule of application according to their respective order. Otherwise, the simultaneous mention of synonymous terms would be purposeless. As it was stated previously: "Having placed the fuel while wearing the *prācīnāvīta* [sacrificial cord]," according to the *Āśvalāyana-Śrautasūtra*. Or, as in "or indeed in the hands," this should be understood to apply when fire is absent: "In the absence of fire, however, one should place [the offering] in the hand of the Brahmin."

This is because of the statement of Manu (3.212): "If in the hands. If the offering is made into the hands, then one "assigns" or gives other food once they have sipped water (*ācamana*). This sipping of water is an occasional rite (*naimittika*) occurring both before and after the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). One must not entertain the suspicion that what has been given is for consumption, for there is a censure found in this very context: "The ignorant eat first the food given upon the palm of the hand."
The Baijavāpa-gṛhya:

Having addressed [the fire] with the words, "Wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, I shall perform the offering in the fire," the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa) is performed like the Piṇḍapitṛyajña; or one may follow the entire procedure according to the [standard] ritual sequence.
The Nigama says:

"Having sprinkled water for purification and taken up the food, he should sprinkle it with clarified butter and ask, 'Shall I perform the offering in the fire? Being authorized with the words, 'Do so,' he offers oblations into the fire, preceded by the placing of fuel sticks."
"Having performed the *avanejana*": having offered water into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa immediately after presenting the *arghya*.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

Having adorned [the site] with incense, perfumes, and garlands, and having offered food with ghee to the Brahmins with their permission, one should strew darbha grass around the fire while facing south and offer oblations, saying: "Svāhā to Yama, the descendant of Aṅgiras, accompanied by the Pitṛs; svāhā to Agni Kavyavāhana; svāhā to Soma, accompanied by the Pitṛs."
[163] Hārīta says:

Having approached the water-vessels with the verse "They come together," he pours water into them, cleanses the *sumanas* flowers, and, being permitted by the Brahmins, places the fuel on the fire with the formula "Be kindled. Having invoked the Agniṣvātta ancestors and others, he honors the Brahmins standing there with the water-vessels as appropriate. Holding the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) in his hand, he is then granted permission. When he offers to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, he thereby gratifies the Pitṛs who have Soma as their chief and those who drink Soma; when [he offers] to Yama Aṅgiras, he gratifies those who have Yama as their chief and those who sit on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad*); and when [he offers] to Agni Kavyavāhana, the Sviṣṭakṛt, he gratifies the Agniṣvātta ancestors. When they take up the stirring-spoon, he gratifies his own self. Having given the remnants of the oblation to the Brahmins, he should set aside what remains for the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*).

"Having approached" the water-vessels; "having purified" them like the *prokṣaṇī* waters, but without the mantra. "Permitted by [the Brāhmaṇas] with the words 'kindle the fire,'" meaning permitted by the Brāhmaṇas with the words "Kindle the fire."
[164] Viṣṇu [73, 5–14]: [The section on Viṣṇu].

In *āmaśrāddhas* (funeral rites with raw food) and those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), one should offer oblations into the fire with the first pentad of verses; in *paśuśrāddhas* (animal sacrifice rites), with the middle pentad; on the new moon days (*amāvāsyā*), with the final pentad; and following the *Āgrahāyaṇī* festival, as well as on the eighth days of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇāṣṭakā*) and the *anvaṣṭakā* days, one should proceed respectively with the first, middle, and final pentads. Then, having been authorized by the Brahmins, he should invoke the ancestors with the two verses beginning, "May the gods come" (*āyantu surāḥ*) and "May the Asuras depart" (*apayantv asurāḥ*). Having performed the expulsion of the *yātudhānas* (demons) with sesame seeds, he performs the invocation with the verses, "This is for you, O fathers," "All of them, O Agni," "May they come to me," and "This is for you, O fathers. Having offered water for washing the feet (*pādya*) mixed with *kuśa* grass and sesame, using the verses "Those who stand immortal" (*yās tiṣṭhanty amṛtāḥ*) and "That which my mother" (*yan me mātā*), and having presented the guest-water (*arghya*), he honors the Brahmins according to his ability with ointments, garments, *kuśa*, sesame, flowers, ornaments, and incense (as well as lamps). Taking food soaked in ghee and looking at it while reciting, "The Ādityas, the Rudras, the Vasus," he says, "I shall perform the fire-oblation" (*agnau kariṣye*). Being authorized by the Brahmins with the words "Do so" (*kuru*), he offers three oblations into the fire as before. Having consecrated the entire offering with the mantras, "Those who are my fathers," "This is for you, O fathers," and "This sacrifice is yours," he places the food—preferably in silver vessels—in appropriate vessels. First, he presents the food to the two facing east with the mantra, "Salutation to all the gods" (*namo viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ*). Then, he presents it to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, addressing them by name and lineage (*nāmagotra*), to those facing north.

The *āmaśrāddha* is that which is performed without meat at the commencement of rites such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*, according to the *Laugākṣi-gṛhya-sūtra*. The *kāmyaśrāddha* is that performed by one desiring a son on the fifth lunar day and other such occasions. Regarding the phrase "by the first pentad," this very [section] consisting of fifteen verses is recited as an *anuvāka* in both the Taittirīya and Kāṭhaka schools; its first, second, and third pentads are respectively employed for the *sthālīpāka* and the *agnaukaraṇa-homa*. The *paśuśrāddha* is the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa-śrāddha* mentioned by Hārīta, stating: "When the year is completed, one should duly perform the animal-śrāddha. "Having looked [at the Brahmins] with the words 'ādityā vasavaḥ'" means having gazed upon the Brahmins while reciting the mantra beginning with "ādityā vasavaḥ."
Baudhāyana [2.14.7–14].

Then, having caused them to accept water mixed with sesame seeds and having adorned them with perfumes and garlands, and being permitted by saying, "I shall perform the fire-rite," he prepares the fire, strews grass around it, and—having performed the *agnimukha* rite—offers three oblations: "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors (*pitṛmat*), who has been drunk by the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā!* To Yama accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā!* To Agni Kavyavāhana, the maker of good offerings (*sviṣṭakṛt*), *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā!*! With the remainder of that [water], he sprinkles the food and should offer these same three oblations over the food. He should give balls of food to birds. For it is known from scripture: "The ancestors move about in the form of birds. Then, having presented the other food to the Brahmins, he assigns it with the thumb of a Brahmin: "For you, who are equal to the earth, Agni is the witness; the greatness of what is given is for the sake of non-negligence. The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid. Into the mouth of the Brahmin, I offer nectar into nectar. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brahmins. You are imperishable; may you not fail among the fathers in that world, in yonder world. *Svadhā*! Adoration to the fathers! He assigns a second portion: "For you, who are equal to the intermediate space, Vāyu is the listener; the Yajus formulas are your greatness, for the sake of non-negligence of what is given. The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid. Into the mouth of the Brahmin, I offer nectar. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brahmins. You are imperishable; may you not fail among the grandfathers in that world, in yonder world. He assigns a third portion: "For you, who are equal to the sky, Āditya is the beholder; the Sāman chants are your greatness, for the sake of non-negligence of what is given. The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid. Into the mouth of the Brahmin, I offer nectar. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brahmins. You are imperishable; may you not fail among the great-grandfathers in that world, in yonder world."
Regarding this, they also cite an example:
"One should sprinkle that food with the remainder of the *agnaukaraṇa* offering;
once that has been consumed, one should give the food that was originally prepared."
But that śrāddha which is performed without the thumb does not gratify the ancestors.

‘Then’ means immediately after seating [the guests]. ‘With the remnant of that’ means with the remnant of the clarified butter (ājya) offered in the oblation. By the words beginning with ‘of birds’ (vayasām), it is stated that one should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to the birds only after performing the piṇḍa-offering following the fire-oblation (anvāhāryahoma). And this is the practice of the Baudhāyanas in certain Śrāddha rites. ‘In the form of birds’ (vayasāṃ pratimayā) means in the shape of birds. — Paiṭhīnasi.

Having requested permission with the words, "I shall invoke the gods and the ancestors," and having said, "May they be auspicious," and having requested permission for the fire-rite with the words, "I shall perform it in the fire," and being told, "Do so," he should say, "The oblation," while touching the food with his thumb; having thus designated the preparation of the food as "the oblation," he should give it to the Brahmins.
The meaning is: having said "this is the oblation" regarding the rule for food—that is, the manner of food which involves the thumb—one should give that food to the Brahmins.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: Then, having taken the prepared food smeared with ghee while it is still warm, he, being self-restrained, requests the twice-born, saying, "I shall offer these into the fire."
Being told by them, "Oṃ, do it," he should summon the Dakṣiṇāgni fire;
having strewn darbha grass in the four directions around the Dakṣiṇāgni, he should remain silent.
And one should offer three fuel-sticks of the length of a span (prādeśa) into that fire.
And the Palāśa tree is to be employed for the purpose of sacrificial fuel in rites for the ancestors.
Having offered oblations of fuel-sticks smeared with ghee, with their tips pointing southward and accompanied by mantras,
one should offer three oblations using a stirring-ladle smeared with ghee.
Likewise, he who offers oblations while afflicted by hunger, thirst, or anger, or with an inferior mantra,
or when the fire is unawakened or smoky, shall become blind in another birth.
When the fire is very small, dry, or consists of sparks; when it whirls to the left and appears terrifying;
or when it is filled with moist wood and crackles with hissing sounds.
If one should offer an oblation into a fire that has black flames, emits a foul odor, and likewise licks the earth,
his destruction will certainly occur.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
Having been thus permitted by the best of the twice-born with the words,
"Perform [the rite]," he should take his wife and sons and offer oblations into the fire.
Likewise: Having carefully brought forth the Dakṣiṇāgni for the purpose of the oblation,
or even the common (laukika) fire for the sake of the fire-ritual, one should offer the sacrifice for the successful completion of the rite.
"For the sake of fire" means for the purpose of the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation. "Worldly" refers to the domestic (*āvasathya*) fire. Likewise:
"Of flowers, of fruits, of edible foods, and likewise of cooked grain."
Having extracted the foremost portion of all [the offerings], one should offer it into the fire, the carrier of oblations.
One should always offer oblations to Agni on the south, likewise to Soma on the north,
and always to Vivasvat between these two.
Likewise: the palāśa, phalguna, nyagrodha, plakṣa, aśvattha, vikaṅkata, udumbara, as well as the bilva, sandalwood, and those trees that are fit for sacrifice.
The *sarala*, the *devadāru*, the *sāla*, and likewise the *khadira*—
these trees are especially recommended for the purpose of sacrificial fuel.
Those trees that have thorns and those which are fit for sacrifice should be gathered and honored for the purpose of sacrificial fuel,
according to the word of the ancestors.
Listen as I describe to you the fruit that belongs to the rite of one who offers oblations into the fire with fuel-sticks produced from the six fruits.
Indeed, that yields inexhaustible fruit equal to the merit of a horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) and fulfills all desires.
[170] Śleṣmātaka, naktamāla, kapittha, and likewise śālmali;
The nīpa, the vibhītaka, the ciribilva, the aṅkola, the tinduka, and the āmrātaka are likewise censured for use in the performance of śrāddha rites.
The Bakula and the Kovidāra trees are censured at ancestral rites; likewise, those trees in which insects dwell and those that do not produce sacrificial fruit are censured.
One should avoid those trees that are entwined with thickets, completely covered by creepers, and serve as dwellings for birds.
One should avoid all other such things that are unfit for sacrifice.
As stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa* (18.32–33):
"A Brahmin, authorized by the Brahmins, should perform the rites in the fire according to the prescribed rule."
Then, having prepared the sacrificial oblation (caru) in a bronze vessel according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra;
Then, he should perform the satiation with the two mantras addressed to Agni and Soma;
or, for that best of the twice-born who maintains only a single fire, he should do so when the Dakṣiṇa fire has been brought forward.

"In the consecrated" means set apart from the *āvasathya* fire. "Possessing a single fire" means one who maintains only the *āvasathya*. Furthermore, this *agnaukaraṇa* oblation for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) is performed specifically in the *dakṣiṇāgni*; in its absence, in the *āvasathya*; and in the absence of that as well, in the hand of a Brahmin or similar locations.
[171] In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* (3.15.26): "Then one should offer food, excluding meat, condiments, and salt, into the fire.
Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
And the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*),
facing eastward, because of the Vedic revelation stating, "One offers to the gods facing east."
Or it may be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder while facing south;
for once the oblation has been set aside from one [deity], it is not offered to another.
One should utter "svāhā," but neither at the end of this [mantra] nor should one offer the oblation;
having offered into the fire with the word "svāhā," one should then conclude the mantra.

Regarding the alternative "or it should be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (*apasavyena*), this option between the left and right shoulders is to be understood as being established according to the distinction of Vedic schools (*śākhā*) in accordance with one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. The meaning of the passage beginning with "one should utter *svāhā*" is as follows: having first uttered "svāhā," the mantra "to Soma accompanied by the ancestors" (*somāya pitṛmate*) is to be concluded. The same applies to "svāhā to Agni, the carrier of offerings to the ancestors" (*svāhāgnaye kavyavāhanāya*).
Manu and Śātātapa state in the first [chapter]:
"In the absence of fire, one should offer the breaths themselves into the mouth of a Brahmin;
for that twice-born man is declared by Brahmins learned in the mantras to be the very fire itself."

The ancients speak of these best of the twice-born as those who are free from anger, possessed of great serenity, intent upon nourishing the world, and who have the ancestors and the gods as their deities at the śrāddha rites.
"In the absence of fire" means in the absence of both the Śrauta and Smārta fires that are prescribed for the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation.

[172] In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "In the absence of fire, however, for a Brahmin, [the offering may be made] either in the hand, or even in water, or in the ear of a goat, or in the ear of a horse, or in a cow-pen, or in the presence of Śiva."
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* states:

"Having offered [the food] with the sacred formula into the hand of that person who is at the head of the row for the ancestors, one who does not maintain a sacred fire should silently deposit it into the vessels of the others."
Yama says: One should present the remainder of the *agnaukaraṇa* offering to the ancestors;
having presented it to the ancestors, one must not give it to those of the *vaiśvadeva* rite.
Now follows the procedure for the serving of food.
Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi states:
"Having adorned the Brāhmaṇas, one should set before them meat, cakes, curd, ghee, honey, milk-rice, rice-and-pulse mixture (kṛsara), preparations of fruit, and fish.

Here, the word *iti* has the sense of "and so forth," referring to vegetables and other such items. "One should set before them" (*upasādayet*) means one should present them immediately after the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
Manu and Bṛhaspati [state]: "Having personally taken a portion of the increased food with both hands,
one should place it slowly near the Brahmins while meditating on the ancestors."
For the food that is offered with both hands held away is indeed snatched away suddenly by the evil-minded Asuras.
Being self-restrained and composed, he should first place on the ground itself the various qualities of food— soups, vegetables, and so forth— as well as milk, curd, ghee, and honey.
Various kinds of food and edibles, roots and fruits,
heart-pleasing meats, and fragrant drinks.
Having brought all that, he should serve it slowly and with great composure; being self-restrained, he should do so while extolling all its qualities.
Whatever may please the learned Brahmins, that he should give without stinginess;
and he should engage in discourses on the Veda, for this is what is desired by the ancestors.

The genitive case in the word "annasya" is used in the sense of the instrumental. "Vardhitam" means filled. "Muktam ubhābhyām" means not held by both hands. "Guṇān" refers to subordinate items, because food is the primary substance in a meal.
Devala says:
"Then one should cause the twice-born to eat the food remaining from the *piṇḍas* according to the prescribed rule."
With foods mixed with sesame seeds, fats, and various kinds of eatables and cakes.
Then, remaining thus restrained, joyful, respectful, and pure, the performer should feed those best of the twice-born with food according to their desire.
Yama says:
Then, having brought pure food, one who is self-restrained should feed the twice-born:
rice, soup, clarified butter, vegetables, meat, curd, milk, and honey.
Likewise: One should, free from envy, give parched grains mixed with honey, sugarcane with milk, and all kinds of sugar, fruits, and roots.
"Viśadam" means stainless.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"Then, being free from envy, one should give abundant food according to one's desire—sesame, meat, vegetables, soups, *kṛsara*, milk-rice, cakes, lentils, *bhavya* fruits, drinks, honey, ghee, curds, and milk-rice."
‘From desire’ means from one’s own wish.
Gautama [15.5–6]:
[The rule regarding time] is according to one's ability; one should perform the rules for the refinement of qualities with excellence regarding the food.

"Guṇasaṃskāravidhīn": "guṇāḥ" refers to the seasonings (vyañjanas), and "saṃskārāḥ" refers to qualities such as fragrance; the meaning is that one should "prakarṣet," i.e., make these excellent or superior.
Kātyāyana says: "One should give warm and well-prepared food, or according to one's ability."
"Well-offered" means *sviṣṭa*.
[Regarding] the conch:
having performed the *śrāddha* with diligence, free from haste and anger.
One should devoutly offer warm food to the twice-born.
Except for fruits and roots and various drinks,
the wise man should afterwards feed the twice-born according to the rules, adorned with fragrant garlands.

In the phrase "having made an offering of faith," the anteriority of time is not intended to be expressed. Regarding the rule "except for fruits and roots," this should be understood as being in relation to hot food; therefore, even non-hot items such as fruits and roots may be given.
Yājñavalkya [1.240]: Free from anger and without haste, one should give food that is desirable and fit for sacrifice.
Bṛhaspati [Śrāddha, 36]:
Because refined side dishes and the like, accompanied by milk, honey, and ghee,
are given with faith (śraddhā), it is therefore called śrāddha.

Āpastamba [2.19.13–16; 20.1–2]: One should offer the obligatory (naiyamika) Śrāddha with oily substances. Ghee and meat is the primary rule. In their absence, oil and vegetables. On the Maghā day, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas with ghee according to the ritual procedure for Śrāddha. At the monthly Śrāddha, one should employ a *droṇa* of sesame seeds by whatever means one is able. And one should feed those who have risen together [with the invited guests].

The *naiyamika* [śrāddha] is the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha*; one should not offer that without [using] oil. The grammatical connection is: "One should feed the Brahmins with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) in abundance according to the ritual procedure for the śrāddha. The intended meaning is that even oil may optionally be given at the *maghā-śrāddha*. "One should employ a *droṇa* measure of sesame seeds" refers to the alternative where there is a greater number of Brahmins. "By whatever means one is able" refers to methods such as sweetmeats (*modaka*) and so forth. "Those who have risen together" means those who possess virtuous qualities.
Manu [3.229–230]: He should never shed tears, he should not become angry, and he should not speak untruth;
he should not touch food with his foot, nor should he shake it.
Tears send the hungry ghosts (pretas) away; anger, enemies; falsehood, dogs;
the touch of one's feet, the rākṣasas; and shaking [the limbs], evildoers.
"Duṣkṛtīn" means evildoers.
Devala says: One should not shed tears at a śrāddha, nor chatter, nor laugh with others in private.
One should not be deluded, nor should one become angry, nor should one ever be agitated therein.
Even when the cause for anger has arisen, one should never give way to wrath;
nor should one remain standing in the presence of the ancestors while weary or with limbs perspiring.
And one should not ward off birds such as hawks or crows from this place;
for it is a Vedic teaching that the ancestors arrive there in those very forms.
The word "in the cause" implies "of anger"; "should manifest" means he should express it; "dependent" means not dependent [on others].
Viṣṇu [81, 1–3]: One should not place food upon a seat; one should not touch it with the foot; nor should one spit upon it.
Yama says:
The Yātudhānas plunder whatever is sacrificed, offered, given, eaten, muttered, performed as austerity, or studied by a twice-born man who has fallen away from purity.
Likewise, whatever is given in anger and whatever is eaten in haste—
both of these the Yātudhānas along with the Rākṣasas plunder.
Having invited the ancestors, one should not become subject to negligence;
therefore, having restrained both speech and anger, one should perform the śrāddha.
One should not harbor anger toward anyone for any reason whatsoever;
for when served by one who is free from anger, the ancestral spirits (pitṛs) are satisfied at the śrāddha rite.
"Uncaused by the improper" means that he should not be the cause of improper things, such as incoherent prattle and the like.
Baudhāyana says:
Lack of faith is the supreme evil; for evil is said to be ignorance.
Through ignorance one's dharma is lost, and one whose dharma is lost is remembered as the lowest.
By faith the intellect is purified; by faith the mind is purified.
By faith dharma is attained; faith is the deliverer from evil.
Therefore, the deities do not eat the oblation of one who lacks faith;
here, "mind" (mati) refers to desire, because it is mentioned separately from the intellect (buddhi).
Kātyāyana:
One endowed with faith should perform a śrāddha even with vegetables alone. Manu [3.275]:
Whatever one gives according to the rule, properly, and endowed with faith,
that becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the next world.
Yama said: Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows,
so does the mantra bring the ancestors to the sweet food at the śrāddha rites.
Manu [3.233]: Being satisfied himself, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them gradually;
he should repeatedly encourage them with food and drink as well as with words of praise.
Bṛhaspati [Śrāddha, 100]:
Having described the qualities of the various kinds of food, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas slowly;
one should gladden them with narratives, including Itihāsas and accounts of past events.
Āpastamba [2.17.4]:
Being self-restrained and with a serene mind, he should, having been invited, feed the Brāhmaṇas.
"Sṛṣṭaḥ" means one who is energetic.
Yama and Śātātapa [state this] in the second [chapter].
As long as there is sacrificial food (haviṣya), as long as that which is well-offered is given.
The ancestors eat only so long as I do not say, "I give."
When a Śūdra gives food to Brāhmaṇas, or a Brāhmaṇa gives food to Śūdras, the food of those two is unfit to be eaten; having consumed it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If one commits an offense against the four [rules], one should wipe away the clarified butter with the hand;
both the giver and the eater are indeed affected by the offense, there is no doubt.
If one should offer ghee with four fingernails or with the hand,
the giver does not obtain merit, and the eater goes to a state of even greater sin.
Clarified butter brought by the hand of a Śūdra is Śaudra; whatever else may be brought is also Śaudra. Cold food is Śaudra, and that which is served by Śūdras becomes Śaudra.
Having eaten or having given with the hand honey, molasses, vegetables, cow's milk products, salt, or ghee, one should perform the Sāntapana penance.
Alms-food, water, and condiments that are given directly from the hand—
having eaten these, one becomes impure, and the donor does not go to heaven.
"Śaudra" means that which is fit for a Śrāddha only for a Śūdra; furthermore, whatever food and so forth is brought after asking, "What shall be brought?"—that too is "śaudra."
One should not give salt directly with the hand, nor ghee, side dishes, and so forth. One should provide vessels made of metal, especially those made of silver.
[180] The conch shell,
rock salt, and likewise that which originates from Lake Mānasa—
these are indeed supremely purifying, even though they are perceptible to the senses at all times.
Śātātapa, Vasiṣṭha, and Vṛddha-Śātātapa state in the first [section]:
"But those oily substances, salt, and condiments that are given with the hand do not reach the giver; the eater consumes the sin."
Therefore, the offering should be given using something intermediate, such as a leaf or a blade of grass;
one should never give it with the hand, nor ever with an iron vessel.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa and Laghu-Hārīta state:
"If food is served in an iron vessel,
the eater consumes what is equal to excrement, and the giver shall go to hell."
"Even water given with faith in silver vessels, or in those adorned with silver, results in inexhaustible merit for them."
Hārīta says:
A gift given with a vessel made of gold, silver, or udumbara wood, as well as one made of steel wrought by a noble artisan, becomes inexhaustible.
An "āryakṛta" vessel—that is, one fashioned by members of the three higher castes—is also desired. Viṣṇu [79.22] states:
"For the offering of ghee and other substances, vessels made of metal (taijasa), [swords], and vessels of phalgu wood are recommended."
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"If one feeds the ancestors at a śrāddha ceremony using an earthenware vessel,
then the donor, the officiating priest, and the eater shall all go to hell."
Paiṭhīnasi states:
"Lentils, beans, and kodrava grain are unfit for sacrifice; likewise, among metals, lead, tin, stone vessels, and broken vessels [are forbidden]."
Regarding the term "of metals," this is a selection made by virtue of suitability with respect to lead and tin. "Inferior" means extremely base.
Hārīta says: To those seated in a row, one should offer equal portions of perfumes and other items for the meal;
one should not give unequally in the row, nor should one ask for more, nor cause it to be given.
Both the beggar and the giver go to hell.
"Food" (*bhojana*) refers to rice and other such items that are consumed; thus says Yama.
One should not give unequally in a row, nor should one beg for it, nor cause others to give it;
the one who begs, the one who causes it to be given, and the giver—all go to hell.
Therefore, a wise man should neither give, nor beg, nor cause to be given;
for he who bestows unequal gifts upon those seated in a single row [incurs sin].
He who takes food from a row where it has been given commits a misdeed;
so does he who builds a bridge across a small stream and he who creates obstacles for a maiden.
[182] Furthermore, no atonement is possible for one who gives unequally in a row.
A "small river" (*kunadī*) is one with little water; because the flow of water is completely cut off there by a dam, great suffering arises for the many who depend upon it.
— Hārīta.
But he who, out of affection, fear, or for the sake of wealth, makes a distinction within a single row regarding the Smṛti composed by the sages and witnessed by the Vedas—
The sages call that the murder of a Brahmin.
Now follows the consecration of the food (*annasaṃkalpa*).
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya [1.238] states:
"Having offered the food, one performs the consecration of the vessel with the mantra: 'The earth is the vessel.'"
Having performed this with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should place the thumb of the twice-born into the food.
Yama said: "The blessed Viṣṇu, the size of a thumb, wanders the earth for the sake of slaying the Rākṣasas; who will strike me today?"
Therefore, in all śrāddha rites, the grasping of the thumb is prescribed;
for a śrāddha that is performed without the thumb or outside the knees is [considered invalid].
Whatever is eaten with the knees outside [the thighs] becomes entirely demonic.

One should first offer food to the Viśvedevas, saying "Salutation to the Viśvedevas," to two [guests] facing east; and to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, by name and lineage, to those facing north.
Śāṅkhāyanagṛhya [4, 1,8]:
And he should feed him food, addressing him by name with the words, "This for you."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: Then, having taken warm food smeared with honey and clarified butter and mixed with sesame seeds,
he should do so again with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) using the *devatīrtha*.
Having said, "This food is for you," he should worship the Viśvedevas;
then he should offer food to the ancestors with an invitation.
"O you of such-and-such lineage, this food is for you; *svadhā*! *Namaḥ*!
Having thus given the water, the food, and the meal in their proper order, [one should proceed].
One should perform the offering to all the Śrāddha-deities;
holding the thumb of the twice-born guest, one should recite the mantra while remaining silent.
Reciting "The earth is your vessel," one should contemplate the food that has been taken;
then one should proclaim, "O Kṛṣṇa, protect this my sacrificial offering."
Furthermore, with that very same mantra, he should offer it to the ancestors,
respectfully taking hold of the thumb of each individual Brahmin.
"O you of such-and-such a lineage, this food is for you; Svadhā! Homage!
With that [food], along with sesame seeds, rice, water, and kuśa grass, [one should offer] in front."
He should scatter [food] for the ancestors and the servants while reciting "apahatāḥ" (driven away).
To them he should give the *apośāna* water, saying, "May you partake."

Then, having announced the remainder to the Brahmins, he assigns it with his thumb, excluding the nail, saying: "Equal to the earth is that for you; Agni is your witness; the Ṛg-verses are your greatness, so that what is given may not be lost. The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer the nectar into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not fail among the fathers in yonder world, in such-and-such a place. He assigns a second portion, saying: "Equal to the intermediate space is that for you; Vāyu is your listener; the Yajus-formulas are your greatness, so that what is given may not be lost. The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer the nectar into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not fail among the grandfathers in this world, in yonder world, in such-and-such a place. He assigns a third portion, saying: "Equal to the heavens is that for you; Āditya is your announcer; the Sāman-chants are your greatness, so that what is given may not be lost. The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer the nectar into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not fail among the great-grandfathers in yonder world, in such-and-such a place."
Moreover, they also cite this:
"When the food is sprinkled with the remainder of the *agnaukaraṇa* offering,
and that has been consumed, one should give whatever other [food] is prepared."

A śrāddha performed "without the thumb" (niraṅguṣṭha) does not gratify the ancestors. "The other" refers to the rice, side dishes, and so forth. "With the remnant of the *agnaukaraṇa*" means with the remnant of the clarified butter used for the *agnaukaraṇa* rite. "Food" refers to that which was set aside for the *agnaukaraṇa*. "When it has been consumed" means when it has been cast into [the fire], that is, offered as an oblation (*huta*). "The other, the prepared [food]" refers to the rice, side dishes, and so forth, which were cooked for the purpose of eating. "Without the thumb" means devoid of the aforementioned manner of touching with the thumb.
Regarding the statement "one should give," Kātyāyana says in the *Śrāddhakalpasūtra* (2.2–3):

Having given the remains of the oblation and touched the vessel, he mutters: "The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer the nectar into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa, svāhā! Then, with either a verse addressed to Viṣṇu (*vaiṣṇavī ṛc*) or a sacrificial formula (*yajus*), he inserts his thumb into the vessel.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"One should give the food-preparation to the Brāhmaṇas with the thumb, saying, 'This is the sacrificial oblation (havis).

The meaning of this is as follows: 'The food-preparation' refers to the types of food such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and the like; 'with the thumb' means preceded by the placing of the Brāhmaṇas' thumbs [into the food]; having declared, 'This is the sacrificial oblation,' it should be formally dedicated (*saṅkalpanīya*)."
Hārīta says: A śrāddha performed without the thumb does not gratify the ancestors;
therefore, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind while pressing down upon the thumb.
The mantra is: "Viṣṇu strode across this [universe]. Likewise:
"Then the food was placed in a vessel and covered with a larger one."
In the same way, that which is produced by the thumb reaches the conditioned state.
"By the larger" means by one that is greater than the lower bowl.
Now, the rules for eating.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya [1.239] states:
"Having recited the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis and the three verses beginning with 'madhu vātā,' they should eat while remaining silent, after having been told to do so as they please."
Manu, Hārīta, Viṣṇu, Yama, Śātātapa, and Uśanas [state] in the second [chapter]:
"All the food should be very hot; they too should eat while remaining silent.
And the twice-born should not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering when asked by the giver."
As long as there is heat in the food, as long as those who eat remain silent,
and as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been mentioned, so long do the ancestors partake of it.
The qualities of the sacrificial oblation must not be mentioned until the libation for the ancestors has been performed;
once they have been properly satisfied by it, one may then speak of the excellence of the oblation.

Since it is already established by the very mention of "restraint of speech" (*vāgyatatva*) that the eater of the *śrāddha* must not describe the qualities of the sacrificial food (*havirguṇa*), the repetition of the phrase "and the twice-born should not speak" is intended to prohibit the communication of such qualities even by means of hand gestures and the like.
Devala says:
And just as a pure Brāhmaṇa, with his senses and mind serene,
should partake of the ancestral food (paitṛka-anna) without agitation and with a joyful heart.
"Prasannavān" means one who is gracious. Likewise:
"For Avalokita grants food, drink, and cool water to those who give."
When there is a reason to speak, he should eat using his hand while making a sign.

The meaning of this is as follows: having been presented with food and the like, one who has been looked upon by the giver for the purpose of giving it should indeed make a sign. "When it is to be spoken" refers to the cause—the reason for acceptance or non-acceptance.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

Brāhmaṇas should not speak of the qualities or defects of the food; they should not speak untruthfully; they should not praise one another. They should not say "the food and drink are abundant," except by means of a hand gesture. The ancestors eat as long as the food remains on the ground, as long as it is not yet praised, and as long as it is still warm—except for fruits, roots, and drinks.

The phrase "as far as the ground" implies that the food vessel remains [on the ground]; therefore, it should not be lifted up. "Inauspicious" means one for whom no blessing has been recited. And so it is stated in the Varāha Purāṇa:
"If a Brāhmaṇa, weak in knowledge, should lift up the vessel..."
"O Vasundharā, the Rākṣasas carry away the food of one who eats [with his hand] while it is still on the palm," so says Yama.
Furthermore, he who eats with his hand in the palm, as well as he who eats with his mouth full, [is likewise affected].
And his ancestors do not eat [the offering], nor does he who praises it first.
One engaged in a *śrāddha* ceremony should not ask for salt or other items while eating;
for if he asks, his ancestors depart as if defiled—of this there is no doubt.
The arm of the giver falls [to the ground] and the tongue of the eater is split;
"with breath" means accompanied by hissing.
[This is stated] in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*.
The ancestors do not eat that which a twice-born man eats making a hissing sound, nor that which he eats with his palms; rather, they eat that which he consumes together with his breath.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"If a Brahmin devoid of knowledge begs from a donor, his ancestors do not eat [the offering]—of neither the giver nor the eater; of this there is no doubt."
And the Brāhmaṇas should eat while maintaining silence; not with their heads covered; not wearing sandals; nor with their feet placed upon a stool.
Manu and Śātātapa:
Whatever one eats with the head wrapped, whatever one eats facing south,
and whatever one eats while wearing shoes— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
That brahmin who eats with a mind lacking faith, or while wearing sandals,
or who is prone to idle chatter, or is angry— he is a defiler of the ancestors.
He who eats while laughing does not nourish the ancestors;
nor does he who eats with his head covered, or he who eats while disparaging [the food].
Yama said: Whatever one eats with his head covered, whatever the husband of a *vṛṣalī* eats, whatever one eats while wearing shoes, and whatever one eats with contempt; [all such food is unfit].
Brahmā assigned all of that as a share to the lord of the Dānavas. Hārīta said:
Raising his hand, smiling yet filled with anger and wonder—
Whatever one eats at the times of ancestral rites does not indeed gratify the ancestors.
Food offered with astonishment is known as *āsura*; food offered with anger is known as *rākṣasa*;
that which is offered disrespectfully and with contempt is declared to be *paiśāca*.
[190] Vasiṣṭha [11.25–26]: When food has been released from both hands and offered to the ancestors,
the evil-minded Asuras watch for that interval.

Therefore, with a hand not empty, a wise man should offer food that has been brought; or, having touched the vessel, he should remain standing until the remnants are cleared away. "With a hand not empty" means accompanied by a connection to either the giver or the eater.
Baudhāyana [2.15.3–9]:
When food has been offered to the ancestors from both branches,
the evil-minded Asuras wait in the interval.
Yātudhānas and Piśācas plunder that sacrificial offering;
likewise, at the offerings of sesame seeds, the non-heirs [plunder it], and at those of Krodhavaśa, the Asuras do so.
Whatever recitations, burnt offerings, or acceptances of gifts one performs while wearing saffron robes—
that oblation among the offerings to gods and ancestors does not reach the deities.
That which is given without the thumb, that which is accepted in the same manner, and he who sips water while standing— by such acts, one does not attain prosperity.

The offering of water at the beginning and the end occurs in all cases; from the recitation [of mantras] onwards, it is according to the prescribed rule. The remainder has been stated in the section on the *aṣṭakā* oblation.

"Without heirs" means those who have no kin. "In the presence of one under the sway of anger" implies that the giver is so disposed; this is the ellipsis. "At the beginning and end of the offering of water": "at the beginning" refers to the initial offering of water, which is the drinking of water; "at the end" refers to the conclusion of the meal. By the word "etcetera" (*prabhṛti*), the meditation on the ancestors and other such acts are included.
Śātātapa says:
Having placed the sacred thread around the waist, one should apply ointment to the body;
and he who eats while wearing only a single garment—his ancestors depart disappointed.
[191] Then, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītī), one who has been invited to a śrāddha should apply ointments.
Unless specifically enjoined, he should not wear a garland on his head, except for the lock of hair at the crown (śikhā).
One should know that he who has a single garment fallen from his left shoulder and resting at the region of the navel is unfit for rites dedicated to the gods or the ancestors; one should avoid him.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
One should not eat before another who is seated on a superior seat; one should not give more than is required; nor should one accept more.

"Seated on the foremost seat" means seated at the head of the row. "Previously" means before the commencement of the meal for the other Brahmins. "Excessively" means unevenly, due to affection and so forth.
Yama says:
That ignorant twice-born man who, seated at the head of the row, eats first while many look on, takes upon himself the sins of the entire line.
Śātātapa says:
If a twice-born man, having washed his hands, should always drink water after eating,
that food has been consumed by the Asuras, and the ancestors depart disappointed.
"Having eaten" means having finished the meal. "Water" here refers to the water held in the final mouthful at the end of the meal. Yama says:
"That which one eats again after having already eaten, and that which is smeared with oil..."
Whatever is seen by women in their courses, that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
That which is eaten or served without the utterance of "Oṃ," that which is eaten with anger,
and that which is eaten by one of evil soul— verily, that goes to the Rākṣasas.
That food which has insects or hair in it, that which is sneezed upon, looked at by dogs, wept over, or shaken about— verily, that goes to the Rākṣasas.
[192] Those of the twice-born classes who do not observe the Vedas, vows, or conduct are served by the three castes with mantras; that [offering], indeed, goes to the Rākṣasas.
That which is devoid of ritual rules, food that is not purified, that which lacks mantras and sacrificial fees,
and that which is offered or given without faith— verily, that goes to the Rākṣasas.

"Anointed with oil" (*tailābhighāritam*) is used when clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is unavailable. "Devoid of the *oṃkāra*" (*niroṅkāraḥ*) means entirely devoid of Vedic mantras. "Shaken off" (*avadhūtam*) refers to [the garment], as indicated by the word "clothing" (*vāsasā*) understood from the context. "Devoid of mantra" (*mantrahīnam*) means lacking the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) with the mantra beginning "The earth is yours" (*pṛthivī te*).
Uśanas said:
If one who has been invited to a śrāddha should avoid anything whatsoever,
his ancestors will remain in a state of hopelessness for that entire month.
Even if the food served in the row does not appear appetizing, one should eat at least something according to one's ability.
Vasiṣṭha [11.34]:
But an ascetic who has been appointed to a Śrāddha or a rite for the gods should not reject meat;
for as many hairs as there are on the animal, for so many years he falls into hell.
Āpastamba [2.18.12]:
"And one should not give the leavings to one who does not possess those qualities.
"One who does not possess those qualities" means one who is devoid of the qualities of a recipient at a *śrāddha*.
Manu [3.249]: "That fool who, having eaten at a *śrāddha*, gives the leavings to a *vṛṣala*,
goes headlong to the Kālasūtra hell."
Devala says:
If one who has eaten at a śrāddha gives his leavings to Śūdras, that fool is without purification; they say he becomes pure only through an expiatory rite (prāyaścitta).
"Without expiation," they say, "there is no atonement for him except through penance."
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"One should not cause the remnants of a *śrāddha* to be given to a woman, a *śūdra*, or one who has not been initiated (*anupeta*).
If one should give it out of passion or delusion, that [offering] certainly does not reach the ancestors."

Therefore, in the performance of a śrāddha rite, no food or other edibles that have been tasted by others should be given as leavings; with the exception of curd and clarified butter, this applies except when giving to a disciple or a son.

"Except for curd and clarified butter"—meaning that food left over from a meal (ucchiṣṭa) other than curd and clarified butter must not be given to anyone at all; however, curd and clarified butter may be given even to disciples and sons who possess the qualities required of those partaking in a *śrāddha* feast.
Now follows the procedure for recitation and other rites.
In that regard, as for the one who has renounced his body (*kāyātyana*):

while [the others] are eating, he should recite the *gāyatrī* preceded by the *vyāhṛtis*, together with the *praṇava*, once or thrice; as well as the *rakṣoghnī* verses, the mantras dedicated to the ancestors (*pitryamantra*), the *puruṣasūkta*, and other purificatory texts (*pavitra*).

The "verses that destroy demons" (*rakṣoghnī*) are the *ṛc*s beginning with "kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ. The "mantras dedicated to the ancestors" (*pitryamantra*) are those beginning with "udīratām avara. The "purificatory texts" (*pavitra*) are the *śatarudrīya* and so forth.

The rule: While they are eating, he should mutter the Sāvitrī mantras, verses from the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda, as well as the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Rakṣoghna hymns, the Pāvamānī verses, those beginning with "udīratām avare," and the Madhumatī verses.

[195] Viṣṇu [73.15–16]: Then, while the Brahmins are eating, he should mutter: "Whatever I have done out of excess, by day and by night, whatever [sin] of yours [is like] a flesh-eater. And [he should recite] the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras.
Baudhāyana [2.14.5]:
One should cause the *rakṣoghna* Sāmans, the *svadhāvat* Yajus formulas,
the honey-verses (*madhūc*), and the purifiers (*pavitra*) to be heard, while seating them quietly.

"The *Sāmans* that destroy Rākṣasas," such as "O Viśvapati," and so forth, are produced from the *Ṛgveda*. "The *Yajus* formulas containing the word *svadhā*," such as "To the ancestors who possess the *svadhā*-offering," and so forth. "The honey-verses (*madhvṛcaḥ*)," such as "Honeyed are the winds for the one who follows the cosmic order (*ṛtāyat*)," and so forth. Thus says Hārīta.

Whatever he considers pure, he should recite the sixteen *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "May the fathers purify me," and the first three [of these]. Here, "O fathers" (*atra pitaraḥ*) is a *yajus*; "Homage to you, O fathers" (*namo vaḥ pitaraḥ*) is a *yajus* ending with the word "beings" (*syāmāntam*). Then the three verses beginning with "The winds are honey for the one who follows the Law" (*madhuvātā ṛtāyate*), and the section beginning with "May the fathers purify me" (*punantu mā pitaraḥ*). Also, this hymn "O Soma, you have been stirred" (*tvaṃ soma pracikitaḥ*) is the *pitryā-saṃhitā*. By reciting these, he pleases the ancestors, and for him, there is an inexhaustible supply from the ancestors.

The meaning is that one should always recite three mantras at the *śrāddha* ceremony, beginning with "May the ancestors purify me" (*punantu mā pitaraḥ*). The mantra ending with "may we be the Yajus" (*yajuḥ syāma*)—that is, ending with "may we be honey-sweet" (*madhutvaṃ syāma*)—is as recited in the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"With hands joined in the *pavitra* position, sitting upon *darbha* grass, one should mutter 'Honey the winds' (*madhu vātā*). Having caused the *pavitra*, the *Dharmaśāstra*, and the *Apratiratha* hymn to be heard, one should recite the *Gāyatrī* in the middle."
"Apratiratham," "Āśuḥ śiśāna," and so forth. "Anuśrāvya" means having caused [the announcement] to be heard.
Manu [3.132]: At a rite for the ancestors, one should cause [the guests] to hear the Vedic study, as well as the treatises on Dharma,
the narratives, the histories, the Purāṇas, and the supplementary texts.
The *khalas* are the *Śrīsūkta* and other such hymns.
As stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"And the various hymns of praise dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka (the Sun), and Rudra."
One should recite the hymns dedicated to Indra, Īśa, and Soma, as well as the Pāvamānī verses, according to one's ability.
Likewise, the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans], the Jyeṣṭhasāman, and similarly the Bṛhat; as well as the Śāntikādhyāya and the Madhubrāhmaṇa.
[197] Likewise, he should recite all those [mantras] that bring joy to the Brāhmaṇas of the maṇḍala as well as to himself.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Or else, one should offer the sound of the lute and the flute to the Brahmins."
[Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.15.31–37]:
Having recited mantras that destroy demons and having spread the ground with sesame seeds,
those very best of the twice-born ancestors should be meditated upon.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather,
abiding within the bodies of the learned, attain satisfaction today.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through this rice-ball (piṇḍa) offered by me upon the earth.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through devotion to me; this has been proclaimed by me.
May his maternal grandfather attain satisfaction, as well as his father and whoever else may be his paternal grandfather;
and may the Viśvedevas attain the highest state.
May the Yātudhānas meet their destruction and find no satisfaction.
Lord Hari, the Master of Sacrifice, the imperishable Self who partakes of all sacrificial offerings (havya) and ancestral oblations (kavya), is the Sovereign here;
by His presence, let [all obstacles] depart immediately.
All the Rākṣasas without exception and all the Asuras.
Based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "This has been proclaimed by me," this hymn should be recited while meditating upon the ancestors at the time of feeding the Brahmins.
[198] In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "I shall proclaim the auspicious Saptārcis, which grants all desires."
Of the formless ancestors and those with form, who possess radiant splendor.
I always pay homage to those meditators who possess the eye of yoga,
as well as to Dakṣa and Mārīca, the progenitors of Indra and the other gods.
I bow to those who grant desires— the Seven Sages and the Pitṛs—
as well as the progenitors of Manu and the others, and likewise to the Sun and the Moon.
Having paid homage to all those ancestors,
as well as to Prajāpati, Kaśyapa, Soma, and Varuṇa, one should offer [oblations] even in the waters and in curd.
With palms joined in reverence, I always bow down to the lords of yoga,
as well as to the stars, the planets, wind, fire, and the ancestors.
And likewise, with palms joined in reverence, I bow to Heaven and Earth,
and to the progenitors of the divine sages, who are honored by all the gods.
With palms joined in reverence, I bow always to those who grant fearlessness;
homage to the seven groups of ancestors throughout the seven worlds.
Salutations indeed to Svayambhū, to Brahmā, who possesses the eye of yoga;
this has been declared by the seven-flamed one (Agni), who is worshipped by the hosts of celestial rishis.
For this is indeed the supreme purifier, glorious, and the dispeller of obstructing spirits.
Now follows the ritual procedure subsequent to the Śrāddha.
Yājñavalkya [1.240–248]:
Having recited the purificatory mantras until satiety, as well as the previously mentioned prayers.
Having taken food and being satisfied, and having obtained permission regarding the remainder,
one should scatter that food upon the ground and offer water once, then once again.
Having taken all the food together with sesame seeds, facing south,
he should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) near the remains of the meal, as in the Pitṛyajña.
In the same manner, one should likewise offer water for sipping (ācamana) to the maternal grandfathers;
thereafter, one should perform the recitation of "Svasti" and the offering of the inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka).
Having given the sacrificial fee according to his ability, he should utter the word *svadhā*.
Being authorized with the words "Let it be spoken," he should say, "Let *svadhā* be pronounced for the ancestors."
When they have said, "Let it be, svadhā," one should pour water on the ground;
and when the brahmins have said, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," one should mutter this:
May our donors increase, as well as our Vedic knowledge and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give.
Having spoken thus and having uttered affectionate words, he should bow down and dismiss [the guests],
saying "vāje vāje" with joy, performing the dismissal starting with the ancestors.
[200] Having turned face upwards that ancestral vessel into which you previously poured the remnants, you should dismiss the Brahmins.

The "prior recitation" consists of the Gāyatrī with the Vyāhṛtis, the verses beginning with "madhu vātā," and so forth. And one should give water "once each": having given water for rinsing the mouth at the conclusion of the meal, one should give it to the Brahmins once each with the formula "amṛtāpidhānam."
Kātyāyana [Śrāddhakalpasūtra, 3, 7–18]:

Knowing them to be satisfied, he scatters food, gives water once for each, and as before recites the *gāyatrī* mantra and the "honey-verses" (*madhumatī*), saying "honey, honey, honey. He asks, "Are you satisfied? They respond, "We are satisfied. Having requested permission regarding the remainder of the food with the words "The rest of the food," he gathers all the food together, places it on *darbha* grass near the remains of the meal, sprinkles water over it, and offers three balls (*piṇḍas*) for each. According to some, this is done after they have sipped water. When they have sipped water, he should offer water, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and the "imperishable water" (*akṣayyodaka*). When they say, "May the ancestors be free from evil (*aghorāḥ*)," he says, "May they be so. When they say, "May our lineage increase," he says, "May it increase."
May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give.

Having accepted these benedictions, he spreads out *kuśa* grass with *pavitra* blades upon which the *svadhā*-invocations are to be recited; then he asks, "Shall I cause the *svadhā* to be recited? Being permitted with the words, "Let it be recited," he says: "Let the *svadhā* be pronounced for the fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers. When the reply is given, "Let there be *svadhā*," he pours water over the items for the *svadhā*-recitation while saying, "For strength (*ūrjam*). Having turned the vessel face upwards, he should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins according to his ability. Having caused them to recite for the *Viśvedevas*, "May the *Viśvedevas* be pleased," and having dismissed them with, "In every battle (*vāje vāje*), protect us," he should follow behind them while reciting, "Come to me with strength (*ā mā vājasya*"), circumambulate them keeping them to his right, and then sit down (or enter).

Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra [4.9.10–14]: Having ascertained that they are satiated, he should cause them to hear the *madhumatī* verses and the verse beginning with *akṣann amīmadanta*. Having asked, "Is it well-prepared? and having set aside portions from each of the foods that were consumed along with the *sthālīpāka* for the sake of the *piṇḍas*, he should present the remainder. Whether by invitation or by consent, while those who have eaten have not yet rinsed their mouths, he should place the *piṇḍas*. Having scattered food and offered water for sipping, he should dismiss them with the words, "Let the *svadhā* be uttered," or [they may reply], "Let there be *svadhā*."

Because of the statement "together with the *sthālīpāka*," those who maintain only the domestic fire (*āvasathya*) should cook the *sthālīpāka* for the sake of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, perform the *śrāddha* up to the point of giving food, perform the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* before the *sthālīpāka*, feed the Brahmins, and then, having combined the *sthālīpāka* rice with the remaining food of the *śrāddha*, they should perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). "In what is approved" means when it has been accepted by the eater of the *śrāddha*. "In what is permitted" means when he himself has given permission, saying, "Let it be eaten together with [your] loved ones."
Śaṅkha and Likhita [state]:

Having caused the *gāyatrī* to be recited, and having ascertained that they are satisfied, he asks, "Is it well-tasted? Having obtained permission regarding the remaining food, he should scatter the original portion of food. Having caused the word *svadhā* to be uttered, he should place three *viṣṭara* (seats). He should also offer three water-vessels containing sesame seeds and *pavitra* grass, made either of clay, stone, or udumbara wood; and he should present incense, perfumes, garlands, a mirror, a lamp, collyrium, and other such items. Taking all varieties of food, he should place the *piṇḍas*. With his left hand placed over the right, he should consecrate each *piṇḍa* with three mantras, saying, "O [Name], this is for you," and wipe his hands on those very *darbha* grasses. Having sprinkled water from the vessels around them, he should say, "May there be givers," and "May we have much to give."
Yama says: Then, after they have eaten, one should present the remaining food to them;
as those twice-born ones may direct, so should he act, being authorized by them.
Having asked whether they are satisfied, he should diligently offer water for sipping;
once they have sipped, he should dismiss them with palms joined in reverence after greeting them.
"Sirs, rejoice here, having recognized the characteristics of permission;
one should say, 'Svadhā! and 'May the ancestors be pleased!'"
The twice-born, being satisfied, should declare, "May the food and drink be inexhaustible";
immediately thereafter, one should perform the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
In a pure and secluded place, one should diligently prepare three seats; there, one should offer them, accompanied by the [deceased's] name and lineage.
Having sprinkled [the hand] with water according to the rule and having scattered sesame seeds over it,
he should then wipe that hand on the darbha grass for the sake of those entitled to the scrapings.
Then, being self-restrained, he should satisfy the ancestors with a jar of water;
he should offer the first funeral cake (piṇḍa) while reciting "pṛthivī" and "pitryam."
One should cause [the offering] to be given to the grandfather in the intermediate space,
and then one should present the third to the great-grandfather.
"This is the eternal Vedic revelation: 'The sky is the giver.
Therefore, having offered salutations and bowed down, one should request boons from the ancestors."
May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give.

By the statement, "Having asked, he indeed gives with effort," this is meant: the solicitation for permission regarding the remaining food is not by mere words alone; rather, one should personally exert effort toward its giving. Here, the verb *dadāti* (he gives) refers to the purpose [of the action], as in the expression "standing, he performs the oblations. "Knowing the sign of permission" means knowing the mark indicating consent, such as saying, "We are satisfied. "*Viṣṭarān*" refers to the *kuśa* grass used as seats for the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*). "He should scatter them there"—the word "rice-balls" is to be supplied. "*Lepabhāginām*" refers to those beyond the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*).
Bṛhaspati [Śrāddha, 106–108, 104, 105, 129, 109]: He should ask, "Are you satisfied? and then he should do whatever they say.
Thereafter, he should perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa) in their presence.
[204] From all the food prepared, one should offer balls of rice mixed with honey and sesame seeds for the ancestors, maternal grandfathers, and others, according to the rules of the Gṛhya-sūtras.
Having worshipped them with lamps, perfumes, garlands, incense, as well as garments, collyrium, and so forth, one should place a vessel of water upon them.
Then, in front of the Brāhmaṇas who have sipped water,
he should scatter food mixed with water and recite this mantra:
May those living beings of my family who have been consumed by fire, as well as those not so consumed, be satisfied by what is given upon the earth; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal.
Having uttered "vāje vāje," he should dismiss those Brahmins;
having circumambulated the Brahmins from left to right, he should request boons from them.
May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give.
Hārīta says:

When they are satisfied, he should ask, "Was it well-tasted? and they reply, "It was well-tasted. At rites for the gods, one says "It is cooked" (*śṛtam*); at private rites, "It is life-giving" (*āyuṣyam*). When they have sipped water, he should pour out the scattered food (*vikira*) on the ground. When they have sipped water again, he should pour it into the hands of the Brahmins along with roots and sesame seeds. They say, "Oṃ Svadhā," and they reply, "Let there be Svadhā. Then follows the formula of permission; some say, "May you be delighted," and they reply, "We are delighted. Having walked around [the Brahmins] while reciting "Vāja-vāja," he should place the portions of the remainder as *piṇḍas* according to the ritual of the Pitṛyajña. One who desires prosperity in the Śrāddha should perform ten or eleven items: the sprinkling around, the sprinkling upon, the handful of water, the vessel for the *arghya*, the water for the secondary rinsing of the *arghya*, the cleansing and the leading away, the water for the scattering, and whatever else is done silently. These constitute the tenth and eleventh [items].
Regarding the term "cooked" (śṛta) in the context of the gods: that śrāddha which is performed with reference to the gods is called *daivika* (pertaining to the gods).
It should be performed with effort on the seventh lunar day and other such days, using distinguished sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
