[205] Thus ends the *deva-śrāddha* as described in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*. In that context, one should ask, “Is it cooked? (*śṛtam*). “Cooked” (*śṛtam*) means prepared; this is due to the irregular form (*nipātana*) “*śṛta* in the sense of cooking. Regarding “in private matters” (*svaireṣu*), it refers to those *śrāddhas* mentioned in the passage, “And indeed, the inclination toward the *śrāddha*. “With roots and sesame seeds” (*samūlatilaiḥ*): here, “with roots” (*samūlāḥ*) refers to *kuśa* grass; therefore, it means together with *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds. “One should pour out” (*ninayet*); the word “water” (*jalam*) is to be supplied. “Then the words of permission” (*tato ’nujñāvacanam*); the word “should be performed” (*kāryam*) is to be supplied. And that [permission] is such as, “Stay as you please,” and so forth. “‘Be pleased,’ say some”: some maintain that the rule for the words of permission is the phrase “be pleased” (*abhiramyatām*).
Furthermore, Hārīta states: A wife, being well-restrained, should likewise offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) for her mother-in-law and the others,
as well as handfuls of water, a lamp, collyrium, and ointment.

Regarding the phrase "of the mother-in-law and others": in that Vedic school where the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa) to the mother and so forth is prescribed separately, it is performed without mantras because [the performer] is the sacrificer (yajamāna). This offering of rice balls to women belongs only to certain followers of specific Vedic schools.

*Śāṅkhāyana Gṛhyasūtra* [4.1.5–9]: When they have finished eating, one should offer the *piṇḍas*. According to some, [they are offered] beforehand. Behind the *piṇḍas*, having placed something as a partition, [he offers] for their wives. He should inform the Brahmins of the remainder. The ritual beginning with the *agnaukaraṇa* is explained by the procedure of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*.

"Before" means prior to the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas. "Some" refers to this distinction being established according to different Vedic schools (śākhā). "To the west of the rice-balls" means in the western region of the rice-balls for the ancestors and others, at a short distance, having placed some intervening object between them. "By means of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, including the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa)" means by means of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña which includes the ritual procedure beginning with the offering into the fire. [206] This is the scriptural citation (nigama).

When they are satisfied, he should dismiss them by asking, "Are you satisfied? as before, and having poured water as previously described, he should cause the ancestors to pronounce a blessing. Then, having said, "Oṃ, let the *svadhā* be uttered," and "May you be pleased; depart at your ease," he should honor them and follow them for a short distance.
"Having sprinkled as before," having performed the ritual rinsing; "having caused the benediction to be recited," having caused them to say, "May there be well-being."

Uśanas says: When these [ancestors] have been satisfied and have said "Enough, enough," one should sprinkle them with water mixed with sesame seeds accompanied by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and then recite the names of the three ancestors who preceded them. One should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) upon the ground strewn with *darbha* grass. Then one should cause the word *svadhā* to be uttered. Having set down the rice-balls and sprinkled them again with water, one should set aside the water vessels. "Accompanied by a sacrificial fee" means together with the substance of the fee. "Having sprinkled" means having performed the ritual washing (*pratyavanijya*).
While the phrase "among Brahmins who do not give" continues [in the context], Viṣṇu states [Viṣṇusmṛti 73.17–28.32]:

In the vicinity of the remnants of the meal, upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing southward, he should place one rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) for the father with the mantra: "The earth is the ladle; may it not be destroyed. A second for the grandfather with: "The intermediate space is the ladle; may it not be destroyed. A third for the great-grandfather with: "The sky is the ladle; may it not be destroyed. He should give a garment with the verse: "Those ancestors here who have passed away... Food with the verse: "O ancestors, grant us heroic sons... At this point, he should sprinkle water from his own hand at the roots of the *darbha* grass with the words: "O ancestors, rejoice according to your respective portions. Having scattered water around the rice-balls clockwise with the mantra "Bringing strength... while accompanied by water, he should present offerings of *arghya*, flowers, incense, ointments, food, and other edibles. He should also provide a water-vessel mixed with honey, ghee, and sesame seeds. When the Brahmins have eaten and reached satiety, he should sprinkle the food along with the grass with the mantra "May it not be exhausted for me," scatter the remains of the food before the remnants, and ask, "Are you satisfied? and "Has it been well-prepared? Then, having given water for sipping (*ācamana*) and so forth to those facing north, and subsequently to those facing east, he should sprinkle the site of the *śrāddha* with the words "It is consecrated" (*saṃprokṣitam*). Holding *darbha* in his hand, he should perform all these acts. Then, while facing east, he should circumambulate the area clockwise with the mantra "Whatever [fault] I have committed, O Rāma," and returning, he should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his ability. Saying, "May you be pleased," and when they reply, "We are pleased," he should mutter the mantra "The gods and the ancestors... Having given the water for inexhaustibility (*akṣayyodaka*) according to their names and lineages, and saying "May the Viśvedevas be gratified" to those facing east, he should then, with palms joined and mind focused on that, make his request.
"May our donors increase, as well as our Vedic knowledge and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
Then, with the words "In every contest," he should dismiss the Brahmins after honoring them according to the rule,
following them for a short distance, and saluting them.
The mantra beginning with "O Rāma who belongs to me" and "O bird who belongs to me," and so forth.
Having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) toward the fire, one should perform the entire circumambulation in reverse order.
One should offer pure water with the hand kept in the *apasavya* position.
[208] But from that remaining sacrificial food, one who is composed should form three balls and offer them facing south, according to the very same procedure used for the water libation.
Having offered those rice-balls (piṇḍas) according to the rule while remaining pure,
he should wipe that hand on those Darbha grasses for the sake of the "partakers of the smearings" (lepabhāginaḥ).
Having sipped water and turned away from it, and having sipped water three times slowly,
the knower of mantras should pay homage to the six seasons and to the ancestors.
One should slowly pour the remaining water near the rice balls;
then, being composed, one should smell those rice balls as they have been placed.
Having taken very small portions from each of the rice-balls in succession,
he should first cause those same seated Brahmins to eat according to the prescribed rule.
Having placed the *tilodaka* together with the *pavitra* into their hands,
he should offer them the first portion of that *piṇḍa*, saying, "May there be *svadhā* for them."

‘Apasavyaṃ’ means counter-clockwise (not to the right). ‘Āvṛtparikramaḥ’ means by turning around ‘apasavyena’, that is, toward the south. ‘Nirvapet’ means he should place; the remainder of the sentence is “upon the kuśa grass spread for the sake of the piṇḍas. ‘Śuci’ means unspoiled. ‘Tasmāt’ means from that remnant of the oblation, which is what remains after the *agnaukaraṇa* offering. ‘Audakenaiva vidhinā’ means by the procedure involving the offering of water for the washing (*avanejana*). ‘Nyupya’ means having given. ‘Vidhipūrvakaṃ’ means accompanied by the method of the ritual prescribed in one’s own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. ‘Udakparāvṛtya’ means having turned around so as to face the north. ‘Mantravat’ means accompanied by the mantras beginning with “*namo vaḥ pitaraḥ rasāya*. ‘Ninayet’ means he should pour out or give. ‘Śeṣaṃ’ refers to the remainder left after the first washing, following the honoring of the Brahmins.
Devala says:
Then, having taken a pitcher filled with water and containing darbha grass,
and having sat down in front of them, he should announce the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍāvāpa).
[209] Then, having been permitted by them, he should go toward the southern direction and prepare a sandy site in a clean, smeared place.
The maṇḍala should be large, square, and sloping toward the south;
one should scratch its center three times with a single blade of darbha grass and discard that [blade].
Then, in that place, he should evenly spread many auspicious darbha grasses with single roots,
all of which have their tips pointing southward and their bases toward the north.
Then, rising with palms joined in reverence and standing, one should invoke the ancestors:
"May my fathers be gracious; may my grandfathers depart."
Reciting this, he should remain silent for a moment without breathing out;
having invoked them, he should prepare their seats with the tips of darbha grass.
When they are seated, he should offer water for rinsing into their vessels;
he should scatter flowers there, as well as sesame seeds of various colors.
Then, taking the sacrificial porridge with his hand holding the purifier (pavitra),
he should indeed divide the balls of rice, smeared with ghee, into four portions using a vessel.
Having anointed them with honey and clarified butter, he should plant them in a heap of *kuśa* grass,
in the shade of an elephant, or in the shade of a goat, in the presence of a grandson of a goat.
And one should slowly recite the names of the three [ancestors], preceded by their father's name,
with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), the thumb tucked inside, preceded by the mantra, and ending with "svadhā."
"O father, this for you and those who follow you"—with these words and others, he should scatter [the rice] for the father;
likewise for the grandfather, and he should act similarly for the father of that [grandfather].
[210] One should pour out the fourth ball of rice for the remaining [ancestors] with the words "The common one. Having thus placed those balls of rice, one should adorn them as before.

Having adorned [the fire] according to the ritual manual, the wise one should offer oblations into the purifier with sacrificial offerings and the *kavya* mantra, while pronouncing the sound of *svadhā*.
Having thus offered the oblations of fire, immediately thereafter,
the twice-born man should present an offering of cooked food to those funeral cakes.
Then, from the portions of the *piṇḍas* over which the *bali* offerings have been made,
he should offer water for sipping (*ācamana*) using that very same alms-bowl (*piṇḍapātra*), preceded by the recitation of mantras.
Then, taking a handful of the remains of the oblation from the beginning,
one should perform the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa) for the wives of the ancestors in successive order, one by one.
Then, taking a large portion of the prepared sacrificial oblation,
he should offer it as common to the entire circle of his kinsmen.
One should cause to be given for each individual ball of rice a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), all enjoyments,
as well as foods to be chewed, cakes, sugarcane, condiments, and solid meals.
Then, having taken up water with sesame seeds in the alms-bowl,
he should walk three times continuously around those funeral cakes, keeping them to his left.
Then, having offered salutations with a disciplined mind, he should request a boon from the ancestors:
"May our lineage increase further, and may we have much to give."
In the case of an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite performed in another month or likewise in the anniversary year, this same procedure shall apply; however, only a single *piṇḍa* is offered there.
Having thus honored the rice-balls and offered oblations into the fire according to the rules,
he should approach the place where the Brahmins are seated and honor those Brahmins.
Then, one should feed the twice-born with the remains of the rice-balls according to the prescribed rite.

"Of these" refers to the Brahmins seated for the *śrāddha*. "To the south, etc. is relative to the performer of the *śrāddha*. "Having come" means having reached. "Sandy" means consisting of sand (*vālukā-maya*). [211] "Three times" means three rounds. "That" refers to the *darbha* grass. "Single-rooted" means many blades joined at a single root. "With the tips pointing north" means with the roots facing north. "Simultaneously" means at one time. "Of them" refers to the ancestors. "One should prepare their places" implies that this is done upon the spread *darbha* grass. "Water for sprinkling" (*mārjana-udaka*) is the water for the ritual washing (*avanejana*). "Basta" means a goat. "Without the thumb" means separated from contact with the thumb. One should employ the address "O Father, etc. (*etat te tata*), using the vocative case of the words for the ancestors. "Of the remaining ones" refers to the great-grandfather (*vṛddha-prapitāmaha*) and others. "As before" means as in the worship of the Brahmins. "With the *kavya* mantra" refers to the mantra beginning with "To Agni Kavyavāhana," etc. "Proclaimed" means uttered loudly; "one should do so" is the implied completion of the sentence. "Water for sipping" (*ācamana-udaka*) is the water for the subsequent washing (*pratyavanejana*). And as for "then": the meaning is that after that, one should wrap the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) three times with water mixed with sesame while the sacred thread is over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). Although this procedure for the rice-balls was stated by Manu and Devala prior to the feeding of the Brahmins, it is written here in accordance with the section on the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-prakaraṇa*).
Śaṅkha says: The wise should perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) either in the vicinity of the food leavings,
or they should first perform the fire-rite (agnikārya) according to the prescribed rule.
Whatever is cooked in the house, whether it be solid food (bhakṣya) or soft food (bhojya),
one must never eat it without first offering it at the base of the *piṇḍa*.
Having fed them according to his devotion, and once they have sipped water and been given sacrificial fees,
he— being of a serene mind— should cause them to pronounce a blessing, follow them for a short distance, and then bid them farewell.

The meaning is that one should offer all the prepared food as *piṇḍa-bali*, according to the rule: "One must not eat without having offered [the food]. "At the base of the *piṇḍa*" means near the *piṇḍa*. Manu and Viṣṇu state in the first [chapter]:
"Having collected all kinds of food and sprinkled them with water..."
He should cast it away and scatter it upon the ground in front of those who have finished eating.
Having asked, "Was it well-tasted?", he should then cause those who are satisfied to rinse their mouths; and once they have rinsed, he should dismiss them with the words, "Be happy, sirs."
Immediately after that, the Brahmins should say, "Svadhāstu.
For in all rites for the ancestors, the utterance of *svadhā* is the supreme benediction.
Then, he should inform those who have eaten about the remainder of the food.
Having been authorized by the best of the twice-born, he should act exactly as they may direct.
At a rite for the ancestors, the formula is "Svaditam"; at a rite for cattle, "Suśrutam";
at an auspicious rite, "Saṃpannam"; and at a rite for the gods, "Rocata" may also be used.
Having dismissed those Brahmins, being self-controlled, restrained in speech, and pure,
he should look toward the southern direction and request these boons from the ancestors:
May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give.
"Sārvavarṇikam" means all that has been prepared. "Sannīya" means having mixed together. "Ākāṅkṣan" means looking on.
Vasiṣṭha [3.69–71]:

One should praise the evening and morning meals with the words "it is pleasing"; at ancestral rites (pitrīya), with "it is well-flavored" (svadita); and at rites for prosperity (ābhyudayika), with "it is excellent" (saṃpanna).
Devala says: When they are thus satisfied, one should offer water for drinking as well as water for sipping (ācamana);
one should also remove the remnants of the food, but avoid pronouncing the names of the ancestors.
Then, having taken all the food into the vessel according to the rules,
he himself should pour it out into that same vessel at the place where their leavings are kept.
Then, after the twice-born have sipped water, he should bestow upon them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to his own ability,
consisting of gold, gems, objects of enjoyment, and other things.
Then, taking a handful from within the sacrificial oblation himself,
and having grasped both that and a jar filled with water;
Flowing from the tips of the hands of the ancestors and the Brahmins,
he should move counter-clockwise past all of them, turning his face outward as he passes the funeral cakes.
Having circumambulated the water three times in this manner, one should cause it to be heard slowly;
then, having carried that vessel around, one should overturn it right there.
Then, indeed, one should have Brāhmaṇas representing the Viśvedevas recite a blessing;
for those representing the ancestors, one should have them recite "May it be inexhaustible," last of all, with water and sesame seeds.
Then, he should salute the Brahmins who have received their portions and are fully satisfied, according to the rules:
first those belonging to the Vaiśvadeva rite, and then again the ancestors, beginning with the father.
First, he should cause those belonging to the ancestors to rise while saying, "May it prosper!
He should follow them once they have risen and collect the remainder from them.
Afterwards, one should likewise cause the Brahmins dedicated to the Vaiśvadeva to rise;
for these who were seated first are the ones who rise last.
‘Pānīyaṃ’ (water) is that which is designated as ‘Amṛta’ at the conclusion of the meal. ‘Evam-patanaṃ’ means that whose falling occurs in the manner thus described. ‘Caramaṃ’ means afterwards.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
“One should cause [the recipient] to place Darbha grass with sesame seeds upon the leavings, with their tips pointing toward the south.”
Whatever has been offered there to the ancestors, and whatever else [has been given] in that place;
Therefore, having taken a portion from each of those [substances] into equal and auspicious [quantities],
one should offer the "lid of nectar" (amṛtāpidhāna) to the Brahmins, one by one.
"O Brahmins, is this of mine well-prepared?"—thus he should say to them;
"It is very well-prepared," they reply, and he should address each of them again.
"Aha! May you be satisfied! they said, "We are satisfied. He spoke to them again: "What remains? And what food is still to be given?"
They say to him, "Let this be given to those who are disciplined.
Then, having ascertained that they are satiated, he should scatter food and water upon the ground.

Those ancestors born in our family for whom the rites of the rice-ball and water libations have been omitted, those who died before the tonsure ceremony was performed, and those who perished while still in the womb— [may they all attain satisfaction].
May those for whom no cremation is performed, as well as others who have been consumed by fire, be satisfied by what is offered upon the ground; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal.

Then, having washed his hands and likewise performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should remember Hari; thereafter, for the sake of pacifying the expiation, he should relinquish the portion belonging to the deceased (preta).
Then one should mutter the Gāyatrī together with the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava;
likewise, one should recite the meritorious Madhumatī verses and the words "Madhu, Madhu."
"In the remnant" means in the vicinity of the remnant. "For the pacification accomplished by expiation" means for that pacification which is to be achieved through expiation.
Likewise; there, in the southeast direction, an altar (vedi) should be prepared.
It is four finger-breadths high from the ground, which extends for one cubit.
Especially for the purpose of offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), this place is most delightful. Oṃ! I destroy everything that is impure;
and all the asuras and dānavas have been slain by me.
The yakṣas, the rākṣasas, the hosts of piśācas,
and all the yātudhānas have been slain by me.
With this mantra, one whose self is well-restrained,
desiring firm and auspicious wisdom, should once sweep the entire sacrificial altar.
And one should scatter kusha grass there with the tips pointing toward the south.
Likewise:
Having taken a bunch of *darbha* grass with his left hand,
he should cross over a line with its tips pointing southward using that [grass], and recite [the mantra].
With the sacred grass (pavitra) in hand and reciting the supreme mantra that destroys demons,
he should spread the kuśa grass along with their roots upon the line, with the tips pointing toward the south.
[215] Then, indeed, taking handfuls of flowers along with water for the guest-offering (argha) from the cups and other vessels, he should place them individually behind each of those [seats].
One should wash [the vessel] counter-clockwise, while consecrating it with the lineage name:
"O [Name], of the [Gotra] lineage, this food is for you; svadhā, obeisance!"
At the end [of the mantra], one should recite "avanenikṣa" while remaining well-composed;
then, as before, one should place the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) into the three *argha* vessels.
Having taken warm food mixed with honey, clarified butter, and water, and combined with all kinds of seasonings, one should form it into a ball the size of a bilva fruit.
One should offer [the rice balls] to the grandfather and the others at the base of the *darbha* grass in due order, and should recite: "O you of such-and-such lineage, this rice ball is for you."
One should recite the mantra "ye ca tvām" separately for each of them;
then, having duly wiped both hands upon the darbha grass, one should proceed.
Then, having washed [the hands] with water and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) three times, one should remember Hari;
from those vessels containing the remnants, the ceremonial sprinkling (avanejana) should be performed with water alone.
Having offered [the water] there, he should stand facing north and recite "datvātra pitaras ca," while contemplating all the ancestors as satisfied and possessing radiant forms.
Seeing [the ancestors], he should recite "amī madanta pitaras tv" with focused meditation;
then, loosening his waist-knot (nīvī), he should mutter "namo vaḥ pitaras tv."
Just as here, having recited that mantra with palms joined in reverence, one should speak to each [ancestor] individually, saying: "O ancestors, this is your garment."
Then one should recite: "O you of such-and-such lineage, this garment is for you. Thereafter, one should present the garments in sequence, including fringes made from white cloth.
When one's age has advanced and one's own hairs have turned grey,
one should provide a new thread made of linen, hemp, or even cotton.
One should avoid black wool, as well as silken garments dyed blue or red; likewise, one should avoid honey, ointments, water for the guest-offering (argha), flowers, incense, and unguents.
One should offer the bali-oblation according to the rule so that the piṇḍa becomes eightfold;
having worshipped the ancestors residing in the piṇḍas, one should pay homage to the seasons.
Oṃ! Homage to you, the Spring; and repeated homage to the Summer.
And always homage to the Rains, and to the season known as Autumn.
Homage to you for the winter season, homage to you for the cold season;
and always homage to the months, the years, and the days.

"Having taken a bunch of *darbha* grass" means that having taken a bunch of *darbha* grass with the left hand, one should scratch [the ground] with both hands; this is because of the statement in the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "A twice-born man should perform the scratching with the left hand placed over the right. "He should recite the mantra that destroys demons" refers to the mantra beginning with "avahatāḥ" and so forth. "On their backs" means upon the *kuśa* grass spread for the sake of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). "Having given" means having deposited [the water]. "As before" means as in the case of the *arghya* vessels for the father and others. "In due order" means according to the rule, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*) and accompanied by the mantra. "Having sprinkled" means having consecrated [the water]. "To them" means to the ancestors present in the rice-balls. "From those [vessels] containing the overflow" means having taken water from the vessel containing the overflow and having given the water for washing the feet (*avanejana*); such is the meaning.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"A twice-born man should perform the scraping with both hands, the left one being uppermost."
Likewise: "I shall destroy everything that is impure, and all the asuras and dānavas have been slain by me."
The rākṣasas, yakṣas, along with the hosts of piśācas,
and all the yātudhānas have been slain by me.
With this mantra,
the wise man, his self well-restrained and desiring certain auspicious wisdom, should once sweep the entire sacrificial altar.
The twice-born man should cast [it] toward the northern direction.
Thus it has been observed regarding the ancestral rites of that twice-born man:
the Asuras avoid the śrāddha in whatever place this mantra is recited.
The Rākṣasas indeed avoid that place.
"He should cast"—the ellipsis is "the instrument for scratching."
Likewise:

One should take up the *darbha* grasses for the sake of the *piṇḍas* all at once, facing southward, with their tips pointing toward the east-south; being self-controlled, the procedure here shall also be explained.
Devoted to the ancestors, the wise man, having placed his left knee upon the ground, should offer three balls of rice mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
One should properly scatter the morsels of food, moving counter-clockwise and without weariness,
using various kinds of food, water, flowers, fruits, and edible offerings.
Some men desire that there be separate [offerings] for the maternal grandfathers as well—
three rice-balls (piṇḍas) in successive order, held with the thumbs and grasped in a fist.
One should diligently offer [the oblation] separately and in due order to those accompanied by their followers;
with both hands—the left and the right—one should always recite this mantra.
Saying "Homage to you, O ancestors! May you be satisfied," he should then, with faith, offer the first *piṇḍa* with both hands—the left and the right.
"Obeisance to you, O Pitṛs, who are gentle; thus, being ever vigilant, one should perform the pouring of water from a vessel onto a line drawn with water."
One should provide new linen thread, as well as flaxen or cotton thread, and silk thread or woven silk;
however, one should avoid silk produced from wild silkworms.
A wise person should avoid [using] the ash even if it is unblemished;
for they say that collyrium from Mount Trikakuda is always the best.
Having taken three blades of *darbha* grass, he should perform the rite according to the prescribed rule;
then, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), he should offer the excellent collyrium to the ancestors.
And oil from black sesame seeds, carefully preserved with great effort.

There is an option between facing south and having the tips [of the grass] pointing southeast. "One should encircle" means one should surround it with the water, flowers, and so forth to be mentioned later. "Counter-clockwise" (apasavya) means not in the direction of the sun's movement. The instruction "and one should avoid the fringe" refers to fringes other than those of white cloth, according to the statement in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "One should offer garments in sequence, including the fringe produced from a white cloth. "Traikakuda" is antimony from the Sauvīra region.
Likewise,
having properly ground the collyrium, the twice-born man [should place it] to the north of the altar.
Likewise: "Oil should be offered along with the rice-ball (piṇḍa), for it is the anointing of the rice-ball;
likewise, ointment, anointing, perfume, and the offering of the sacred thread."
One who desires the fruit of the horse sacrifice should perform [the rite] with new, spun silken cloths;
for these ancestors are indeed gods, and gods are likewise ancestors.
This mantra has been proclaimed for these flowers, perfumes, incenses, and so forth;
and at the śrāddha ceremony, being composed, one should recite the Sāvitrī over each individual piṇḍa.
And one should say "to Soma," as well as "to those who have a father."
Likewise: "And here, the Earth is to be praised as the sustainer of the funeral offering—
she who belongs to Viṣṇu, she who belongs to Kaśyapa, and likewise she who belongs to Ikṣvāku."
And when fetching water, the Lord Varuṇa should be praised. Śātātapa says:
"Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability."
For the sake of accomplishing one's intended purpose, one should cause [the deity] to utter desired boons.
The long rivers and streams, and the three steps of Viṣṇu—
by sprinkling water in this manner, one shall obtain a long life.
The gods abide in the midst of the waters; everything is established in the waters.
May the waters, placed in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa, be auspicious for us.
Fortune dwells in flowers; Fortune dwells in the lotus;
Fortune always dwells in the cow-pen; may there be constant mental well-being for me.
May my merit remain unimpaired; may there be peace, nourishment, and steadfastness for me.
May whatever brings about the highest good in this world be granted to me always.
"May there be much to give everywhere in the south; so may it be for us.
Having received their blessings and having circumambulated the brahmins, [he departed].
Then, having circumambulated them once more with palms joined in reverence,
and having spoken kind words, he should prostrate and bid them farewell.
When the twice-born perform the rite for well-being while the food remains,
that food is consumed by the Asuras, and the ancestors depart disappointed.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "When they have sipped water (ācānta), one should offer water, flowers, and seats,
while reciting the mantra 'yavo 'si' (Thou art barley), endowed with faith and devotion."
One should offer that inexhaustible water, combined with sesame seeds, clarified butter, and honey;
likewise, having spread kusha grass together with purifiers upon the ground, one should offer water.
Then, taking water from the vessels of remnants and having honored it,
while reciting the mantra "ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ," he sprinkles the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) as well.
Having sipped water and become purified, he should smell the middle portion;
they give that to his wife, and he should have the remainder placed in a vessel.
He places those kusa grasses, along with their roots, into the fire; that is the firebrand (ulmuka).
Then there are beautiful and auspicious vessels made of gold and silver.
Elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles; beds and houses; sandals, shoes, umbrellas, chowries, and fans.
Reflecting in his heart that sacrificial fees at sacrifices are meritorious,
even a poor man should give a fee to a Brahmin according to his ability.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "Then, having offered water signifying *svadhā* to the Viśvedevas, the twice-born man, facing eastward, should receive blessings from the twice-born."
"May the ancestors be non-terrible," [he said]; "So be it," was the reply. Then the twice-born man [said], "May our lineage prosper"; and they replied to him again, "So be it."
"May our givers increase, and may our food likewise," he should utter;
and when they have replied, "May these true blessings be fulfilled," he should say, "So be it."
One should perform the recitation of auspicious verses (svastivācana) after having removed the rice-balls (piṇḍas) according to one's ability.
Likewise:
"Then, standing before them and taking hold of a water-vessel..."
Reciting "vāje vāje," one should dismiss [the deity] with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass.
He should perform a circumambulation outside and follow for eight steps,
accompanied by his circle of kinsmen and together with his sons and wife.
In the Mahābhārata:
At the conclusion of the śrāddha, for a Brahmin it should be said, "May it be well-savored" (svaditam bhavet);
for a Kṣatriya, one should likewise say, "May the ancestors be pleased" (prīyantām pitaraḥ).
But at the conclusion of a Brahmin’s Śrāddha rite, O Bhārata, one should utter "May it be inexhaustible" (akṣayyam); for a Śūdra, O Bhārata, one should say "Svasti."
The recitation of the Puṇyāha formula is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in rites for the gods;
this very same rite, performed without the syllable Om, is prescribed for a Kṣatriya.
And for a Vaiśya, it should be said: "May the deities be pleased.
[221] In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: some teachers desire the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) afterwards.
And the worship of Brahmins must always be performed here first of all.
For Bṛhaspati, who was skilled in both dharma and worldly affairs, said "no" to that;
one should first present the rice-balls (piṇḍas) and afterwards feed the Brahmins.
Yama said:
That food which, after the twice-born have been satiated,
is designated by the name "viśada" but is not actually called by that name, and which is given upon the ground— [that is what is meant].
For those whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, for infants, for those who have just emerged from the womb,
and for unmarried maidens who have died, the offering is given upon the ground.
Whatever is given according to this rite near water, upon *darbha* grass, or in sand, shall become inexhaustible for the ancestors.

"Viśadam" means pure; the sense is that one should scatter [the offering] on the ground after making it fit for scattering. Regarding "by the twice-born who have been gratified," this refers to the time characterized by the phrase "on the new moon day of the year"; thus, the meaning is "when the twice-born have been gratified. "And it is not designated by name" means it is not specified by a particular name of the person intended. The passage beginning with "near water" and so forth constitutes an injunction regarding secondary results (guṇaphala).

Manu and Viṣṇu [Manu 3.247–246; Viṣṇu 81.22–23]: For those who died before receiving the sacraments, for those who have abandoned their families, and for women of the household, the food-leavings and whatever is scattered upon the *darbha* grass shall be their allotted portion.
The remnants that have fallen upon the ground at a rite for the ancestors are declared to be the share of the group of servants who are upright and free from deceit.

"Of those who abandon their family women" means those who, without cause, cast out women of good family. "Leftovers" refers to what remains in the vessel for those such as the uninitiated or the deceased. "That which has fallen on the ground" refers to the "remnant," that is, the leavings, intended for the class of servants. "In the rite for the ancestors" (pitrye) means during the ancestral ceremony.
Vasiṣṭha [11.23–24]:
"Regarding those who have died before initiation and those who were servants, such is the Vedic revelation;
Manu has declared that both the leavings of food and the scrapings from the dish are their allotted portion."
One should scatter on the ground the remnants of food, as well as the scrapings and water used for rinsing;
one should cast these away among those who have not yet departed [from this world], who are childless and short-lived.

"Those to be sent forth" (*saṃpreṣyāḥ*) refers to the slaves (*dāsāḥ*). "The water-wash of the smear" (*lepam audakaṃ*) means the wiping of the hand smeared with food and water upon *darbha* grass. Regarding the phrase "among those who have died following the ancestors" (*anupreteṣu pitryādyanuyāyiṣu mṛteṣu*), the meaning is that one should "release"—that is, designate as their portion—the "remnant" (*uccheṣaṇaṃ*), the scattered food (*vikiraṇaṃ*), the smear, and the water-wash for those who are "childless and short-lived" (*aprajānām anāyuṣām*).
Bṛhaspati [Śrāddha, 110]: Those who dwell among the gods are satisfied by what is offered into the fire; those who dwell among the ancestors by the gratification of the twice-born;
and those who dwell in hell are satisfied by the three funeral cakes (piṇḍa) given upon the earth.
Śātātapa says:

The ancestors dwelling in the gods are always satisfied by what is offered into the fire; those dwelling among the ancestors are satisfied by the twice-born who have been gratified with libations; and those dwelling among animals are satisfied by what is given upon the ground.
Hārīta says: "The first rice-ball is known as the giver of long life; the second is remembered as the giver of sons;
the third indeed is the giver of prosperity; therefore, one should feed the middlemost [son]."
If a wife should desire a son, she may eat the middle *piṇḍa* according to the ritual prescribed for Prajāpati; it is traditionally taught that this bestows a son upon her.

[223] "This is the rite of Prajāpati: 'I cause thee to consume the essence of the waters and the plants; do thou conceive a fetus created by the beings,' [saying this] he gives the middle *piṇḍa* to his wife. 'Bestow a fetus, O ancestors—a boy adorned with a lotus-wreath, so that there may be a man here'—with these words the wife should consume it," according to the statement of Āpastamba.
Yama says: One should cause one rice-ball to float in the waters, one should present one to the wife, and one should offer one into the fire; thus three rice-balls are prescribed.
The moon satisfies himself with that ball of food which floats upon the waters;
the highly illustrious moon, as the hare-marked one, gratifies both the gods and the ancestors.
And likewise, the wife, remaining silent, eats the middle ball;
the great-grandfathers make her, who desires a son, one who possesses a son.
When the best of the twice-born thus offers another ball of rice into the fire,
he attains eternal worlds, and his great-grandfathers are satisfied.

"By the words 'eternal ones' (*śāśvatān*), [it means] having been satisfied (*parituṣya*) by the great-grandfathers; 'he,' the performer of the *śrāddha*, 'attains' (*prāpyate*), meaning he obtains, 'the eternal worlds.
Manu [3.267–268]: Having thus performed the offering, immediately thereafter those *piṇḍas*..."
One should cause a cow, a Brahmin, a goat, or fire to eat it, or one should throw it into water.
Some perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) even beforehand;
they cause birds to eat them, or they cast them into fire or water.
A devoted wife, faithful to her husband and intent on the worship of the ancestors,
desiring a son, should then properly eat the middle *piṇḍa*.
One should know that such a son is long-lived, endowed with fame and intelligence,
wealthy, possessed of progeny, righteous, and likewise virtuous.

Regarding the phrase "the offering is thus," when the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa) precedes the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas, three methods of disposal—namely, giving to birds and so forth—are prescribed as mandatory. The statement "they throw [it] into fire or water" is a restatement (anuvāda) of the previously mentioned fire and water, intended to enjoin the consumption by birds.
Bṛhaspati [Śrāddha, 123, 125]:
One should give the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) to cows, goats, or Brahmins, or cast them into fire or water;
however, a woman desiring a son should properly eat the middle cake from among them.
If the wife has gone to another country, or is pregnant, or likewise ill,
then that aged bull or goat deserves to eat [the offering].

The meaning of this is as follows: first, all the *piṇḍas* (funerary cakes) are offered with the understanding that they pertain to cows, water, and so forth. However, when the middle *piṇḍa* is offered to a bull or a goat, it is [offered] when those have been consumed.
As stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "One should give the *piṇḍas* to cows, goats, and Brahmins, or even into fire or water."
Or he may scatter it at the edge of the Brahmins' seats, or have it eaten by birds.
Let them return; let her eat the middle ball of rice, she who is endowed with discipline.
O ancestors, bestow upon her a fetus that shall increase our lineage.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "A man desiring worldly enjoyment should always offer a pinda into the fire;
indeed, for the sake of offspring, he should offer the middle pinda to his wife, preceded by the appropriate mantra."
Seeking the highest state, one should always bestow [the merit] upon cows;
one should always deposit command, wisdom, glory, and fame within the waters.
Desiring long life, he offers [the food] to the crows;
standing in water or facing south, he may cause it to go into the sky.
"Space and the southern direction are the abode of the ancestors," so say Śaṅkha and Likhita.

Having thus requested boons and offered salutations, one should cast the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) either into the fire or into the water; or the wife, having bathed after her menses, may eat the middle cake.
Yājñavalkya [1.257]:
One should give the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to cows, goats, or Brahmins, or else throw them into fire or water;
while Brahmins are present, one must not wipe away the remnants of the twice-born.
Regarding this, Devala says:
"When the Pitṛmedha has concluded, having extinguished the lamp with his hand,
and having sipped water (ācamana) and washed his hands, he should satisfy his kinsmen with the remnants."
Then, when the kinsmen have been satisfied, he should honor his own servants;
afterwards, he himself, together with his wives, should partake of the remains of the offering to the ancestors.
In the case of Ekoddiṣṭa rites, one should offer the remainder to the Brahmins;
thereafter, one may eat oneself, following this with an auspicious meal.
"Having extinguished [the fire] in the shade," he should "recite"; "in the Ekoddiṣṭas" means in the Śrāddha rites performed on the first day and so forth.
Manu [3.264–265]: Having washed his hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should provide for his kinsmen.
Having given honorably to his kinsmen, he should also honor his relatives.
The remnants of the meal should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
thereafter, one should perform the domestic bali offering—thus is the dharma established.

"Abounding in kinsmen" (*jñātiprāyam*) means having many relatives. Regarding the phrase "then the domestic offering" (*tato gṛhabalim*), the term *gṛhabali* denotes the sacrifice to spirits (*bhūtayajña*) and serves as an indicator for the daily great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), such as the *vaiśvadeva*.
Thus it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Having performed [the rites] for the sake of fulfillment and having sprinkled water around the fire, that knower of mantras..."
One should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite as well as the regular bali offering.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: Having gratified the ancestors according to the rule, one should offer the bali-oblation according to the injunction;
thereafter, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite, and after that, the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas.
For this very reason, the sequence for the Bali and Vaiśvadeva offerings should be understood according to the Matsya Purāṇa.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Some excellent men desire the daily rite for the ancestors;
others likewise do not [desire it] for the ancestors; one should perform the remainder as previously described."
Others say not by means of separate cooking; some say everything is as in the case of the *apūrva* (newly prepared) offering.
Vasiṣṭha [11.21–22] states:
"In a *śrāddha*, the remnants of food must not be removed until the end of the day."
Indeed, streams of nectar flow down, and those who have not yet performed their water-libations drink them.
One should not wipe away the remnants until the sun has set;
thereafter, inexhaustible streams of milk flow for those who partake in the distribution.

‘*Cyotante*’ means they leak. ‘*Nodvāsanīyāny ucchiṣṭāni*’ (the leavings are not to be removed) refers to leavings that have fallen on the ground. ‘*Ucchiṣṭaṃ na pramṛjyāt*’ (one should not wipe away the leavings) refers to a vessel containing leavings that has been placed on the ground. ‘*Saṃcarabhāginaḥ*’: that food which, having been given to one person, is passed on (*saṃcarati*) to another is called *saṃcara*; those who partake of it are the slaves and others. [As stated] in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: “Then, after the sun has set, the vessels of the Brahmins [should be placed] in water.”
Having become purified, one should cast down all of them with their faces turned downwards.
On the second day, the washing of all the vessels likewise brings about infinite satisfaction for the ancestors at all times.
Whatever food, whether solid, soft, or liquid, is cooked in the house,
none of it should ever be consumed without first being offered to the ancestors.
Having constantly given to his kinsmen, he should also honor his relatives; Bṛhaspati [Śrāddha, 155]:
"In this manner, having gratified the gods and the three classes of ancestors according to the rule..."
A householder, together with his sons, servants, and others, is entitled to eat.
Śātātapa says: After that, the wise man, being composed and acting according to the rules, should eat the remaining food with his loved ones, having received their permission.
Uśanas says: "Permitted by them, he should give the remainder to those he loves, or he himself should eat it.
The word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "or himself" (*svayaṃ vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*).

[228] Āpastamba [2.17.16]: Having taken portions from all [the food], he should eat of the remainder an amount no less than a mouthful, as prescribed. "An amount no less than a mouthful" means at least one mouthful. "As prescribed" means as stated in the Gṛhyasūtra, with the mantra: "Seated in the vital breath, I offer the nectar; may my self enter into Brahman for the sake of immortality."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa* (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka*, 10.34.1):
"Sisters and kinsmen are indeed always to be honored at *śrāddha* ceremonies."
Likewise: "Bards, panegyrists, and genealogists, as well as those skilled in the triple symphony (song, dance, and instrumental music),
if they receive no gain at the ancestral rites (śrāddha), destroy one's great fame."
Therefore, those [factors] must also be analyzed; both in their entirety and through their divisions.
Yājñavalkya [1.249]: Having circumambulated [the place] clockwise and followed it, one should eat what was consumed by the ancestors;
one should remain celibate for that night together with the Brahmins.
The village rule: Having been permitted, he should satisfy his household members and the young and old, and then eat.
On that day and for both nights, both of them should remain celibate.
Vasiṣṭha and Vṛddha-Śātātapa state in the first [chapter]:
"If one engages in sexual intercourse after having given or eaten at a *śrāddha*,
his ancestors become consumers of semen for that month."
The child born from that [woman], having been given and having consumed what belongs to the father,
does not acquire knowledge and is born with a diminished lifespan.
Bṛhaspati, Manu, and Devala state that on the second day [of the lunar fortnight],
both the one who performs the śrāddha and the one who eats at it should observe celibacy for that night;
otherwise, if they behave differently, both would go to hell.
If one who has partaken of a śrāddha feast approaches the bed of a low-caste woman on that same day,
his ancestors lie for that month in her excrement.
Therefore, both the giver and the eater at a śrāddha must be restrained; if the worshipper and the one worshipped are not honored, both shall go to hell.
The phrase "the bed of a *vṛṣalī*" is an elliptical expression for sexual intercourse. Śātātapa says:
"Those who, being distracted, eat at another's *śrāddha* after having already performed their own *śrāddha*..."
The ancestors of those for whom the rites of the rice-ball and water libations have been omitted fall [into misfortune].

In the Matsya Purāṇa: "The performer of a śrāddha and the eater at a śrāddha should both avoid all of these: eating a second time, traveling on a journey, gambling, physical exertion, and sexual intercourse."
One should always avoid private recitation of the Vedas, quarreling, and sleeping during the day.
As stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Whether one is engaged as an eater at a Śrāddha, or having fed others, or being appointed [to perform it],"
The profligate man causes his own ancestors to sink into the pit of semen.
*Vyavāyī* means one who engages in sexual intercourse.
Now, the nature of the father and others.
In this regard, Manu [3.284] says: "They call the Vasus the fathers, the Rudras the grandfathers, and the Ādityas the great-grandfathers; such is the eternal Vedic revelation."
Devala said:
The ancestors are to be honored in every way; they are the deities of the deities, pure, stainless, and meritorious, residing in the southern direction.
The Basavas are to be known as the fathers, the Rudras are to be known as the grandfathers, and the Ādityas likewise as the great-grandfathers; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
Whatever rite is performed here by humans with reference to the *pretas*,
the ancestors (*pitṛs*) are satisfied by it, for the *pretas* are not remembered as being the ancestors.
Yājñavalkya [1.269]: The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the śrāddha;
when satiated by the śrāddha, they gratify the ancestors of human beings.
Paiṭhīnasi says: "He who, knowing this, worships the ancestors—the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas—becomes dear to them.
Who indeed are these called 'ancestors' to whom what is given here becomes inexhaustible?"
The Vasus are the fathers, the Rudras are the grandfathers, and the Ādityas are the great-grandfathers; what is given to them here becomes inexhaustible.

In this regard, although the status of the Vasus and others as deities (*devatā*) in the *śrāddha* rite is understood from such statements as, “The ancestors (*pitaraḥ*), the sons of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, are the deities of the *śrāddha*,” nevertheless, their status as deities is established by the scriptural injunctions: “O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, this is for you,” and so forth; specifically, by the hearing of the words “this is for you” addressed to the sacrificer’s father, “this is for you” to the grandfather, and “this is for you” to the great-grandfather, accompanied by the proclamation of their specific lineage, name, and relationship, and by their being heard in the dative case (*caturthyanta*). They are to be meditated upon in the form of the Vasus and others, according to the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: “He who, knowing thus, sacrifices to the ancestors.”
Now follows the praise of the Śrāddha.
In this regard, Yama says:
"Those who worship the ancestors, the gods, the Brahmins, and the sacrificial fires—
they worship Viṣṇu alone, the inner self of all beings."
By giving according to this procedure, one obtains four boons;
the ancestors bestow wealth, food, sons, and long life upon the person on earth.
Through the worship of the ancestors, one shall obtain long life, sons, fame, heaven, renown, nourishment, strength, prosperity, cattle, happiness, wealth, and grain.
Devala says:
One who is free from disease, natural, healthy, long-lived, possessed of sons and grandsons, wealthy,
and an enjoyer of wealth shall be one who desires to perform the Śrāddha here in this world.
That man who performs the *śrāddha* attains supreme satisfaction in the hereafter, vast and auspicious worlds, and extensive fame.
Yājñavalkya [1.270]: When pleased, the ancestors bestow upon men long life, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and pleasures, as well as sovereignty.
Hārīta [A.
12]: Whoever performs or even recites this meritorious rite for the Śrāddha, being endowed with all desires, indeed attains immortality.
[233] Bṛhaspati [Śrāddha, 41]: "The wise man who understands this obtains the fruit of the śrāddha;
both the instructor and the one who gives consent are recorded in the world as having equal merit."
Hārīta [A. 12]:
"Neither heroes, nor those free from disease, nor those who live a hundred years are born there, nor do they attain any higher good, in that place where the śrāddha is avoided."
Even with roots, fruits, or likewise with offerings of water, one should perform [the rite] when [proper materials] are unavailable; one must never completely abandon the Śrāddha.
Now follows the *āmaśrāddha* (the śrāddha performed with raw food).
In that regard, the Matsya Purāṇa states:
"When the knower of the rules performs an *āma-śrāddha*,
the giver of the śrāddha should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* with that [uncooked food] and offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) with that very same [food]."
Jābāli says:
One who offers a *śrāddha* with raw food and is without a sacred fire is so for all wise men;
he should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* rite [with that food] and offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) with that very same [food].

The purport here is as follows: "In all cases"—that is, when an occasion for a *śrāddha* such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) has arisen—one who lacks a consecrated fire (*anagni*) should perform an *āma-śrāddha*. Here, "one who lacks a fire" means one who is devoid of a fire capable of cooking; this is an elliptical expression indicating the absence of the entire apparatus for cooking. It does not, however, mean one who has not formally established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), because the performance of a *śrāddha* by means of cooking is prescribed for those who are uninitiated (*anupanīta*), those whose wives have passed away, and those living in exile. Thus it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "Having brought [the food] with both hands, he should serve it."
With a tranquil mind and darbha grass in hand, he should drink the water without leaving any remainder.
But auspicious soups, vegetables, and so forth, as well as various kinds of foods;
and food with curd and milk, along with cow's ghee and sugar.
Likewise,
O King, when they have finished eating at the conclusion of the meal,
one should eat all kinds of food, having rinsed it with water.
One should cast away [the remains] before those who have eaten, scattering them upon the ground.
Likewise:
"Having known them to be satiated, one should likewise offer water once into the hand of the Brahmin."
Even when they have already sipped water, he should again sip water himself and offer water once to each.
Likewise: "That remnant, however, should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed."
Having thus described the *śrāddha* by means of cooking with such introductory statements, it is stated in that very chapter:
"Even one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) should perform this *śrāddha*, known as the 'common' (*sādhāraṇa*), on all festival days (*parvan*); it bestows the fruits of all desires."
"Even one separated from his wife, even one staying abroad,
even a Śūdra who is devoid of mantras, a wise man should perform this according to the prescribed rule, provided he is devoted.
By this it is meant that, in times of distress, both those with sacred fires and those without may perform a funeral rite (śrāddha) with uncooked food (āma-śrāddha).
For one who possesses a sacred fire as well as for one without a fire, an *āmaśrāddha* (a śrāddha with raw food) is always appropriate in times of distress;
likewise, a Śūdra may always perform the common *vṛddhiśrāddha* (an auspicious śrāddha).
"A wise person should perform [the rite] with the *namaskāra* mantra as if it were raw grain (*āmānna*)," because this is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa* itself.
Now follows the Śrāddha for those whose father is living and so forth.
Regarding this, Manu (3.220–222) states:
"While the father is still living, one should perform the offerings for the ancestors alone;
or else, like a Brahmin [at a guest-offering], one should feed one's own father at the śrāddha."
But if one's father has passed away while the grandfather is still living,
he should pronounce his father’s name and then proclaim the name of the great-grandfather.
"Or the grandfather may eat that śrāddha," so Manu declared;
"or, with his permission, one may perform it oneself at will."

‘Dhriyamāṇe’ means while he is staying alive, that is to say, while he is living. Here, the mention of his name is intended as an indication for the *śrāddha* rite; ‘*śrāddham*’ here refers to the purpose of the *śrāddha*. Regarding the phrase ‘or at will, with his permission,’ this is an alternative to the feeding of the father and others. The meaning is: permitted by that father or other relative, he may ‘at will’ perform whatever he desires. Likewise [Manu 3.246]: “Water should be offered to three; the *piṇḍas* proceed for three.”
The fourth among these is the giver; a fifth does not exist.

If one should perform the *śrāddha* while his father is still living, he should perform it for those for whom his father performs it. While both his father and grandfather are living, he should perform it for those for whom his grandfather performs it. While his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are all living, he should not perform it at all. He whose father has passed away should, having placed the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) for his father, offer to the two ancestors beyond the grandfather. He whose father and grandfather have both passed away should, having offered the two rice-balls to them, offer to the great-grandfather of the grandfather. He whose grandfather has passed away should, having placed the rice-ball for him, offer to the two ancestors beyond the great-grandfather.
In this same manner, a wise person should perform the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) for the maternal grandfathers as well;
according to the rule, it should be performed with the modification of the mantras, while for the remaining [ancestors] it is performed without mantras.

The phrase "the father may have died" means that the father alone has passed away, while the grandfather and great-grandfather are still living. "By the modification of the mantra" means by the insertion of words such as "maternal grandfathers" (*mātāmahāḥ*) in place of "fathers" (*pitaraḥ*) within mantras such as "May the fathers be purified" (*śundhantāṃ pitaraḥ*). "Of the remaining [relatives]," namely paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and so forth; "devoid of mantras" means that the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) should be performed excluding the mantras.
Hārīta says: "A son should indeed avoid the time for the Śrāddha while his father is alive;
or rather, it is prescribed that he should perform it for those for whom his father would have offered it."
If the grandfather is indeed living, one should complete [the rites] with the father;
one should diligently offer a handful of water, a lamp, and collyrium.

[238] On the strength of the scriptural injunction, "One should not offer [the śrāddha] by bypassing a living [relative]," one should perform the śrāddha for only a single person even on occasions such as the new moon (*amāvāsya*). Furthermore, because of statements such as "a handful of water" (*udakāñjali*), Jayasvāmin maintains that this is an original (*apūrva*) rite, similar to the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice.
The *Yajñapārśvapariśiṣṭa*:
"For one who knows [the ritual], the Pitṛyajña should conclude with the *homa* if his father is alive;
having fed his father, he should offer the two subsequent rice-balls (*piṇḍa*)."
To those same ancestors to whom one’s father would offer funeral cakes, the son should also cause them to be offered;
one should not offer to one who is still living—this is the Vedic revelation of the learned.
The wise have declared that if the grandfather is living while the father is deceased,
the offering should be given to the father alone.
Having formed three balls of food, he should feed the middle one to him;
he should give two balls to a Brāhmaṇa, or cast them into the fire or into water.
If both [the father and grandfather] have passed away, but the great-grandfather still lives,
one should offer two rice-balls for the former ancestors and feed the great-grandfather.

The *Nigama* states: "Or rather, one should feed him among the ancestors who is still living. Some say [it should be offered] to the *sapiṇḍas*. Hiraṇyaketu says that it must indeed be given, whether they are living or dead. Why? Because the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) is a ritual injunction and this is an auxiliary part of it; and because of the Vedic scripture stating, "He makes this portion for these very [ancestors]," Kātyāyana maintains that there is no non-giving even when only one [of the ancestors] is living.

Regarding the phrase "because it is enjoined as a sacrifice" (*yajñavidhitvāt*), what is intended is either its being a means of livelihood or its not being so; however, it means that because it is enjoined as necessary due to its nature as a sacrifice consisting of renunciation (*tyāga*) performed for the sake of the ancestors and others. Regarding "because it is a subsidiary part of the *Darśa*": the meaning is that the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the ritual known as the *Darśa*.
Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"One who has a father living has no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the rites involving the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*)."
"One should not give anything by bypassing a living person," so says the Śruti.
While the grandfather is living, one should offer for the deceased father;
even if that father is aged and the great-grandfather is still living,
one should pronounce the name of the father and then proclaim the name of the great-grandfather.

One whose great-grandfather is deceased should offer three rice-balls for his father, his grandfather, and even the father of that [grandfather]. Or, O twice-born, one may offer food and water to the deceased while bypassing those who are still living.

"Or he should give to the father's fathers; he is the father"—this is another Vedic text. By the phrase "of that elder," the grandfather is referred to. "Of him also"—that is, of the father's grandfather, the great-grandfather. "Saṃsthitaḥ" means deceased.
[240] This is from the *Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra* regarding the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.

One who has a living father may offer to the ancestors even when [the father] has passed away; for one with a living father, the rite ends with the *homa*. Or rather, there is no undertaking [of the Śrāddha at all]. Jātūkarṇya says it is not interrupted [by the presence of the father], because of the Vedic revelation: "One does not pass over one who is alive."

There are three views regarding one whose father is living: first, that one should offer to those same ancestors to whom the father would have offered, bypassing the living father; second, that there is only the offering into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire up to the end of the *homa*, beginning with "To Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.6.12) and so forth; third, that there is either non-commencement or simply non-performance. The phrase "not separated" (*na vyavete*) means that the offering should not be made when anyone who is living intervenes.
This is stated in the context of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña concerning the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, in the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra (2.6.22–24).
One should offer oblations to the living; for all those who live, it is an offering made to all. Not knowing their names, one should call them "father," "grandfather," and "great-grandfather."

Regarding the phrase "one should offer to those who are living," one should offer the rice-ball (piṇḍa) to whichever among the father and the others is alive. To the deceased, however, one should give it according to the procedure for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. The meaning is that if all are living, then one should offer three rice-balls.
Now follows the śrāddha for one who has two fathers.
In this regard, the *Śāṅkhāyana-sūtra* states:

"Having placed the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) according to the manner of the water-offering (*avanejana*), both [ancestors] are mentioned in a single rice-ball even when there is a distinction among the ancestors. There is no [offering] for one whose father is living; nor for one who has died while another is still living. Or, the son [performs it] for those [ancestors] for whom his father did so, up to the end of the oblation (*homānta*).

Regarding the phrase 'both in one': both the progenitor (*bījika*) and the owner of the field (*kṣetrika*) [are meant]. Regarding 'in a single rice-ball': the meaning is that he should mention them both even within a single rice-ball."

The Chapter on Genealogy (*Pravarādhyāya*). Now, if they are born through a paternal uncle or a relative of the same lineage, they belong to the adoptive father alone. Furthermore, if these [adopted sons] have no offspring by their own wives, they shall inherit his estate. They shall also offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to him for three generations. Even if [the biological father] still exists, they shall offer [the cake] to both; such is the teaching of the Teacher (*Ācārya*). One may perform two *śrāddha* rites, or one. Or, having designated two separately, one may mention both the adoptive father and the biological progenitor in a single funeral cake. The adoptive father [is the primary recipient] until the third generation.
"Of these" refers to the seed-givers, beginning with the field-owner, the paternal uncle, and so forth.

Hārīta says: "A field does not bear fruit without seed, nor does seed sprout without a field; because both are observed [to be necessary], the offspring belongs to both. According to others, among these, the first *pravara* (ancestral invocation) belongs to the progenitor. At the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), they should offer two rice-balls, or else mention two [ancestors] in a single rice-ball. The son [belongs to the second], the grandson to the third, and the great-grandsons to the *lepins*. Some say that when reciting the three [ancestors], one should go back as far as the seventh.

Regarding the phrase “of them”: among those ancestors, both the seed-givers (*bījin*) and the field-owners (*kṣetriṇ*), one should first specify the most eminent *ṛṣi*-lineage (*pravara*) of the seed-giver. Then follows that of the field-owner; thus there is a state of having two *pravaras*. In the *nirvāpa* (offering of rice balls) during the *pitṛyajña*, which is an ancillary part of this ritual, one should mention both [names] in each single [ball]. Here, a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is to be understood, in accordance with the statement of Āpastamba: “If he has two fathers, he should designate two for each. Therefore, the meaning is that in each single *piṇḍa*, both fathers, both grandfathers, and both great-grandfathers are to be mentioned. “In the second”: in the *piṇḍa* of the grandfather. The word “second” is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *piṇḍa* of the great-grandfather. “The son”: of the *dvāmuṣyāyaṇa* (one belonging to two lineages). Here too, the connection “he should mention both in each” is to be supplied. “In the third”: in the *piṇḍa* of the great-grandfather. “The grandson”: of the *dvāmuṣyāyaṇa*. Here too, the construction “he should mention both in each” applies. “And the *lepinas*” (those who partake of the smearings): the ellipsis is “he should mention them. “Reciting three,” i.e., reciting the *piṇḍas* of the father and the others. “Up to the seventh,” meaning up to the seventh person.
Yājñavalkya [2.128]:
A son begotten by means of *niyoga* upon the wife of another by a man who has no son,
according to the law, shall be the heir to the property and the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to both fathers.

Marīci: Whether he be of the same lineage or of a different lineage, the son of a widow should first cause the performance of the piṇḍa-śrāddha rite to be offered to the owner of the field (the biological father).

But if, after that, the offspring should live in the field of the owner of the soil, they should first give [the inheritance] to the owner of the seed; however, if he has died, it is given afterwards.
If both should die, then one should first give [the estate] to the progenitor;
it should not be given first to the owner of the field, for if it were not given first to the progenitor, it would not accrue to him.
"From one of the same lineage or from another lineage" means from anyone of the same caste (savarṇa).
Nārada says: Those who are born of a woman not authorized [to bear children], whether by one man or by many, none of them are sharers of the inheritance;
they are the sons of the seed-givers alone.
If the mother was taken for a bride-price, the seeders shall give the funeral cake;
but if she was obtained without a bride-price, those who give the cake are the husband's kin alone.
"Non-partakers of the inheritance": the biological fathers do not share in the inheritance.
Now follows the Śrāddha for the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra).

Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "According to Pracetas, a *putrikā* (appointed daughter) is like a son; her offspring, the *putrikāsuta*, is the giver of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) to both maternal and paternal grandfathers. There is no distinction between a son and a daughter’s son in terms of bestowing favor.

The phrase "of the maternal and paternal grandfathers" is an indication of both lineages. "Of the son and the daughter’s son" refers to the biological son (*aurasa*) and the son of the appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*). "In terms of bestowing favor" refers to the nature of such acts as rescuing [ancestors] from hell.
Manu [9.132]: "For the daughter's son shall take the entire inheritance of his father who has no [other] sons;
he alone shall offer two funeral cakes, one to his father and one to his maternal grandfather."
The second [portion] belongs to her father, and the third belongs to her father's father.

"Daughter's son" (*dauhitra*) here refers to the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). Thus ends the section on those who belong to two lineages (*ḍyāmuṣyāyaṇa*) in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Śrī Hṛdayadhara, the great minister for peace and war under the illustrious King Govindacandra.
Now follows the rite for a single deceased person (ekoddiṣṭa).
Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"The *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha which is here called occasional (*naimittika*) must also be performed on that very day; one should feed an odd number of twice-born brahmins."
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Then, on the eleventh day, one should feed exactly eleven twice-born men;
however, for those of the Kṣatriya and other castes, one should feed an odd number of twice-born men at the end of the period of impurity (*sūtaka*)."
On the second day, one should again perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite in the same manner.
Yājñavalkya [1.251–252] states:
"The *ekoddiṣṭa* is devoid of the deities; it has a single *argha* offering and a single *pavitraka*."
For it is indeed devoid of the invocation (āvāhana) and the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), and is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).
At the dismissal of the Brahmins, in place of saying "May [the gods] attend upon you," he should say, "May you be delighted"; they should then reply, "We have been delighted."
In the context of employing the term *akṣaya* (inexhaustible), one should use the expression "may it be present" (*upatiṣṭhatām*).

Śāṅkhāyana says: Now, therefore, follows the *ekoddiṣṭa* (rite for a single deceased person). There is one purifier (*pavitraka*), one offering of water (*argha*), one rice-ball (*piṇḍa*); there is no invocation (*āvāhana*), no offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and no Viśvedevas here. The question regarding satisfaction is "Is it well-eaten? (*svaditam*). In place of the word "imperishable" (*akṣayya*), one says "may he approach" (*upatiṣṭhatām*). The dismissal is with the words "may you be pleased" (*ābhiramyatām*). This is done thus for one year after death. [245] In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
One should say "Svaditam" when scattering the food, and "Abhiramyatām" upon its dismissal.
From the *Āśvalāyanagṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"Therefore, on the eleventh day, the Śrāddha for him is prescribed."
But the śrāddha performed for a single deceased person is called "without a rival" (asapatna); such is the established rule.
Having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, one should leave a remainder for three fortnights;
this includes the food scraps fallen on the ground, the scattered offerings, the smears, and the water offerings.
One should offer [the food] among the Anupretas for those who are childless or short-lived;
in all Ekoddiṣṭa rites, there is neither the word "svadhā" nor the formula "abhiramyatām."
The mantra for the offering into the fire and the single offering of water with sesame seeds are always presented everywhere without specifically designating the deceased.
For all those who are childless, it is ordained that there be one purifier, one offering of water, and one rice-ball; there is no utterance of "svadhā," nor the formula "may you be satisfied."
One should thus release [the food] with the words "May there be well-being," omitting the *praṇava* (Om) only once;
however, in the case of the *piṇḍa* offering for an *ekoddiṣṭa*, the word "after" (*anu*) is not employed.
One should not utter the word "father," for one becomes a parricide.

"Without a rival" (*asapatnam*) means being free from a second [offering]. The meaning of the passage beginning with "having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*" is as follows: he who has not performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* within three fortnights should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha once the three fortnights are complete. Regarding the phrase "but without designating the deceased": wherever—in an *ekoddiṣṭa*, a *pārvaṇa*, or elsewhere—the deceased is designated and then released, in all such cases where the deceased has not yet passed [into the state of the ancestors], the leftovers, the scattered grains (*vikira*), and so forth must be offered in this very manner. "No *svadhā*" means that one should not perform the recitation of the *svadhā*. This is a prohibition of the final utterance of *svadhā* prescribed by Āśvalāyana in the rule: "One should dismiss [the guests] saying, 'Let the *svadhā* be uttered. The phrase "let them be satisfied" (*abhiramyatām*) refers specifically to the *ekoddiṣṭa* for the deceased. As for the statement of Śāṅkhāyana, "The dismissal is with the words 'let them be satisfied,'" that refers to other types of *ekoddiṣṭa* rites. Regarding the word "after" (*anu*): the mantra containing the word "after," such as "And those who follow you," etc., should not employ the word "father"; that is to say, one should not recite mantras such as "Obeisance to you, O fathers."
Bṛhaspati [Śrāddha, 128, 132, 135, 136, 138]:

That which is offered to a single person according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* is devoid of the invocation (*āvāhana*), the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and is excluded from the portion for the gods (*daiva*).

Having honored with perfumes and garlands the clothing, ornaments, beds, and so forth, as well as the vehicle and weapons of the deceased father, one should present them to the recipient of the śrāddha meal.
One should cause various kinds of food and condiments to be prepared,
and according to one's ability, one should likewise give gifts such as cows, land, gold, and so forth.
Nine, seven, or thirteen learned Vedic scholars (śrotriya) should be fed,
as well as kinsmen, relatives, the indigent, and other guests.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to all of them in accordance with their merit;
for a Śrāddha performed without those learned in the Vedas is destroyed, and sacrifices without a sacrificial fee are destroyed.
Therefore, one should give as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in a sacrifice even a paṇa, a kārṣāpaṇa, or even a fruit or a flower; by that, one becomes equal in merit.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"On the eleventh day, one must diligently perform the śrāddha for the deceased;
having resolved, 'I shall perform it tomorrow,' one should carry out the act of inviting the brāhmaṇas."
Having bathed and become pure, one should assign the deceased among the Brahmins, saying:
"You have gone to the divine world by the path ordained by Kṛtānta."
"O Brahmin, with my mind transformed into the wind, I shall employ you;
I will honor you with enjoyments. In this manner, one should invite the Brahmin.
When the sun had set, he went to the brahmin’s residence,
offered water for the feet according to the rules, and paid homage to that best of the twice-born.
Having washed the feet of the deceased with oil out of a desire for his welfare,
when the night has turned to dawn and the sun has risen;
Having had the shaving of the beard performed, and after that the clipping of the nails,
one should provide the Brahmin with a bath and anointing according to the prescribed ritual.
One should take a portion of ground and, immediately thereafter, a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
having selected the site for the offering, a large sacrificial mound should be prepared.
One should designate a cremation ground on the bank of a river;
for those who perform the funeral offering without having set aside a portion of the earth, [the merit does not accrue].
O blessed lady, the entire world is dependent on that; it would become defiled by his leavings, and neither the gods nor the ancestors will ever accept offerings from him in this world.
By that leavings, O beautiful one, they fall into a terrible hell;
therefore, having gone to a great river, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
Having meditated upon the sacred fords with his mind, the wise man should sprinkle himself with their waters;
having thus performed purification, he should then quickly summon a Brāhmaṇa.

O Mādhavī, upon seeing a twice-born guest who has arrived, one should perform the rites of welcome; having then offered water for the hands and feet, one should act with a heart pleased by the sight of him.
And one should prepare a seat according to the ritual procedure with the mantra:
"May you rest upon this seat, permitted by the deities."
A Brahmin, having purified his hands with the fire of knowledge, should purify the seat that has been sanctified by household rites;
then, having washed his hands and saluted with his head bowed, he should proceed.
And having rested his knees while reciting the mantra.
Having seated [the recipient] on an auspicious seat, one should provide an umbrella there;
