that umbrella is given to the Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of protection.
Afterwards, one should give two sandals that touch the feet,
for [the traveler must cross] the ground of scorching sand as well as that which is thorned with sword-blades.
By giving a pair of sandals to a brahmin with a self-controlled mind, having performed the offering of sesame seeds, one causes the deceased to cross over difficult passages.
Having uttered the name and clan of the preta immediately thereafter,
one who holds darbha grass in his hand should quickly summon him to the ground upon the earth.
[248] ‘Mantra’: “Having abandoned this world, you have gone to the supreme goal.
Having thus invoked him, one should offer perfumes, flowers, and incense.

The mantra for incense is: "All fragrant scents. The mantra for flowers is: "By the Goddess Śrī. The mantra for incense is: "O Bṛhaspati, [accept] the excellent essences. Then, O Vasundharā, one should provide all garments and ornaments to the Brahmin, and furthermore, one should prepare cooked food.
O fair-faced one, cooking and eating must be performed by the three castes for Śūdras who have entered into service.
When the thirteenth day has arrived, one should feed the twice-born with cooked food;
such is the procedure to be employed for Śūdras, performed without mantras.
And for a Śūdra who lacks a mantra, a Brāhmaṇa is taken as the mantra;
he is entirely the recipient of the portion belonging to the deceased while being enjoyed by the Brāhmaṇa.
Among his kinsmen, friends, relatives, and own people,
a share should be given to each according to the need of each.
Having become pure and having duly performed the rites of propitiatory water,
O Goddess, he bowed his head and arrived at the place of the libations.
And the mantras to be praised are established with equal devotion.
The mantra:
"Homage, homage to you, O Earth, supporter of the world!"
O wide one, great one, bearer of mountains and peaks, O Earth, homage to you!
O Dharaṇī, daughter of Kaśyapa, foundation of the world, O Vasudhā, supporter of beings, daughter of Viṣṇu, homage indeed to you!
Homage be to you, the foundation of all flavors;
homage, homage be to you, O Nivāpa-nāvīti!
One should offer sesame-water while pronouncing the person's name and lineage.
Having massaged his feet and paid homage to that best of the twice-born,
he should take the hand of the twice-born man with his own hand and help him rise while reciting the mantra.
O Goddess, he should likewise give a bed and seat, as well as collyrium and a comb;
having taken the collyrium and the comb, that twice-born man ascends the bed.
Having rested there for a moment, he arrived at a sacred place.
Having lifted up the tail of a cow and placed his hand there, the Brāhmaṇa should pour water mixed with sesame seeds into an udumbara vessel.
The twice-born offer that water, which destroys all sins, with mantras from the Sāmaveda, preceded by the recitation of those mantras.
Taking a vessel made of udumbara wood, a brahmin of restrained mind should sprinkle with water,
while reciting the mantra, everything that remains within his own house.
Having gratified all the gods, whose mouth is Agni, in their respective portions,
one should offer the bali-oblation to the spirits and provide food to the Brahmins.
Having honored the twice-born by giving them the portion intended for the departed spirits,
one should indeed provide for the deceased an inexhaustible [merit] by addressing him by name.
Having caused a Brahmin to pronounce a blessing, one should perform the dismissal of the deceased;
then, one should cause [the Brahmin] to consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) combined with the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
In the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa: "When ten days had passed, having performed purification according to the prescribed rule,
he performed the twelfth-day śrāddha as well as the thirteenth-day śrāddha."
Vehicles, male and female slaves, very large houses,
and the finest ornaments— these were for the funeral rites of that king.
Vasiṣṭha, on the duties of kings [19.29–30]:
"And when the king has died, one should give what is incidental; by this, the conduct toward mother and father is explained."

"Prāsaṅgika" means incidental; "prasaṅga" refers to the enjoyment of objects, and for that purpose, one should provide bedding, seats, and so forth. "Mātāpitṛvṛttiḥ" means that even toward one's mother and father, one should act by giving them incidental gifts such as bedding during the śrāddha ceremony.

Then, upon the cessation of the period of impurity, having bathed well, having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, and having sipped water according to the rules (*svācānta*), he should feed Brāhmaṇas of the same kind as before, facing north, according to his ability, after honoring them with perfumes, garlands, garments, ornaments, and so forth. In the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, he should modify the mantras to the singular. In the vicinity of the food remnants, he should offer a single *piṇḍa* using the deceased’s name and lineage. When the Brāhmaṇas have finished eating and have been honored with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and when the water for imperishability (*akṣayyodaka*) has been offered with the deceased’s name and lineage, he should prepare three trenches—four finger-breadths wide, of the same depth and interval, and one span long. Having established three fires near the three trenches and strewn grass around them, he should offer three oblations into each fire: "Svadhā! Adoration to Soma accompanied by the ancestors (*pitṛmat*); Svadhā! Adoration to Agni, the bearer of the *kavya*; Svadhā! Adoration to Yama, the descendant of Aṅgiras. In the three locations, he should perform the offering of the *piṇḍas* as previously described. Then, having filled the three trenches with rice, curds, honey, clarified butter, and meat, he should mutter: "This is for you. He should perform this every month on the anniversary of the death.
"One should modify the mantras into the singular," means that wherever a word ending in the plural occurs in a mantra, it should be modified into the singular form.
Yājñavalkya and Vṛddha-Śātātapa state:
"On the anniversary of the day of death, the rite should be performed every month for a year."
And every year, on the eleventh day of the month of Māgha.

The phrase "on the eleventh day" is intended to indicate the day immediately following the cessation of impurity, according to the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: "Now, [the rite is performed] upon the removal of impurity."
Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"The *śrāddha* for one who maintains the sacred fires should be performed on the eleventh day after cremation;
however, one should always perform the obligatory (*dhruva*) rites on the anniversary of the day of death."
The monthly rites for twelve months, the first six-month rite,
and the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa— these are the sixteen śrāddhas for the deceased.
If six months should be completed in a single day, or even in three days,
then both the annual and the six-monthly rites should likewise be performed.
"Of one who possesses a sacred fire" refers to the deceased. "Fixed" means the necessary rites to be described hereafter. The construction is: "[rites] for less than a year."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "For men who have abandoned their bodies, the sixteen śrāddhas are always [performed] on the fourth, the fifth, the ninth, and likewise the eleventh [days]."
Then, for twelve months, the faithful should perform the śrāddha rites twelve times; being pure, they should there gratify the brahmins with offerings for them.
This [rite] is distinct from the sixteen śrāddhas beginning with the eleventh day, because there is no śrāddha intervening between the fourth-day śrāddha and the others.

Immediately after the rites of the ten days have been completed, Hārīta says: "On the following day, having offered the *ekānuddiṣṭa* [offering], they perform the duties for the sake of dharma, such as the recitation of auspicious benedictions (*svastyayana*) and so forth."
‘Ekānudiṣṭa’ means performed with reference to a single person. Baijavāpa says:
“Having approached water after the tenth day, one performs the *śrāddha* for him; and its procedure is the same as that of the *gavāśvinājya* and the *aṣṭakā*.”

The *āvṛdaṣṭakā* is that *aṣṭakā* on which the offerings of the omentum (*vapā*) and other rites of the *āvṛt* [sacrifice] take place. Paiṭhīnasi states: "One should perform the *śrāddha* for the deceased month after month; at the end of the year, there is a dismissal (*visarjana*). Some say it lasts for nine months."
Devala says:
One should perform the nourishment of the deceased through the eleventh-day rite and others;
when a full year has properly elapsed, he attains the station of the ancestors.
Hārīta says:
When the father has died, the son should indeed perform the piṇḍa offering at the end of the year;
he should also give food and a water-jar to a brahmin according to the dharma prescribed for the deceased.
Yājñavalkya [1.255]:
For one whose Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite has taken place before the completion of a year,
one should give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man on the anniversary of the death.
Regarding the section on the *preta*, Pāraskara [3.10.54–55] states: "Day by day, one should give food to this Brāhmaṇa and a water-pot; some also offer a funeral ball (*piṇḍa*)."
Now follows the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite.
Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"The Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa should be understood here as occurring at the end of one year;
the rites for the deceased (pretakriyā) are to be known by the wise as ending with the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa."
One should perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha preceded by the rites for the gods;
there, one should feed the ancestors alone, yet designate the deceased (preta) once again.
Having prepared four balls of food, the giver of the pindas, addressing each by name,
should divide the first ball into three parts while reciting the two verses beginning with "ye samānāḥ."
First, the knower of mantras should perform the single rite for the four arghya vessels;
he should then sprinkle the vessels of the ancestors with water from the vessel of the deceased.

The term *pretakriyā* refers to that rite which is performed by mentioning the word *preta*. Consequently, even in the view that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is to be performed earlier [than usual], the mention of the word *preta* should not be made when offering the water-pot (*udakumbha*). "To the ancestors alone" means not to the maternal grandfathers and others. "The noble one" refers to the *preta*-piṇḍa.
The Āśvalāyana-Parīśiṣṭa.

Now follows the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. There are four water-vessels: one for the deceased and three for the others. One should pour the first vessel into the [other] three vessels with the verse, "United indeed be our intention... In this very same manner, one should join the first *piṇḍa* (rice-ball) to the [other] three *piṇḍas* with the two verses beginning, "O honey-sweet ones, come together! Thus, the fourth [deceased] becomes admitted. And at this point, one should not feed the *daiva* (the gods). Having already offered half of the food and drink to the *daiva* portion and having honored the vessel with perfumes and garlands, one should place the remains of the oblation into the hands of the ancestors; and that same [remainder] again.
[254] In the past, the unintelligent ate food given upon the palm of the hand;
by that, the ancestors were satisfied, yet they did not obtain anything at all.
That which is placed in the palm of the hand and that food which has been prepared—these should be eaten as one; no separate portion exists.

‘Anujñapitaḥ’ means dismissed. ‘And not here’ means that one should not cause a confusion of items—such as the offering of seats for the ancestors and so forth—with items belonging to the deities, such as their seats, within the section concerning ritual objects. ‘Hutaśeṣa’ refers to what remains after the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation has been performed in the fire.

At the end of the year, one should feed Brāhmaṇas for the deceased, his father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather. One should perform the *agnaukaraṇa*, the invocation (*āvāhana*), and the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*). One should pour the water from the deceased’s foot-basin into the three basins of the ancestors with the verses “May the earth unite you” and “The same is yours. Near the remains of the food, one should prepare four rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). After the Brāhmaṇas have sipped water and been given sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), one should follow them and bid them farewell. Then, like the water from the *argha* vessels, one should place the rice-ball into the three rice-balls. The same applies when they are near the three pits (*karṣū*). Thus, having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* after performing the monthly *śrāddhas* for twelve days—or on the thirteenth day—one should perform it. For Śūdras, however, it is on the twelfth day, excluding the recitation of mantras. If an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) occurs within the year, one should increase the day by one for the purpose of the monthly rites.

"Even when in proximity to the three furrows (*karṣū*), it is likewise"—thus, one should join even those rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) associated with the *ekoddiṣṭa* for the deceased (the *preta*) to the rice-balls of the ancestors (*pitṛ*). "Like the purpose of the monthly rites": the monthly rites are those performed in each month; their purpose consists of the nourishment of the deceased and so forth, and the *śrāddhas* connected with that are "for the purpose of the monthly rites. Having performed them during the twelve days following the end of the period of impurity (*āśauca*), one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the thirteenth day. And the first *ekoddiṣṭa* is performed at the very end of the period of impurity. The *ūnaṣāṇmāsika*, *ūnābdika*, and so forth should also be performed on the sixth and twelfth days respectively. Thus, according to this view, there are sixteen *śrāddhas*. This should be understood as applying to both those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgni*) and those who do not (*niragni*), provided there is a cause for the postponement, such as a festive occasion (*vṛddhi*). And a festive occasion is a cause for the postponement of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.

It should be understood from the observation of a restatement in the words of Śātātapa: "Those deceased ancestors who have been made *sapiṇḍa*— whether before a year or when the year is complete— at [the time of] prosperity."
Paiṭhīnasi states: "At the end of the year there is the dismissal [of the deceased]; some say it is at the end of nine months.

This rule regarding the nine-month period for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be understood as applicable when an occasion for a *vṛddhi-śrāddha* arises at the beginning of the tenth month or thereafter; the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must not be performed prior to that.

Baijavāpa says: Now follows the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* (the rite of unification with the ancestors). For one year, one does not offer a separate rice-ball (*piṇḍa*). When the year has elapsed, he joins together four water-vessels: one for the deceased and three for the ancestors. He pours that vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the ancestors while reciting the two verses beginning with "Those who are common... (*ye samānāḥ*). In the same manner, he merges the rice-balls as he touches them, saying: "O fathers, this deceased one has followed you; I give him to you."
"May there be auspiciousness for the rest; may they become long-lived."
May your intentions be as one, may your hearts be united;
may your mind be the same, so that you may dwell together in harmony.
"Come together, speak together; may your minds be in harmony, just as the gods of old, being in agreement, partook of their portion.
One should not extend this [rule] to those who have been accused, the outcaste, the killer of an embryo, or an unfaithful woman.
Hārīta says: When the [ancestral rite] is completed, one should duly perform the animal-śrāddha;
one should offer four pindas, and among them, one should first offer [to the ancestors].

Having offered the omentum, the animals, the sacrificial porridge, and whatever portions are to be cut off according to the prescribed ritual procedure, he should place the remaining portions into the funeral cakes.
From that time forward, the deceased indeed attains the commonality of the ancestors;
he finds the world of the ancestors, and from that point the śrāddha ceremony proceeds.
For as many hairs as there are on the animal, for that many thousands of years shall the offering be inexhaustible for the ancestors, provided it is performed according to the prescribed rite.
For that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world;
and the performer of animal sacrifice undoubtedly binds himself with all objects of desire.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Having taken one of the four *argha* vessels with the left hand,
[he should take] the water with sesame seeds with the right hand alone."
Recalling the mantra "May the Earth unite you with those who are equal," one should pour a fourth part of water into the hand of the deceased Brahmin.
Then, one should offer that water to the Grandfather (Brahmā) and the others individually with their respective mantras, using the two verses beginning with "ye samānāḥ."
Having offered the *argha* from the vessel according to that very rite and in accordance with the rules,
and having presented half of it to them, he should afterwards perform the rite himself.
Then, by that same procedure, having offered the water for washing at the root of the *darbha* grass to the father, he should devoutly offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) as before.
Having offered the morsel and meditated upon that [deity] as possessing eight limbs and being brilliantly radiant,
one should then divide that morsel into three parts with vessels of gold, silver, and earth.
Having offered [the portion] to the ancestors beginning with the Grandfather, he should present the deceased [with it], saying:
"May the Earth, Vāyu, Agni, and Prajāpati unite with you."
One should recite this mantra with devotion, as well as "samānīvat";
and with the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," one should worship the deceased among the ancestors.
Then, having formed those three balls into circular shapes, one should worship them with water-offerings (argha),
flowers, incense, garments, garlands, and ointments.
But having made the father the primary [recipient], one should then [offer] to the others in due order;
for when the father has died and the grandfather still exists.
By him, three rice-balls should be offered, beginning with the great-grandfather;
and from those, the rice-ball for the father should be joined as before.
But if the mother has died while the paternal grandmother still lives,
then this same procedure should be performed there as well, preceded by the great-grandmother.
Jābāla says: A son who possesses the *asapiṇḍa* fire should not perform the *pitṛyajña*;
for by not performing it, he becomes a sinner and is born as a slayer of his father.

This is the meaning: immediately after the period of impurity has ended, one should perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite—preceded by the monthly śrāddhas and the Piṇḍapitṛyajña śrāddha which must necessarily be performed on the upcoming new moon day.
Yājñavalkya [1.253–254]:
One should prepare four vessels joined with water scented with perfumes and sesame seeds;
for the purpose of the *argha* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessel of the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
With the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," one should perform the remainder as previously described;
this Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for a woman is also performed as an Ekoddiṣṭa.
The meaning is that for a woman as well, the *ekoddiṣṭa*—namely, the rites from the eleventh day onwards—and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed in exactly this same manner. Vṛddha-Śātātapa states:
"A brother, or a brother’s son, or a *sapiṇḍa*, or even a learned disciple..."
Having performed the sapindikarana rite, one should thereafter perform the rites for prosperity.
[258] Viṣṇu [21, 22]: The sapindikarana rite for women must indeed be performed;
likewise, one should perform the śrāddha every year as long as one lives.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
How should the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a mother be performed by her sons?
It is ordained that her *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed together with her paternal grandmother.
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [Gobhila 2.102] states:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a mother is declared to be performed together with the paternal grandmother at the same time as prescribed,
provided she was an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) and has no son."

The meaning of this is as follows: the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for a mother must be performed by her son together with the paternal grandmother and the other ancestors; [likewise] by the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) together with the maternal grandfather and the others. Baudhāyana and Yajñapārśva state: "In the first rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), the son of an appointed daughter should designate his mother."
In the second [generation] her father, and in the third her grandfather.
Śātātapa and Vṛddha-Śātātapa state in the second [section]:
"In the case of an unmarried daughter, the father shall perform [the rite]; but in the case of one who has been given away in marriage, the husband likewise [shall do so].
When she remains established in her own respective lineage, the offering of water with sesame seeds is performed by each according to their own *gotra*."
As long as the wife remains alive, she belongs to the paternal *gotra* until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite;
thereafter, however, she belongs to the *gotra* of her husband’s father.
Upon the performance of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, she attains a single form with her husband’s ancestors; therefore, she becomes a sharer in their lineage.
Whatever is offered to the ancestors after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, [she partakes in that].
"In all matters of law, it is the settled rule that the mother is the heir to all shares."

"In *saṃsthitāyām*" means when she has died. "*Tilodakam*" (water with sesame seeds) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) in general. The authors of the *Smṛtimañjarī* and others maintain that the rule regarding "partaking in the paternal lineage" (*pitṛgotrabhājana*) applies specifically to women married through censured forms of marriage, such as the *āsura* rite. The reason for the statement "but after [death], [she partakes] in the husband's and father's [lineage]" is given by the words "being of one body" (*ekamūrtitvam*), and so forth. By the phrase "after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*," it is stated that when the substance is being manifested specifically for the sake of the father and others, the mother becomes an "inheritress of a share" (*aṃśaharā*), meaning she is a partaker of satisfaction (*tṛpti*). Bṛhaspati [Śrāddha, 85, 29, 26]:
The mother eats the śrāddha consisting of svadhā together with her own husband;
likewise, the paternal grandmother and the great-grandmother eat with their own respective husbands.
The funeral cakes and water for women should be offered by their sons using the name of the husband’s lineage,
as well as for their paternal grandmother and father, each according to his own prescribed rule.
The mantras recited at the taking of the hand (marriage) cause the removal of the paternal lineage;
thereafter, the offering of rice-balls and water for women should be performed with the husband’s lineage.
By means of the mantra of the fourth oblation, [the soul is joined] with skin, flesh, heart, and sense organs.
The wife is united with her husband; therefore, she belongs to his gotra. Viṣṇu [74, 1–8].

Having performed the *śrāddha* on the *aṣṭakā* days preceded by the gods, with vegetables, meat, and cakes, one should then perform the *anvaṣṭakā* rites. Having offered oblations into the fire as at the *aṣṭakā*, and having likewise fed the Brahmins for the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother as before, one should honor them with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), follow them as they depart, and then dismiss them. Thereafter, one should prepare six furrows. At their base, having established the sacred fires facing east and north and having offered oblations, one should perform the offering of three rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) at the base of each furrow. There are three furrows for the males and three furrows for the females. One should fill the three furrows for the males with water mixed with rice; the three furrows for the females with milk mixed with rice; and each set of three furrows [for the grandmothers] with curds, meat, and milk respectively. Having filled them, one should recite: "May this be inexhaustible for you, sirs, and for you, ladies."

The meaning is that one should fill the three furrows for the women with boiled rice and milk; another [teacher] says that one should fill each of the three furrows with curd, meat, and milk respectively.
Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [Gobhila 2.103]:
"One should not give separately to women, except on the anniversary of their death;
for it is traditionally taught that their satisfaction comes solely from the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) offered to their own husbands."
Likewise:
"If the grandfather passes away after the father,
the grandson must perform the sixteen śrāddhas, beginning with the eleventh-day rite."
This should not be performed by the grandson if the grandfather has sons;
having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his father, he should perform the monthly rites.
The two ancestors who have not yet been consecrated are not to be consecrated by the grandson or great-grandson;
rather, one should perform the consecration there for the father—so said Kātyāyana.
It is the settled rule that one should consecrate one’s father with the funeral rites by means of a pure grandfather— even if that grandfather is most wicked— or even by one who has committed a sin.

If the two ancestors—the grandfather and the great-grandfather—for some reason remain "unconsecrated," meaning their *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has not been performed, then one should "consecrate the father" along with them; that is to say, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for him together with them.
Thus ends the section on Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa in the Śrāddhakāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru composed by the illustrious Lakṣmīdhara.
Now follows the Śrāddha performed after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa.
Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"In whatever case these [offerings] are made after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*,
that *śrāddha* should be known as being like the *pārvaṇa*, except for those performed on auspicious occasions (*abhyudaya*)."
Whether before a year has passed or when the year is complete,
for those deceased who have been made *sapiṇḍa*, there is no longer a separate ritual performance for them.
Therefore, the offering of separate funeral cakes (piṇḍa) is prescribed for all the deceased here who have been summoned by means of mantras.
For those who have performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite have indeed achieved their purpose;
having emerged from the state of being a *preta*, they have reached the company of the ancestors.
He who joins a deceased person for whom the sapindikarana has been performed to a separate funeral cake becomes a destroyer of the ritual ordinance and is born as a slayer of his ancestors.

"In a separate *piṇḍa*": where a *piṇḍa* is offered individually (*pṛthak*), that is, without being accompanied by other *piṇḍas*, in the case of an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite; "one should employ" [the deceased] as the deity—this is the ellipsis. Jābāla says:
"But having performed the *pitṛyajña* and the monthly *śrāddha*..."
And when there is a desire for the śrāddha, it should be performed on the anniversary of the death of one's mother and father.
One should satisfy a deceased person for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has not been performed by means of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite;
after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, it is held that [the deceased] shares the same status as the three [ancestors].
The two sons, the aurasa (legitimate) and the kṣetraja (son of the wife), shall perform the pārvaṇa rite every year according to the prescribed rule;
the other ten types of sons shall perform the ekoddiṣṭa rite.
[262] ‘The sacrifice to the ancestors’ (*pitṛyajña*) here refers to the libation for the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*). Yājñavalkya [1.256] states:
"On the anniversary of death, however, it should be performed every month for a year."
And likewise every year, the first [offering] is performed on the eleventh day.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:

"From that time forward, on the occasion of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), during eclipses and other festival days (*parvan*), one should perform the *tri-piṇḍa* śrāddha; for those who have died, the *ekoddiṣṭa* [is prescribed]."
He who abandons the ekoddiṣṭa rite and performs the pārvaṇa rite instead would always be a slayer of his father, and a destroyer of his mother and brothers.
A man who performs the *pārvaṇa* rite on the anniversary of death goes lower and lower;
when the deceased are thus confounded, there arises a state of agitation among them.
Likewise:
"In whatever case an offering is to be made after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*,
it must always be given by one who maintains the sacred fire according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure."

And here, since an equal option between the *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa* rites would otherwise arise for the anniversary of death each year, the settled rule is as follows: the legitimate son (*aurasa*) and the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), if they maintain the sacred fires, should perform only the *pārvaṇa* rite every year, according to the statement of Jābāla: "The two sons, the legitimate and the son of the wife, [should perform] the *pārvaṇa* rite according to the prescribed rule."
Wherever it is to be offered after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite,
it should always be given by one who maintains the sacred fires according to the Pārvaṇa procedure.

And because of this statement from the *Matsya Purāṇa*, the author of the *Mahārṇavaprakāśa* maintains that while the *aurasa* (legitimate) and *kṣetraja* (son born of the wife) sons are without the sacred fires (*niragnika*), the other sons—whether with or without the sacred fires—should perform only the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite every year on the anniversary of the death.
Now, those entitled to perform the Śrāddha.
In that regard, Marīci says:
"When the father has died, the son must perform the rites according to the prescribed rule.
When there are many sons living together as one with their father," [the eldest alone shall perform them].
Whatever is performed by one eldest brother, having obtained the consent of all,
with property that has not been divided, shall be considered as performed by all.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"If many brothers born of one father have separate fields and separate wealth, they share a single funeral cake (piṇḍa) but have separate periods of ritual impurity; however, the offering of the funeral cake extends through three generations."

"Having separate fields" (*pṛthakkṣetrāḥ*) means those born of mothers of different castes. "Sharing a single funeral cake" (*ekapiṇḍāḥ*) means they should offer only one funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), and not offer separate cakes for each individual. "Having separate purifications" (*pṛthakśaucāḥ*) means they have distinct periods of ritual impurity due to their connection with mothers of different castes. As for the phrase "the funeral cake returns within three," the meaning is that *sapiṇḍatā* (the state of being a sapinda) exists among three generations.
Paiṭhīnasi says: "As long as the lineage is unbroken for three generations, the rice-ball (piṇḍa) is offered;
but upon the extinction of the three generations, the rites of the rice-ball and water-libation are performed separately."

"Uninterrupted" means free from interruption caused by the entry of persons of a different caste, by death, or by [the husband] becoming an outcaste. "Upon the destruction of three generations" refers to the entry of persons of a different caste, such as Kṣatriyas and so forth.

[264] Bṛhaspati [on Śrāddha, verse 150]: For one who has passed away, a funeral cake (piṇḍa) should be diligently offered at the śrāddha by sons, as well as by kinsmen, relatives, friends, disciples, officiating priests, servants, and family chaplains.
In this context, it should be understood that the right of succession belongs to each subsequent person in the absence of each preceding one, beginning with the son.

Gautama (GDhS 15.13–14) states: "In the absence of a son, the *sapiṇḍas*, the *mātṛsapiṇḍas*, and the disciples shall offer; in their absence, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*)."

In the Viṣṇupurāṇa (3.13.31–40): "O King, the son, the grandson, or the great-grandson, or likewise the lineage of a brother, or even the lineage of a *sapiṇḍa*, becomes eligible to perform the rites."
In the absence of all these, the sapinda-lineage of those who share the same water [is entitled to the inheritance],
as is whoever has a connection with the maternal side by means of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) or by water.
O King, when both families have been cut off, the funeral rites for the deceased must be performed by women,
or they may be performed by those who have entered into the religious community (saṅgha).
Or, from the inheritance of one whose lineage has been severed, the lord of the earth should cause the prior rites,
the intermediate rites, and likewise the subsequent rites to be performed.
These ritual acts are indeed of three kinds; hear from me their distinctions according to their forms:
those beginning with the cremation, those involving the touching of water, weapons, and so forth, and finally those which are the concluding rites.
These [rites] performed every month—first, middle, and last—are designated as *ekoddiṣṭa*;
they continue after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* once the deceased has attained the status of an ancestor (*pitṛ*).
[265] Those rites performed for the ancestors are declared, O best of kings, to be *pitrya*;
they are likewise performed by the *sapindas* of one's father and mother, as well as by those who share the same water (*samānasalila*).
The earlier rites must be performed by those included within the family group, or by the king, or by one who takes the wealth; however, the later rites must be performed by the sons and others alone.
Or, O best of men, they may be performed by the daughters' sons or likewise by their sons;
on the anniversary of death, the subsequent rites for women must also be performed.
O King, every year, according to the rules for the Ekoddiṣṭa rite, [one should perform the offering].

"Connection by the *piṇḍa* of the mother's side" means through the *sapiṇḍa* relationship with the mother; "connection by the water of the mother's side" means through the *samānodaka* relationship with the mother. "From the inheritance of one whose kinsmen have perished" refers to the estate of one whose relatives have died out. Regarding "until the cremation, from the touching of the water-vessel, the weapon, and so forth, [the rites] beginning with the last": "last" (*antya*) means death; those [rites] occurring therein, beginning with the cremation and ending with the touching of the water-vessel, the weapon, and so forth, are the "prior" ones—this is the meaning. The phrase "month after month" is an elliptical expression for the prior funeral rites, such as those on the eleventh day up to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. In this context, the *sapiṇḍas* of the father and mother and others shall perform only the prior rites, not the subsequent ones. However, regarding the intermediate rites, there is no fixed rule for them. For the subsequent rites, however, the sons and others down to the future progeny, the daughter's sons (*dauhitrāḥ*), and their sons are the fixed performers. The terms "by daughter's sons" and "by their sons" refer specifically to the case of a son born of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*).
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "The Śrāddha should never be performed by those outside one's lineage for one who belongs to the same lineage;
it must also be performed by a religious student (*brahmacārin*), even if he has not yet completed his vows."
He does not perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and so forth for his parents;
rather, while constantly residing in the teacher's house, he performs them for his teacher and his fellow students.
[266] But when a sapinda who has no offspring has died, one who is moved by compassion,
having first completed the period of impurity for that death, should perform the funeral rites for him as if for his own father.
One should perform the rites of cremation and so forth for those in the three [lower] stages of life;
however, nothing at all should be done for an ascetic, nor does he perform such rites for others.
The preceptor always performs the offering of funeral cakes for his disciples,
having first performed the ancestral purification and whatever rites are prescribed for his own caste.
If his wife is not present, the brother himself performed [the rite] for his brother;
for him who has no uterine brother, the son of that brother performed it.
On the fourth day, those who are well-composed should perform the rite for those maidens— whether they have been given away or not— who have been betrothed by their fathers.
The daughters' sons perform [the rites] for their maternal grandfathers on that same day,
while others always perform them for them on the second day.
The father-in-law honored his son-in-law, and those [sons-in-law] were likewise self-restrained;
so too did the teacher honor his friends and their sons who were learned in the Vedas.
And on the following day, having first bathed and performed the water-rites, he should perform the *śrāddha* for all his sister's sons.
When the king has died, if he is a *sapiṇḍa* but leaves no offspring,
the domestic priest or the minister shall first observe that period of impurity and afterwards perform [the funeral rites].
A Brāhmaṇa, however, never performs [such rites] for those of other castes, whether out of desire, greed, or even fear; by doing so, he would descend to the status of that same caste.
Sons born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes perform [funeral rites] for a Brāhmaṇa;
he, however, never performs them for such sons.
Their own mother performs [services] for them, and they also perform [services] for her.

"One who has his own lineage" (*svagotra*) means one who possesses a living member of the same lineage. When the Śrāddha is to be performed for someone, if a member of that person's own lineage is available, the Śrāddha must not be performed by another lineage member, whether he belongs to a religious community (*saṅgha*) or is a king. Regarding the phrase "even for one whose vows are incomplete": "that like a father"—just as a father performs such and such rites for his son, so too should a non-*sapiṇḍa* relative perform them with compassion. The statement "nothing at all should be done for an ascetic (*yati*)" refers specifically to the funeral rites beginning with cremation and ending with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
And so it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"Vidura must never be burned, he must never be burned;
for one whose body has been consumed by knowledge, there is no further burning."
"And that which is prescribed by one's own caste," such as touching water, weapons, and so forth at the end of the period of impurity (āśauca).
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"In the absence of everyone else, women should perform [the rites] for their mothers without mantras."
But in the absence of such persons, the king should cause it to be performed as if for his own family.
"All the rites, such as cremation and the rest, should be properly performed by men of the same caste;
in the absence of all [male kin], women should perform them for their husbands without mantras"—this refers to women other than the wife, such as concubines (*avaruddhā*) and so forth, as it says:
"If the brother's wife is not present, the brother himself performed [the rites] for his brother."
Thus, because the qualification for the wife is seen only with respect to those who are still alive;
and likewise: "In the same way, this Ekoddiṣṭa rite is declared to be for women as well."
The sapindikarana rite for them is not performed in the absence of a son.
Every year, men should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for a woman on her anniversary of death,
according to the rule that has been declared here for men.

"‘The same applies to women as well’ means that by whatever relationship—such as being a paternal uncle or the like—the eleventh-day rite and so forth are performed for men, by that very same relationship they must also be performed for women."
Now follows the rite for prosperity.
In that regard, the Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.13.5–6] states:
"At the weddings of daughters and sons, upon entering a new house,
at the naming ceremony of infants, and likewise at the tonsure ceremony and others."
At the parting of the hair ceremony and upon seeing the face of a son or other offspring,
the self-restrained householder should worship the Nāndīmukha class of ancestors.
Likewise, O lord of men, one should feed an even number of Brahmins facing the east;
[as stated] in the Matsya Purāṇa.
During festivals, the continuity of joy, sacrifices, marriages, and other auspicious occasions,
the Mothers are to be worshipped first, and the Fathers immediately thereafter.
Then likewise the maternal grandfathers and the Viśvedevas; as stated in the Brahmapurāṇa:
"The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather."
For these three ancestors are proclaimed as the "Tear-faced" (aśrumukha) Pitṛs.
Those who are even earlier than them, who possess offspring and have thrived in happiness, are called Nāndīmukhas; "nāndī" is said to mean prosperity.
Likewise: "In rites for prosperity, in auspicious and beautiful ceremonies, such as a birth, an initiation, a marriage, or [the naming] of a son."
One should satisfy the ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas according to the prescribed ritual;
one should recite the Śakuni-sūkta as well as the auspicious Svasti-sūkta.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, one should invoke the Nāndīmukha ancestors with devotion.
Likewise:
"Reciting the purifying mantra, 'O Viśvedevas,
you have come,' he should spread out auspicious darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward."
One should offer great medicinal herbs into the fire as sacrificial fuel for the purpose of destroying demons;
likewise, one should scatter there highly praised sesame seeds and barley grains.
One should not perform any rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya);
one should offer food with the Daiva tīrtha while reciting the *svadhā* mantra.
"Is this well-prepared for me?"—thus he should ask them, gladdening them;
and they should say to him, "It is well-prepared," and then he should cast [the oblation] for the attainment of all success.
He should mutter, "May this be inexhaustible for the Nāndīmukhas," and then he should offer darbha grass and water for rinsing the feet with milk to those facing the east.
Having given [these] to the Nāndīmukha ancestors, he proceeds gradually toward the eastern direction,
offering rice cooked with śāli grains, mixed with curd and honey, as well as jujube fruits and barley.
Having mixed these four together into balls resembling *bilva* fruits,
one should offer them according to the prescribed ritual to the ancestors known as the *nāndīmukha*s.
One should offer water for honor (argha), flowers, incense, excellent unguents,
and a pair of unwashed garments that are new, equal, and flawless.
One should then offer grapes, emblic myrobalan roots, and barley;
likewise, one should always give these to the Brahmins as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, having offered milk and barley water in place of the water for inexhaustibility,
[he offers it] to those known as the great-grandfathers and to the mothers who have the "Joyous Face" (nāndīmukhī).
Indeed, [offerings are made] to the maternal grandmother, the paternal grandmother, and the great-grandmother;
and likewise to the maternal grandfather and those who are the *nāndīmukha* ancestors.
"Let 'svadhā' be uttered by you for those known as the great-grandfathers.
"Let there be svadhā," they replied to him with joyful laughter.
"May the Viśvedevas be pleased," the giver says to them;
"May they be pleased with you," they reply to him in sweet syllables.
Reciting "tam ū ṣu vājinam," he should dismiss them;
then follows the excellent Śrāddha for the Nāndīmukhī Mothers.
By this procedure, the rites such as the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) and others should be performed.

"Equal" (*samaṃ*) means common or one and the same; the meaning is that it is not distinct for each individual lump (*piṇḍa*). "Root" (*mūla*) refers to ginger and the like. "Laughter" (*prahasa*) means excessive laughter. And here, because of the observation of the statement by Kātyāyana—"The Nāndīmukha ancestors, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers"—the deities are indeed the father and the others, characterized by the epithet "Nāndīmukha. As for the fact that the *Brahmapurāṇa* describes the triad beginning with the father as having "tearful faces" (*aśrumukha*) and then designates those beyond them as Nāndīmukhas to be the deities of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, that is for the purpose of establishing that one whose own father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are living is not eligible to have them as deities in the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. Consequently, this [Nāndīmukha rite] must certainly be performed even by such a person. However, he should not perform the *pārvaṇa* and other types of *śrāddha*, because of the prohibition in the *Viṣṇusmṛti*: "One should not perform [the śrāddha] at all while the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are living."
Kātyāyana says:

In rites for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), the ritual procedure is performed clockwise. In the forenoon, one performs the recitation of mantras, excluding those dedicated to the ancestors (*pitrya*). The *darbha* grass blades are straight. Barley (*yava*) serves the purpose of sesame seeds (*tila*). The question regarding satiety is "Is it well-prepared? [The others should reply, "It is very well-prepared"]. The funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) are mixed with curd, jujube fruits (*badara*), and unbroken grains (*akṣata*). He asks, "Shall I invoke the Nāndīmukha ancestors? Being permitted with the words "Invoke them," he says, "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased. In place of the word "imperishable" (*akṣaya*), he asks, "Shall I cause the Nāndīmukha ancestors to be addressed? Being permitted with the words "Let it be addressed," he says, "May the Nāndīmukha fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers—and the maternal grandfather, his father, and his father—be pleased. He should not employ the word *svadhā*. At this point, he should feed an even number of guests.
Yājñavalkya [1.250]: Having thus circumambulated [the fire] clockwise for the sake of prosperity, one should worship the Nāndīmukha ancestors with offerings;
the ritual acts are performed with barley and rice-balls mixed with curd and jujube fruits.
Śātātapa says: A wise person seeking prosperity should perform rites for the gods and the śrāddha ceremony in the forenoon,
using the sacred thread over the left shoulder (savya) and straight blades of darbha grass.
If one should offer the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* out of sequence by keeping it to the left (*apasavya*),
neither the gods nor the ancestors will be satisfied with him according to the prescribed rule.
Assuming the form of the ancestors, he partakes of the food of the deities;
therefore, in rites for prosperity (*vṛddhi-śrāddha*), the offering should always be given with the left hand.
On the occasion of a prosperity rite (vṛddhi), one who is self-restrained and pure should feed an even number of Brāhmaṇas;
he should cause them to recite: "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be satisfied."
The Śrāddha for the mother should come first, followed immediately by that for the paternal ancestors;
thereafter, for the maternal grandfathers—thus, at a Vṛddhi ceremony, three Śrāddhas are prescribed.
In all three of these [rites], one who is pure should feed an even number of Brāhmaṇas;
he should offer them from left to right, beginning with those representing the gods.
The Vasus are to be known as the fathers, the Rudras as the grandfathers, and the Ādityas as the great-grandfathers; such is the Vedic revelation.
One should not perform the *apasavya* rite, nor should one act counter-clockwise;
just as one should worship the gods, so too should one honor the ancestors during the *vṛddhi* rites.
With the sacred grass in hand, having sipped water, seated and composed,
facing the east and remaining silent, he should offer the rice-balls with his left hand during a rite for prosperity.
[272] One should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward during rites for prosperity (*vṛddhi*);
likewise, in the *pārvaṇa* rite and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, they should be placed upon grass with its tips pointing southward.
One should not perform a rite for the gods without first having offered a śrāddha to the ancestors;
even before them, the Mothers must be worshipped with diligent effort.
If one serves food at a śrāddha ceremony without having performed the Mātṛ-yāga,
the Mothers, possessed by wrath, seek to inflict harm upon him.

"Daivika" here refers to the *abhyudayika* (rite for prosperity), because the Nāndīmukha ancestors are treated like gods. "He should cause [the priest] to recite 'May they be satisfied'"—the words "in place of the *akṣayya* offering" are to be supplied. "Mātṛyāga" is the worship of the mothers.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, in the section concerning prosperity (*ābhyudayika*):
"Some men, however, desire [to perform it] even when the *vaiśvadeva* is omitted.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [1.13–19]:
In all rites, beginning with those for karma, the Mothers together with their lords of the hosts must be worshipped with diligence; when they are worshipped, they in turn worship [the worshipper].
And upon pure images, those painted on cloth and other media,
as well as upon heaps of unbroken grains, with various kinds of food offerings.
One should cause a stream of clarified butter to flow against the wall— either seven streams or five streams— neither too low nor too high.
Having recited there with a concentrated mind those mantras that bestow long life for the sake of pacification,
he should then proceed to the offering of the *śrāddha* for the six ancestors.
The entire procedure taught by Vasiṣṭha should be understood here as being free from worldly motives;
beyond this, I shall explain whatever specific distinction there may be in this case.
Having seated the invited Brahmins—both groups being even in number—one should indeed give them straight *kuśa* blades with one's own hand.

The term "longevity-rites" (*āyuṣyāṇi*) refers to the hymns that cause the increase of life. "To six" means to the three ancestors beginning with the father, and to the three beginning with the maternal grandfather. Furthermore, the mention of "six" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother as well. By the statement "invited in the morning," the optional invitation in the evening is also excluded. "Both sides" refers to the side of the ancestors (*pitṛpakṣa*) and the side of the Viśvedevas (*vaiśvadevapakṣa*).
Likewise, Gobhila [1.24–27] states:
"There is never any bending of the left knee;
one should always serve the ancestors here with devotion, just as one would the gods."

Having seated them upon kusha grass after they have been offered [the invitation] with the words "To the ancestors," one should cause the ancestors to be addressed by their lineage names and lineages and cause the arghya water to be offered.
In this rite, the practice of using the left hand (apasavya) is not required, nor is the ancestral (pitrya) part of the hand prescribed;
for the filling of the vessels and other such acts should indeed be performed with the right hand (daiva).

Having placed the hands in pairs with the right hand uppermost and the tips of the fingers joined by the pavitra grass, the arghya should be offered; here, it is not given to each individual separately.

"Jyeṣṭhottarakarān" means such that the hand is placed over the hand of the eldest, who was seated first. "Karāgrāgrapavitrān" refers to those whose tips of the *pavitra* grass are positioned at the tips of their hands.
Likewise, Gobhila [states in 1.39–55]:
"The triple recitation of 'madhu, madhu' intended for those desiring to eat,
which follows the Gāyatrī, is here devoid of the Madhu-mantras."
And one should never recite the *pitṛsaṃhitā* while they are eating;
instead, another auspicious recitation, such as the *soma-sāman* and so forth, should be performed.
Whatever portion of food there is there, like sesame or barley,
which remains in proximity to the leavings— that is what is reversed here when [the guests] are satisfied.
"Is it well-prepared?"—with this question, they are made to express their satisfaction;
when "It is very well-prepared" has been said, one should offer the remaining food.
And upon the darbha grass with tips pointing eastward, having addressed the first ancestor as before,
one should pour water without sesame seeds at the base of the grass, saying, "Ava-nenikṣva" (be cleansed).
The second and third [seats] are for the central region and the foremost region;
however, the maternal grandfather and the others are placed to their left.
Having set aside a portion of all the food, having sprinkled it with condiments, and having mixed it with unbroken grains,
jujubes, and curd, he should then face the east.
Having formed the rice balls (piṇḍas) according to the rite of washing, each the size of a bilva fruit,
one should then wash them once more with the water used for rinsing that vessel.
Even when giving alms-foods one after another,
each subsequent one should be placed below the preceding ones during acts of faith.
Therefore, at all śrāddha ceremonies—
whether those performed on auspicious occasions or others— one should offer oblations that are slightly attached at the base, middle, and top portions [of the sacrificial grass].
One should silently place the fragrant substances and so forth, and then invite the twice-born.
This same procedure, excluding the barley and other grains, should apply elsewhere as well;
[it is performed] in a place sloping toward the south for one facing the south.
On darbha grass with the tips pointing south—this is remembered as the rule for other occasions.
Then one should sprinkle the ground with water, saying, "May it be well-sprinkled," and likewise, "May the waters be auspicious," while offering water to an even number of persons.
After this, one should offer flowers with the thought, "May there be joy," and one should present unbroken grains (akṣata) with the thought, "May there be well-being and freedom from misfortune."
The offering of inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka) is prescribed in the same manner as the offering of the guest-water (argha);
one should always perform it with the dative case-ending alone, and never with the dative-instrumental (caturthī).
When all the requests have been answered by the best of the twice-born,
one who has placed the vessels face-upward should sprinkle water over the rice-balls (piṇḍas) covered by the sacred grass (pavitra).
Having had an even number of Brahmins recite auspicious blessings, and having grasped the thumb of the leading Brahmin, he should then bow and follow after him.

"‘Just as with sesame, so with barley’: that variety of food which is prepared elsewhere mixed with sesame should be prepared here in such a way that it is mixed with barley. ‘In reverse order’ means by a mode of giving such as using the *devatīrtha* [finger-tip] and so forth. ‘The first’ refers to the person.
‘Slightly stuck’ means slightly adhered.
Likewise, [Gobhila 1.68–69]:”
Those rites which are performed by ritual officiants more than once need not be repeated at every performance; this applies to the *mātṛkā-śrāddha* as well.
At the establishment of the sacred fires, at the two daily oblations, and likewise at the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice;
at the offering of bali, at the new moon, and likewise at the full moon.
Regarding both the *navayajña* and the ordinary sacrifice, the wise declare this:
there should be only one *śrāddha* for these, not separate ones for each.

A śrāddha is not to be performed on the Aṣṭakā days, nor is a śrāddha prescribed during another śrāddha; nor is it to be performed during the rites for a woman about to give birth, the birth-rite, or the rites for one returning from a journey.
Regarding the group of rites beginning with marriage that was mentioned, and the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) which we have heard is at the end—
here, one should perform only one [of these] at the beginning of the marriage and so forth.
The śrāddha should not be performed at the beginning of every ritual action.
There should be one *śrāddha* at dusk for both the departure and the re-entry of the cows;
however, it is not appropriate to perform a *śrāddha* during the first rite for prosperity (*puṣṭikarman*).
One should perform the six [rites] beginning with *halādi* and *yogādi* separately for each;
for others, one should perform them all together at the beginning of each individual rite.
For those who serve food for the sake of the welfare of large cattle and small animals,
there is no Śrāddha rite for the two [deities] whose functions are those of the Sun and the Moon.

The *Daśagranthika* alone is not sufficient for the treatment of a wound inflicted by a venomous creature; it is likewise not found to be effective in treating a wound by a worm, nor in other such cases.
When the rites for the Mothers are being performed collectively, the worship of the Mothers should always take place only once;
the Śrāddha should likewise be performed only at the beginning, not separately for each individual rite.

Wherever there may be a *śrāddha*, there the Mothers [are to be worshipped]. By the passage beginning with "At the *ādhāna* and the two *homas*" and so forth, he states a specific restriction regarding the scope of the rule "The rites which have been performed repeatedly. Consequently, in the case of the *Soma* sacrifice and similar rituals, the *śrāddha* must be repeated for each performance. "New sacrifice" (*navayajña*) refers to the *Āgrayaṇa*. "Rites for one who has returned from travel" (*proṣitāgatakarmasu*) refers to what is prescribed such as "Having returned from abroad, he approaches his home; having seen his son, he mutters [the prayer]," and so on. "Collection of rites" (*karmagaṇaḥ*) refers to the *Gṛhapraveśa-caturthī-karma* and others. "Mothers" (*mātaraḥ*) means those related by birth; this is the understood sense.

Likewise: "In the rites of consecrating his sons, a father should offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) to his own ancestors until their marriage; but in his absence, [the son] should do so according to that same order."
"Until the wedding" means up to the point of marriage.
Yama says: "Even for the ancestors, guests are deities on the occasions of *śrāddha* ceremonies."
And the ancestors are always the guests of the deities.

Thus ends the section on the *Ābhyudayika* (rites for prosperity) in the *Śrāddhakāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Akṣamādhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsandhivigrahika*).
Now follows the procedure for the *jīvacchrāddha* (the funeral rite for one still living).
In that regard, the *Brahma Purāṇa* states: "When life— which arises from place, time, wealth, faith, and exertion— still exists, a man himself should offer the *śrāddha* for the sake of the living."
Having observed a fast and bathed well on the thirteenth day, being composed in mind,
one should worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, as both the performer of the rite and the enjoyer of its fruits.

He is omnipresent in water, on land, in the sky, in form, in the water-pot, in the lotus, and in the sun; he dwells in the moon, fire, the preceptor, the cow, the Brahmin, and in one’s mother and father.
With a concentrated mind, he should present three water-cows (jaladhenu) accompanied by sesame seeds and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) before the ancestors.
Recalling, "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, svadhā! Homage! and recalling, "To Agni Kavyavāhana, svadhā! Homage!"
And on the right, he should place the third [offering] accompanied by a sacrificial fee, while recollecting: "To Yama or to Aṅgiras, Svadhā! Obeisance!"
Having placed the Brahmins between those two, one should seat five of them;
and having first worshipped the Viśvedevas with the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites.
"O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Vasus; I feed you for the sake of the Rudras;
I feed you for the sake of the Sūryas, O Brahmin"—thus he should say to them.
One should perform the remaining rites, such as the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, according to the ritual for one's own ancestors;
then, one should give a gentle cow to a brahmin dedicated to Indra.
Then, one should offer a vessel of sesame seeds to all the gods;
having given the water for well-being (*svasti*) and the inexhaustible water (*akṣayya-jala*) to those twice-born ones.
One should dismiss [the deity] while recollecting the all-pervading Lord Viṣṇu through the eight-syllable mantra;
thereafter, at night, one should recollect Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the family of Kāma.
Then, on the fourteenth day, one should go to the excellent river as it may be reached:
by the east for a Brahmin, by the north for a Kṣatriya, and by the west for a Vaiśya.
Likewise, the Śūdra should scatter barley grains on the path to the south,
while recollecting the mantra "jīvanta" (living ones), and [scatter] garments and pieces of iron.
Facing south, he himself should kindle the fire there;
having fashioned an image of Brahmā out of fifty blades of kuśa grass, he should burn it.
Having performed the cremation-ground fire-offering (śmaśānika-homa) up to the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
one who is without a sacred fire (niragni) should then meditate upon the Earth, Yama, and Rudra.
Having offered [the oblation] in the place of the primary deity, one should subsequently have her cremated;
then, one should cook a sacrificial porridge mixed with mung beans in another fire.
And one should fill a second *karṣū* with honey, milk, ghee, and water, mixed with sesame seeds and rice, along with a *pavitra*.
Then, near that [vessel], one should fill three bowls with mung beans;
and one should offer another with the mantra: "Oṃ, salutation to you, O Earth."
"Oṃ, salutation to Yama"—this is the second [mantra] immediately following that;
then "Oṃ, salutation to Rudra, the Lord of the Cremation Ground."
Then, remembering "Oṃ, obeisance to the earth scorched by fire, the consumer of raw flesh," he [should offer] onto the ground a blazing, well-kindled fire that naturally burns.
To pacify that [evil], one should scatter a water-pot smeared with milk;
then, having entered the water up to the navel, one should face the direction of Yama (the south).
One should offer seven handfuls of water to the seven known as Yama:
to Yama, to Dharmarāja, to Mṛtyu, and to Antaka.
To Vaivasvata Kāla, the snatcher of all life-breaths,
[one should offer oblations] seven times, together with the utterances of *svadhā*, *namas*, and the *praṇava*.
[279] Oṃ! Remembering Śiva, Rudra, and the Lord of the Cremation Ground, one should scatter upon the ground a jar filled with parched grain and water.
One should offer the water for washing (avanejana) upon the darbha grass blades directed toward the south,
uttering "Svadhā" joined with the name of the deceased and recollecting "Obeisance to Rudra."
"O you of such-and-such a lineage, may this water with sesame seeds be for you.
He should then offer ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas) accompanied by water-offerings (argha) and flowers.
"May incense, lamps, offerings, and perfumes be inexhaustible for all.
Then, having offered ten rice-balls (piṇḍas), one should meditate upon the gentle face of Viṣṇu."
And having entered that water, which is devoid of heat, up to the navel,
one should pour it separately into the midst of the water with a full jar.
One should then offer fifty-five jars or handfuls of water;
at the threshold of the door or within the house, one should pour out milk and water.
"O living one, bathe here and drink this milk while recollecting [the deceased].
Then, he should sleep facing north upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing toward the south.
Thereafter, on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), he should perform the *jīva-śrāddha*.
One should fill three karṣukas with ghee, rice, meat, and curd.
And one should perform the monthly *māsika* rites every month, as well as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*,
at the end of the period of impurity (*āśauca*), whether for oneself or for another.
One should act with a sense of instability, knowing that power, health, wealth, and lifespan are all transient.

"To the south" means in the southern direction, not far away. "To Vāsava" means for the Brāhmaṇa who has been seated for the Vasus. The same applies to "to Raudra. "In the place of Pradhāna" means at the location of the principal oblation (*pradhāna-homa*).
Thus ends the Śrāddhakāṇḍa (the Section on Ancestral Rites) in the Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and the great minister for peace and war.
May there be auspiciousness.
